stories.Headline: Northwestern researchers develop AI algorithms to help pathologists analyze digitized tissue samples
stories.Summary:
Lee Cooper, director of computational pathology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, said digital imaging methods are becoming more popular in pathology, as Medill Reports described on November 13, 2026. After a blood or tissue sample is placed on a glass slide, the slide goes into a scanner that produces a digital image that can be shared electronically. Cooper runs a lab where researchers develop artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms that review digitized samples. He said the algorithms will help pathologists make more accurate and detailed diagnoses and help researchers interpret how diseases progressed in past patients. The article said glass slides are often still carried between offices so multiple pathologists can look at them.

Cooper said a computer can analyze a sample in much greater detail than a human can, because each image could contain a million cells or more. Researcher Fattaneh Pourakpour, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, uses digitized tissue data from Northwestern’s Mesulam Institute for Cognitive Neurology and Alzheimer’s Disease brain bank, which accepts brain donations upon death from people who had dementia. Her tissue segmentation algorithms distinguish brain regions such as gray matter and white matter, and her cell classifier algorithms identify and categorize cell types within gray matter. Researcher Ramin Nateghi, a post-doctoral researcher with a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Shiraz University of Technology in Shiraz, Iran, applies machine learning to prostate cancer detection. Nateghi said biopsies taken over time might show few differences over 25 years, so detecting subtle changes in slides can help doctors make better decisions.

Cooper said digital pathology tools are meant to augment pathologists, not replace them, because the models he works with operate on the basis of correlation and have no causal understanding inside them. He said an algorithm is less helpful on a rare case it has never seen, and that he does not think the models should be trusted implicitly. Researcher Lawrence Chillrud, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, said the United States has a huge shortage of pathologists but heaps of patient biopsy data that needs to be inspected, analyzed and reviewed. Chillrud develops tools that conduct a preliminary screen of pathology data, sort out the most obvious cases and flag others for fast-tracked, specialized review. His models might also count items such as a certain kind of cell, direct a pathologist’s attention to important areas or review a pathologist’s report for potential errors.

Chillrud is also developing uncertainty tools that quantify the likely accuracy of a model’s prediction, because many models are overconfident and give a false picture of how well their predictions can be trusted. He said models inherit the biases of the data sets they are trained on, giving the example of training on mostly white, affluent patients living in a certain part of a city. Artificial intelligence pathology tools can also help address shortages of specialized pathologists, since a general pathologist might not have the training for a detailed read of a prostate cancer biopsy. Specialists are harder to find in smaller, more rural areas, while large, city-based medical systems might have them on staff. According to Cooper, the Northwestern Medicine health care system generates about 2 million glass slides per year.

Cooper is not sure how quickly digital pathology will become commonplace, because the tools must undergo FDA clearance and be validated on very high-quality data that can be hard to access. Not all medical systems have adopted the digitizing tools and technology Northwestern has access to. In the Cooper Lab, glass slides are digitized using the Aperio slide scanner, manufactured by Leica, which takes about 90 seconds per slide and can hold up to 450 glass slides at a time. Cooper said each image typically has several billion pixels, and pathology at Northwestern generates about 3 petabytes, or 3 million gigabytes, per year. Cooper said he is optimistic about adoption after seeing researchers use the tools to measure patterns in tissue and relate them to metrics such as treatment success.

Cooper said the tools are useful and easy to use, and that it is not just tool developers but scientists using them. The article said pathology data is by far the biggest source of data in the medical field. Whether models possess deep understandings of the subjects they are trained in, or only superficial ones, is an unanswered question, though Cooper said he thinks they can deliver accurate and efficient predictions regardless. Cooper said computers can consider many more properties of the samples than a doctor could, which can help generate a fuller prediction of that patient’s future. The article did not say when the algorithms might receive FDA clearance or reach routine clinical use.

stories.Headline: Colette Kress becomes interim Nvidia CEO to manage legal crises and aggressive AI investments
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia during a dizzying week in November 2026 after thirty three years of leadership. He left the company following an alleged spy scandal and reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs with various women. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has now stepped in as the interim chief executive to lead the company through this crisis. This abrupt departure leaves many questions about the future of an artificial intelligence industry that relied on the company's financial backing. The transition occurs just weeks after Huang delivered a keynote at the GTC event in Berlin on October 21, 2026.

Kress must now manage a situation where Huang committed 120 billion dollars in equity investments and sought 250 billion in guarantees for OpenAI. She previously renegotiated the Ohio data center project to cut that financial commitment in half and checked Vice President Nico Caprez. The company planned to acquire Hugging Face for 12.9 billion dollars in September and invest 10 billion dollars into the firm Anthropic. Kress also faces potential federal and congressional investigations into the dealings of Nvidia involving China and the actions of Alice Huang. These changes may shift the company away from circular financing used by firms like CoreWeave, OpenAI, and also the company Anthropic.

Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus stated that Nvidia acted like a bank by backstopping the industry through a process of circular financing. He described Jensen Huang as a swashbuckler who made bets of arbitrary size while many AI businesses struggle to turn profits. Marcus noted that Kress must clean up the legal mess and answer why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not intervene earlier. He believes lawmakers need to know exactly what information Huang shared with Alice Huang during their relationship and the suspected spy scandal. Kress is expected to focus on managing risk and stability rather than opening new lines of business for the company.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue expressed his dismay on X, calling the current situation deeply regrettable and a truly sad day. Many AI companies are affected because they relied on the aggressive financial backing and the large bets made by Huang. Some Nvidia engineers are unhappy, with over 1,600 comments on an internal post urging the board to bring Huang back. Analysts suggest that a CFO is the best choice for interim leader to send a message of confidence to markets. The board aims to secure steady leadership while the company deals with extreme instability and the fallout from the scandal.

The company previously operated under an arrangement where Huang made business decisions quickly and intuitively while taking reports directly from executives. This aggressive spending strategy allowed Nvidia to bankroll the AI boom but created risks of overextension that Kress internally opposed. The board chair position has remained vacant since the company was founded, which allowed Huang to operate with very little oversight. Kress has spent thirteen years at Nvidia and is known for avoiding the public spotlight and choosing her words very carefully. This background in finance contrasts with the engineering background of Huang, who led the company for over three decades.

Harvey Jones, a mentor to Huang for twenty five years, has been appointed as the new chairman of the Nvidia board. The board will now supervise and check the strategy of the CEO to reduce the financial risk of the company. It remains open whether the long careers of Jones and Kress will prevent them from fully breaking with the past. The planned acquisitions of Hugging Face and the investment in Anthropic may now be subject to revision or total cancellation. It is not yet clear if the board will eventually heed the employee sentiment and find a way to return Huang.

stories.Headline: 42Gears earns ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for its AI management system
stories.Summary:
42Gears announced on Nov. 13, 2026, that it had achieved certification to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the international standard for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems. The announcement was made from Bengaluru, Karnataka, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated Nov. 13, 2026. The certification followed a rigorous independent audit conducted by the British Standards Institution, known as BSI. 42Gears is described in the articles as a global leader in Unified Endpoint Management, or UEM. The certification recognizes 42Gears for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving structured governance across its AI-enabled enterprise capabilities.

The certification covers 42Gears' role as a producer, provider, and user of AI systems integrated within its flagship SureMDM platform. It includes the use of third-party large language models, or LLMs, to deliver AI-powered unified endpoint management services across key global sectors. Those sectors are Banking & Financial Services, Healthcare & Life Sciences, Industrial & Supply Chain Operations, and Consumer & Commercial Services. The certification demonstrates that 42Gears embeds accountability, transparency, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle. It also shows governance frameworks for the responsible development, deployment, and use of AI technologies, including the adoption and use of LLMs.

Onkar Singh, Co-founder and CEO of 42Gears, said enterprise IT teams want the efficiency and intelligence of AI but not at the expense of security, transparency, or regulatory compliance. He said achieving ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification validates the company's commitment to responsible AI innovation. He said customers in banking, healthcare, and mission-critical operations can deploy SureMDM's AI capabilities knowing they are backed by internationally audited governance and strict human oversight. The articles state that 42Gears is responsible for the AI management system covered by the certification. The audit that validated the system was conducted independently by BSI.

The articles list key benefits for 42Gears customers and partners, starting with independently audited AI governance that gives verified assurance that SureMDM's AI management framework meets rigorous international compliance benchmarks. They describe an end-to-end risk and impact assessment that establishes a structured methodology for identifying, evaluating, and mitigating AI-related risks across the entire deployment lifecycle. They describe transparency and human oversight that enforces clear accountability mechanisms and human oversight controls over AI-assisted decision-making and workflows. They describe governed third-party LLM integration that ensures strict security, privacy, and vendor oversight protocols when leveraging external large language models. The articles say the certification complements 42Gears' existing enterprise security and privacy portfolio, including ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, and HIPAA compliance programs, offering heightened confidence for organizations in heavily regulated industries.

The articles state that 42Gears is a trusted authority in Unified Endpoint Management and Security, delivering one strategy to manage, secure, and empower diverse, complex technology environments. They say 42Gears goes beyond traditional MDM and RMM, enabling IT teams and MSPs to start where they are and grow without switching. They say this helps scale from endpoint management and Zero Trust security to identity and access management, automation, and self-healing technology. They say 42Gears products are available in cloud and on-premises deployments across all major mobile, desktop, and specialized operating systems. They say 42Gears products are used by 23,000+ customers across 170+ countries and are available through 1,000+ global partners.

The articles give no further steps beyond the announcement and the listed benefits of the certification. They leave open the date the BSI audit was conducted and the date the certification was issued. They leave open the cost of the audit and certification and the number of AI systems or LLMs covered within SureMDM. They leave open which specific third-party LLMs are used and how the human oversight controls operate in practice. They leave open whether the certification has a defined validity period or a scheduled recertification date, and they give no information on how customers can obtain the audit results.

stories.Headline: Ninepoint files prospectus for Anthropic HighShares ETF with covered call strategy
stories.Summary:
Ninepoint Partners LP filed and obtained a receipt for a final prospectus qualifying units of the Ninepoint Anthropic HighShares ETF, the company announced on November 13, 2026. The ETF is expected to begin trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the ticker ANHI, subject to satisfying the TSX's original listing requirements. Trading is expected to start the business day following the completion of an initial public offering by Anthropic, PBC, currently anticipated on or about November 19, 2026. The ETF combines leveraged exposure to Anthropic, the company behind Claude, with a professionally managed covered call strategy designed to generate income. Ninepoint is based in Toronto and oversees approximately $8 billion in assets under management and institutional contracts.

ANHI will offer a management fee of 0.29% and intends to pay twice-monthly cash distributions, like other ETFs in the Ninepoint HighShares suite. The ETF seeks long-term capital appreciation through purchasing and holding, on a levered basis, Class A common stock of Anthropic, and regular cash distributions. ANHI will hold up to 100% of its total assets, including assets acquired with borrowings, in Anthropic Class A common stock and write covered call options on up to 50% of those holdings. The covered call strategy will be reviewed monthly for cash flow sustainability, and the risk rating is High. The ETF is considered an alternative mutual fund under applicable securities legislation, permitting strategies generally prohibited for conventional mutual funds, such as investing up to 20% of net asset value in a single issuer, borrowing cash, short selling beyond conventional limits and employing leverage.

Karl Cheong, CFA, Executive Vice President and Head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners, said Anthropic's upcoming public listing is an opportunity to invest directly in the company, and he anticipates strong interest from Canadians seeking TSX-listed exposure. Cheong said Ninepoint designed ANHI to provide Canadian investors a way to participate in Anthropic's growth potential while seeking regular income through a covered call strategy. Ninepoint is the investment manager of the ETF. The ETF does not have a fixed distribution amount, and the amount of ordinary cash distributions may fluctuate, based on the Manager's assessment of prevailing market conditions. The amount and date of any cash distributions will be announced in advance by press release.

The ETF intends to pay cash distributions based on its ability to generate monthly cash flows from writing covered call options and any dividends received on portfolio securities, as applicable. The Manager will review the level of distributions quarterly to consider sustainability, and may change the frequency of distributions at its complete discretion, with any change announced by press release. The ETF is generally exposed to risks including absence of an active market for ETF Units risk, ADR risk, artificial intelligence industry and regulatory risk, borrowing risk, collateral risk, concentration risk, covered call strategy risk, currency risk, cybersecurity risk, derivatives risk, equity investment risk, exchange risk, foreign investment risk, foreign withholding tax risk, halted trading of ETF Units risk, inflation risk, interest rate risk, large capitalization issuer risk, leverage risk, market risk, no ownership risk, options availability and liquidity risk, Passive Launch Public Issuer Investment Risk, performance risk, regulatory risk, risk associated with an investment in the Launch Public Issuer, specific issuer risk, tax risk and trading price of ETF Units risk. Commissions, trailing commissions, management fees, performance fees if any, and other expenses may all be associated with investing in the ETF. The ETF is not guaranteed, its values change frequently and past performance may not be repeated.

The forward-looking statements in the release are not historical facts but reflect Ninepoint's current expectations regarding future results or events, and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Neither the ETF nor Ninepoint undertakes any obligation to update publicly or otherwise revise any forward-looking statement, except as required by law. The information does not constitute an offer or solicitation by anyone in the United States or in any other jurisdiction in which such an offer or solicitation is not authorized. Prospective investors who are not resident in Canada should contact their financial advisor to determine whether securities of the ETF may be lawfully sold in their jurisdiction. For inquiries regarding the offering, Ninepoint can be contacted at (416) 943-6707 or (866) 299-9906.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kovind urges lawyers to verify AI-generated citations as AI reshapes legal work
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved into courtrooms, law offices and legal research departments across the country, according to TechSpective on November 14, 2026. The article says the technology is no longer confined to science fiction or Silicon Valley boardrooms. It describes the rise of AI as both an opportunity and a genuine shift in how legal work gets done. It says attorneys, paralegals and clients alike face this change. It adds that understanding these changes is essential for anyone navigating today’s legal landscape.

AI-driven platforms scan thousands of case files, statutes and legal precedents in minutes, work that once took junior associates hours or full days. The tools retrieve information and also analyze patterns and surface insights a human researcher might overlook under time pressure. AI tools help lawyers identify problematic clauses, inconsistencies and missing provisions faster than manual review, and can be trained to flag language deviating from standard agreements or posing legal risks. Predictive analytics tools evaluate how courts have ruled on similar cases, and AI-driven e-discovery platforms streamline document review during discovery. A probate litigation attorney in California may use AI-assisted research and case analysis in complex matters like estate disputes involving contested wills or trust administration.

Former President Ram Nath Kovind said human judgment and oversight must remain indispensable to protect the credibility of courts and the rights of litigants, the Deccan Chronicle reported on November 14, 2026. Speaking at the Justice K. Ramaswamy Endowment Lecture at Dr B.R. Ambedkar College of Law, Andhra University, in Visakhapatnam on Saturday, he cautioned young advocates against blindly relying on AI-generated case laws and judicial precedents. He said, in the article’s words, that professional credibility cannot be transferred to a software provider. He urged advocates to personally verify legal assertions from authentic sources, including original judgments, rather than rely on software to validate its own output. He said technology should democratise access to justice instead of widening the gap between metropolitan law firms and lawyers practising in district courts.

Kovind cited the US case of Mata vs Avianca Inc., in which lawyers were penalised for submitting fictitious case citations generated by AI. He also referred to the Supreme Court case of Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd., where orders based on fabricated citations were set aside. He noted that more than 83,000 Supreme Court judgments were available in 18 Indian languages and said AI could accelerate translations while human supervision preserved the nuances and precision of legal terminology.

He urged law schools to adapt teaching methods to the digital era by emphasising critical thinking, legal research and oral advocacy, and to train future lawyers to examine electronic evidence and identify deepfakes. He said the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and the Bharatiya Nararik Suraksha Sanhita showed India’s legal framework had recognised the growing importance of electronic records and digital proceedings. TechSpective says questions around data privacy, attorney-client privilege and the accuracy of AI-generated outputs are at the forefront of ongoing legal and ethical debates. It says bar associations and regulatory bodies are actively working to establish guidelines keeping AI use within appropriate ethical boundaries.

It warns that over-reliance on automated tools could lead to critical errors if attorneys accept AI outputs without proper scrutiny, and that the most effective approach treats AI as a powerful assistant rather than a substitute for genuine professional legal judgment. It says legal fees may decrease as efficiency improves and turnaround times on documents and case updates can be significantly faster, while AI-powered client portals and chatbots make basic legal information easier to access and let people communicate with legal teams outside traditional office hours. It says the overall client experience is becoming more transparent, more responsive and far more service-oriented. Kovind paid tribute to Justice K. Ramaswamy, recalling his contribution to the landmark S.R. Bommai judgment and the constitutional principle of secularism.

He concluded by urging young lawyers to combine technological skills with constitutional values and a commitment to justice, saying technology provides powerful tools but will never possess a conscience. TechSpective says the human element of law, including empathy, ethical reasoning and nuanced judgment, remains irreplaceable, and that attorneys who thrive will embrace AI as a tool while prioritising the personal and professional skills that define excellent legal practice. It says the future of law is both human and machine working together toward better outcomes. The articles leave open which guidelines bar associations and regulatory bodies will adopt and when.

stories.Headline: Adobe and Google integrate AI models into creative and productivity tools
stories.Summary:
Adobe and Google expanded their strategic AI partnership on November 14, 2026, to integrate advanced models into creative tools. This collaboration brings Google AI models into Adobe software and extends Adobe tools across the Google productivity ecosystem. Adobe also unveiled new AI agents and features at the Adobe MAX 2026 conference in Miami. This annual creative event opened on October 10 and showcased the evolution of the Firefly generative app. The updates aim to turn Firefly into a comprehensive AI creative studio for all digital creators.

Google Gemini models will power Acrobat, allowing users to edit PDFs via conversational prompts through Google Workspace, Drive, and Gmail. Adobe Firefly, Photoshop, Premiere, and Express will integrate Google image and video models, including Gemini Omni, Veo, and Nano Banana. Firefly now supports 36 models, including ByteDance's Dreamina and Seedance 2.5, Runway's Gen-4.5, Kuaishou's Kling 4.0, and OpenAI's GPT. Adobe also partnered with Disney for custom Firefly Foundry models and Microsoft for Arm-based Windows PCs and Microsoft Photos. New tools include Firefly Design in beta, Firefly Builder in private beta, and the CX Enterprise Coworker in GenStudio.

Forrest Key, vice president for Firefly and agentic AI, stated the company wants to help everyone create digital content. He described Firefly as the best platform for both new creators and professionals to build their digital work. Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud, said updates provide professionals with precision, control, and flexibility. She noted that these new tools allow professionals to focus on the decisions that shape their own creative work. The companies are also exploring custom Google image models for Photoshop to enable near-real-time editing through text prompts.

Users of Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, and Lightroom are affected by these updates, including new lighting and color tools. Premiere mobile users gain natural-language editing and licensed music from UMG and WMG for personal, non-commercial video projects. Designers can use Firefly Design to combine illustration, animation, and 3D tools on a single canvas for efficiency. Marketing teams can now use the Ideation Space in Workfront to build campaign strategies and briefs using AI. Business users can coordinate agents and workflows across planning and activation using the new CX Enterprise Coworker interface.

Adobe's multi-model strategy allows users to work with different AI models alongside professional editing tools in the Creative Cloud. Firefly was developed as a generative AI app offering image and video generation, editing, and now agent-based workflow tools. The company introduced a plan mode for reviewing agent plans and a model picker for selecting specific AI models. Always-on agents are being previewed to handle repetitive background tasks like organizing assets and checking content quality. Adobe also developed Firefly Graph in beta for users who want to build repeatable and efficient creative workflows.

Next, Adobe will expand integrations with Gemini and Gemini Enterprise to bring Acrobat and creative tools into those platforms. The company is rolling out beta features like Generative Remove in Premiere and real-time co-editing in InDesign. Local MCP integrations are being previewed to allow third-party agents to edit native project files while keeping layers editable. Adobe continues to test Firefly Builder for turning spoken descriptions into prototypes for websites and mobile apps without coding. The articles leave open how the custom Google models for Photoshop will perform in real-time text-to-image editing.

stories.Headline: Former culture vice minister Yong Ho-seong releases AI-assisted Shakespeare sonnet album
stories.Summary:
Yong Ho-seong, former vice minister of culture, sports and tourism, released his debut full-length album “Fragile Beauty” on Nov. 10 under the stage name Dr. Dragon. The album sets 15 of William Shakespeare’s sonnets to AI-assisted music and vocals. It is the first installment of “DiVerse,” a project to set all 154 of Shakespeare’s sonnets to modern music. Yong gave an interview to The Korea Times at a cafe in Seoul on Thursday, published Nov. 13, 2026. The idea was sparked by a hardcover edition of Shakespeare’s complete sonnets that a British friend gifted him while he was director of the Korean Cultural Centre UK.

The album leans into late-1960s avant-garde folk and chamber folk, using nylon-string guitars, upright contrabass, cellos, violas, flutes, harmoniums and bass clarinets. It features the contralto tones of his AI vocal persona NikkiD. Yong adapted the sonnets’ themes for modern listeners, recasting a verse about passing down family lineage as a message about artists sharing their talents with the world. He said the name DiVerse reflects Shakespeare’s original verse, the newly written lyrics and the diverse genres used to reimagine the classics. In July, Yong won the AI.LOVE.JAZZ.

composition competition in Montreux, Switzerland, with “Frozen Edge,” a vocal jazz piece inspired by Sonnet 97. Yong said he uses AI as a creative assistant rather than a replacement for human artistry. He writes detailed prompts spanning a full page to specify rhythm, instrumentation and musical references, and sometimes regenerates a track 30 or 40 times before editing individual tracks himself. He compared AI to the introduction of digital sampling in popular music in the 1980s, saying it broadens the pool of people who can create music. He said students could turn personal stories and daily emotions into original songs, calling music a powerful tool for self-expression.

He said happiness is not about the high intensity of achievements but the frequency of joyful moments. Yong plans to issue a new sonnet-inspired album every month, spanning jazz, blues, hip-hop, rap-metal and K-pop. He has reached out to Shakespeare-related societies, associations and academic institutions around the world to explore educational and cultural collaborations. He is developing progressive rock operas based on Shakespeare’s tragedies “Hamlet” and “Macbeth,” and a project reinterpreting the poetry of Joseon Dynasty poet Yi Mae-chang (1573-1610).

Before retiring last year, he studied classical music and jazz, collected more than 10,000 records, debuted as a music critic in 1993 and played drums in jazz and rock bands. He composes up to six hours a day and practices drums for two hours, and he recently earned his first musician revenue by composing a theme song for T&C Foundation. In fall 2026, Concord Academy presented Shakespeare’s “Macbeth” in the Hammett Ory Theater, directed by Shelley Bolman P’27. The production used AI-inspired staging to explore the tension between power and technology, with intricate dance and fight choreography.

Bolman said greed for power and artificial intelligence both resonate strongly with the current time. William Jiang-Fogel ’27 played Macbeth, who is consumed by prophecies of his ascent and murders the king to seize the throne. The production retained Shakespeare’s original language and immersed audiences in a world where technology and human behavior are intertwined. Audiences sat on either side of a spare central stage, where a staircase and gate with camouflage paint were entwined with wires and cable extending across archways and pillars.

Live feeds displayed the opposite side of the audience, while screens featured “Heck 8.0,” an AI system that generated prophetic outputs. The production opened in darkness with a flash of lightning illuminating an ensemble in Guy Fawkes masks, and the Weird Sisters were reimagined as analogues for predictive AI. Lady Macbeth, played by Aslan Liu ’27, and Fleance, played by Ren Lipman ’29, were depicted as frequently attached to their phones. Bolman said the play offered an excellent opportunity to bring an over 400-year-old text from the classroom to the stage.

stories.Headline: Character.ai files for bankruptcy as Ollie and Sora shut down
stories.Summary:
Character.ai filed for bankruptcy in October 2026, while the privacy assistant Ollie ceased operations a few weeks before that date. Many other projects failed, including the video platform Sora, which shut down in March 2026 due to high costs. The workflow tool Relay closed in August 2026, and Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22. Humane closed its AI Pin business in February 2025, and the browser ChatGPT Atlas ended on August 9.

The Character.ai sale to Disney involves a bid of 20 million dollars for certain intellectual property rights. Apple paid a 250 million dollar settlement after delaying the Siri AI upgrade, which finally appeared in iOS 27. Humane raised 230 million dollars before HP acquired most of its assets for 116 million dollars in February 2025. Character.ai previously raised 150 million dollars in 2023 and received 2.7 billion dollars from Google for technology licensing. The Rabbit R1 device debuted at CES in January 2024 and reportedly sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

S&P Global Market Intelligence reports that 42 percent of AI projects fail because of funding or weak user demand. CEO Bill Lennon stated that Ollie would shut down on November 6 due to slow growth and funding issues. OpenAI rolled back a July 9 redesign of ChatGPT after users called the new interface confusing and cluttered. Microsoft delayed its Recall feature for nearly a year to reassess security safeguards after receiving strong privacy backlash. Apple cited engineering issues and bugs as the reasons for the repeated delays of its upgraded Siri AI.

Users of ChatGPT criticized the super app redesign, and families sued Character.ai over teen suicides and self-harm. Disney issued cease and desist letters to Character.ai, and customers were warned that Humane charging cases might catch fire. Cybersecurity researchers affected Microsoft by creating a tool that could extract sensitive data captured by the Recall photographic memory. Notion Mail users were already using standalone AI agents, which made the dedicated email product unnecessary for the market. Rabbit R1 users found the device to be unfinished and unstable according to early reviews of the hardware.

S&P Global notes that technical challenges, intense competition, and scaling difficulties contribute to the growing cemetery of failed AI projects. Character.ai was founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas to create customizable bots. Ollie launched in June 2026 as a family assistant and was among the first mainstream apps with SOC 2. Relay operated for five years as a Zapier alternative before major platforms integrated similar automation features into their tools. Microsoft introduced Recall at the 2024 Build developer conference to allow users to search their digital history via screenshots.

The Character.ai transaction with Disney is expected to be completed by late November or early December of the year 2026. Siri AI is currently being rolled out to English users, with support for additional languages expected to follow soon. CFT regulations may influence the future viability of AI projects, though the articles do not specify the exact rules. The articles leave open whether Microsoft has truly fixed the underlying security issues regarding the controversial Recall memory feature. It remains unclear if the Rabbit R1 will be updated to fix the unstable performance noted by early reviewers.

stories.Headline: Hackers steal Uber driver data through Fireworks AI breach
stories.Summary:
Hackers stole the personal information of thousands of Uber drivers by breaking into an AI startup used by the ride-hailing company. Uber filed security breach notices with several state attorneys general this month to detail the specific incident. A third-party service provider notified Uber on October 9 that hackers had stolen internal credentials to access the account. Uber determined on October 13 that the hackers had accessed its data, including personal information belonging to drivers. The breach also affected the productivity app Notion, which confirmed that some of its customers' data was exposed.

The stolen data included driver's license information, and Uber requires drivers to upload licenses, insurance, residency, bank statements, and payment information. In California, a notice dated November 10 stated that approximately 1,873 Rhode Island residents were affected by the breach. South Carolina's Department of Consumer Affairs listed 3,430 affected residents, while 2,567 people in Massachusetts also had their information stolen. The compromised provider was Fireworks AI, a startup that helps developers access and use various open AI models. Notion reported that fewer than 1% of its workspaces were affected, with hackers obtaining anonymized AI chat transcripts.

Fireworks AI said hackers accessed customer account and billing information, datasets, and incomplete AI models belonging to a limited number of accounts. The company stated that hackers gained access to development machines through a separate security incident involving one of its cloud providers. Fireworks notified law enforcement and worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 to conduct a forensic analysis of the event. The company said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group involved in a practice known as LLMJacking. This involves stealing credentials to gain unauthorized access to AI models to use them or sell them to others.

Uber has not disclosed the total number of drivers affected nationwide, but it has alerted almost 8,000 accounts across three states. The company currently operates a fleet of more than 10 million drivers and couriers according to various third-party estimates. Uber stated in its California notification letter that it has not identified any misuse of the stolen information so far. The company is recommending that affected drivers regularly review their account statements and monitor their credit reports for suspicious activity. Uber is offering affected drivers free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through a service called Cyberscout.

Uber previously dealt with a security incident in August when a hacking group claimed to have stolen nearly 1 million files. This earlier attack targeted Uber Freight, which is the logistics subsidiary of the company, though Uber did not verify the claims. In June, Uber announced expanded policies for reviewing and banning drivers based on public records and additional background checks. The company also recently launched a new service that lets drivers reserve parking spots for their vehicles. These events highlight a series of security challenges and policy changes the company has faced throughout the year.

Affected drivers have 90 days from the date of their notification letter to sign up for the free monitoring services. Uber immediately cut off its data connections with Fireworks AI after learning about the breach to prevent further data loss. The articles leave open the total number of drivers impacted across all states beyond the three specifically mentioned notices. It remains unclear if the hackers have sold the stolen LLM tokens or used them to create enormous bills. The company has not confirmed if the August attack on Uber Freight resulted in the loss of any files.

stories.Headline: Pentagon renames its AI office the Super Intelligence Office under Cameron Stanley
stories.Summary:
The Defense Department announced that its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, known as the CDAO, has been redesignated as the Super Intelligence Office, or SIO. The change was reported on November 13, 2026, by Breaking Defense. The department said the new name does not alter the office's mission. It said the change instead lines the office up with a broader push across the federal government to replace references to artificial intelligence with the term "super intelligence."

The department said the transition will roll out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters over the coming weeks. Existing operational programs, industry solicitations and defense partnerships will continue without interruption under the new name. The department has also launched SI.mil, which will serve as the renamed office's main digital domain. The office's portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central data hub formerly known as Advana.

Cameron Stanley, the department's top AI official who also leads the office, said in a statement that the rebrand reflects the Pentagon's priorities going forward. He said the department has moved beyond experimental prototypes. Stanley said the office's mission is to harness the full power of sovereign super intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain. The redesignation follows an announcement by President Donald Trump in September that federal agencies should replace AI references with the term super intelligence, which he argued made the technology sound fake.

The article notes that the terminology has drawn questions in the tech community, where superintelligence has traditionally described a hypothetical form of general artificial intelligence that exceeds overall human intelligence. The Pentagon has been among the federal government's most aggressive adopters of AI, with the CDAO leading efforts to expand its use across military operations. Those efforts include making generative AI tools more widely available to personnel through GenAI.mil, an enterprise platform providing access to commercial generative AI models. The article does not say what the rebrand will cost or whether it will affect the office's budget.

stories.Headline: FAA chief Duffy says aging switches and routers overloaded with data caused the nationwide ground stop
stories.Summary:
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and it said technicians were investigating the preliminary information. Microsoft recorded the start of its Microsoft 365 incident, MO1550821, at November 12, 18:26 UTC, which was 1:26 p.m. EST. The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific, and more than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time. Medevac, critical cargo and law enforcement flights were allowed to continue during the ground stop. It was the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

AP reported that European departures for the United States were suspended at the FAA’s request from November 13, 22:00 UTC, which was 5:00 p.m. EST, until November 14, 05:00 UTC, which was midnight EST. Alaska Airlines’ advisory described the affected U.S. departures as excluding Alaska and Hawaii and offered a flexible change-or-cancel policy. A November 13, 22:46 UTC FAA advisory, which was 5:46 p.m. EST, said the ground stop remained in effect and allowed coordinated departures as facilities recovered, and it expected another update at 04:00 UTC on November 14, which was 11:00 p.m. EST on November 13. The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. Duffy said flights would resume slowly depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the evening news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself and said there was no connection between it and Microsoft. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights. Asked whether a cyberattack or rogue AI could be ruled out, Mullin said there was nothing completely certain right now, that it appeared mechanically driven, and that officials were still looking. Asked whether officials had seen any evidence of a cyberattack, Mullin said they had seen zero evidence. Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific.

Duffy said aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network got overloaded with data and began producing inconsistent information, and that the FAA still relies on 1980s little copper lines. Duffy said the newer equipment held up and that the new IP switches did not go down, while the old hardware did. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, Duffy said. Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing, and that patches, new equipment and new technology were overwhelming the older system. Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

Microsoft attributed the disruption to an earlier network upgrade and a subsequent network change, and on November 13 it said the issue was technical and not related to cyber or AI or agents. Microsoft also told AP it had no indication that the FAA ground stop was related to its disruption, and a company spokesperson confirmed that statement. Anthropic said the Microsoft 365 incident caused failures for Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector and Claude for Outlook, and its retrospective identified the main impact window as November 12 at 16:03 UTC, which was 11:03 a.m. EST, through November 13 at 16:40 UTC, which was 11:40 a.m. EST. Anthropic later marked the incident resolved while warning that occasional errors or delays could continue as Microsoft recovered. OpenAI reported problems with new Microsoft 365 connector connections and connector tools, moved that incident to monitoring at November 13, 16:20 UTC, which was 11:20 a.m. EST, and recorded resolution at 00:18 UTC on November 14, which was 7:18 p.m. EST on November 13.

The FAA unveiled SMART on September 21 and announced expansion on November 10 to the airspace of all 22 centers, and the FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers. The FAA describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes, and FAA specialists review its recommendations while local facilities decide whether to act on them. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, and the FAA awarded Air Space Intelligence a contract for the related Flow Management Data and Services, with SMART described as an enhancement. Air Space Intelligence denied any connection in a post on X, saying the current ground stop was not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or its integration with FAA and ATC. On October 13, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Democrats asked the Government Accountability Office to review SMART and FMDS, requesting scrutiny of safety work, testing, performance measures, training and deployment.

stories.Headline: Stanford review finds most AI education tools do not improve student learning
stories.Summary:
The AI Hub for Education, part of Stanford University’s SCALE Initiative, released a review of 52 studies on artificial intelligence in educational settings on Tuesday, November 13, 2026, Chalkbeat reported. The review found that most AI tools do not help students learn and that education-specific AI tools are not necessarily better than general purpose chatbots. It also found that even tools that help teachers save time can have unintended consequences for students. The report’s authors said they are not throwing in the towel on AI in education. The review is the AI Hub’s second AI research review and incorporates 32 new studies.

The included studies were selected from hundreds in the field and are either randomized controlled trials or have a quasi-experimental design providing strong causal evidence. The goal is eventually to have a robust research repository that teachers and districts can use to inform decisions about whether and how to use AI. The review is a synthesis of findings from high-quality studies, not a meta-analysis. AI in education is not just one thing, with too many different tools used in too many different ways to pile studies together and reach strong conclusions. Many of the studies come from other countries or involve college students, and there is still very little research on AI in K-12 settings in the United States.

Susanna Loeb, faculty director at the SCALE Initiative and an author of the report, said AI tools can be quite powerful to differentiate lessons for students at different levels or support students learning a new language. She said you just have to use them thoughtfully and track how they are doing and whether they are really benefiting students. Loeb said that if a district does not want to think about it and does not want to design its classwork, homework and school day to leverage these tools well, she would not use them. She said that on their own without thought, the tools have some negative effects on learning. She said teachers and district leaders need to proceed thoughtfully and that if they do not have the capacity to do so, it is better not to use AI at all.

Collectively, the studies suggest students do not learn much when they use AI to produce essays or solve problems, and when those students later do work without AI, they do worse than other students. AI shows more promise when students use it to explain concepts and help them practice, but even then the results are mixed or do not show much benefit over traditional study methods. AI tools that provide interactive formats and adaptive practice questions may improve student learning more than static digital textbooks, and students sometimes experience AI-generated feedback as clearer and more motivating than feedback from teachers, but even where students reported positive experiences the evidence of learning gains was mixed. Teachers who used an AI tool to do the first pass on grading assignments provided more and more detailed feedback in one study, and teachers who used AI progress-tracking tools saw students complete more assignments, though students’ grades on those assignments were not necessarily better.

Studies found teachers could save time using AI to generate lesson plans without reducing the quality of those lessons, but students who believed a lesson was AI-generated reported being less motivated, and in one study from Turkey students did worse when teachers who already were lower-performing used AI to generate lesson plans. The review comes as school districts are navigating competing pressures to adopt AI rapidly and to limit technology in the classroom. Google caused an uproar this month when it said that school districts that ban AI will not be able to use Google Search. The American Federation of Teachers has embraced training teachers to use AI while pressing major tech companies to agree to guardrails.

A forensic audit found serious flaws in a number of previous meta-analyses that found positive outcomes for AI in education, such as hallucinated references and statistics that did not make sense, according to The Hechinger Report. Another challenge with studying AI in education, particularly with younger students, is that they often do not want to use the tools. The report’s authors said the technology has potential to provide personalized assistance for students and remove some of the tedium from teachers’ jobs, and Loeb said that potential is worth developing. The articles do not say what specific steps districts or the AI Hub will take next.

The articles do not say how the 52 studies break down by country or age group. The articles do not name the other authors of the report. The articles do not say when the AI Hub’s research repository will be complete. The articles do not say how Google’s statement will affect districts that ban AI.

stories.Headline: Can Artificial Intelligence help with mental health issues?
stories.Summary:
People who struggle to find a therapist or need help faster than a counselling appointment can be set up are turning to general chatbots such as Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT, which seem like understanding listeners, according to an article published by The Star on Sunday, 15 Nov 2026. The article says many of us, especially the young, are using these chatbots as conversation partners for advice and to discuss problems, and it asks why not mental health conditions too. It adds that this comes with limitations and risks, and that psychologists it checked with were clear that AI is no substitute for psychological help from a person. In Germany, anyone looking for a place on a therapy programme has to wait an average of 20 weeks, says Christiane Eichenberg, head of the Institute for Psychosomatics at Sigmund Freud Private University in Vienna.

Eichenberg, a psychologist and author of a book about Artificial Intelligence and Psychotherapy, says the gap in care is by no means the sole reason for the popularity of chatbots, which are available round the clock and are non-judgemental. She says we can communicate with them without having to fear judgement or stigma, and that talking to a computer or phone makes it easier for many people to open up. She says you feel less pressure to put on a brave face and can express feelings such as sadness more intensely. The article says some people turn to general chatbots to discuss their everyday stress, feelings or anxieties, while other AI-based chatbots and applications have been developed specifically with a focus on mental health and are designed to help users reflect on their emotions, overcome fears or manage stress.

Eichenberg says some AI-based mental health programmes have been scientifically evaluated and operate based on a clinically validated treatment protocol, and that the effects are comparable to those of psychotherapy when the systems have been used for four to eight weeks according to the research available so far. However, the article says it remains unclear how stable and long-lasting these effects are. Kevin Hilbert, Professor of Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy at the Health and Medical University of Erfurt, says an attentive, caring and always-available listener is appealing at first for most of us. The article says initial studies suggest that the use of artificial intelligence for mild psychological distress may be more effective than doing nothing at all, and that the systems may help in such cases by empowering users, helping them organise their thoughts and supporting them in their self-reflection.

Hilbert says initial studies have also shown quite good results when it comes to anxiety, high stress or early symptoms of depression, but the article says there is overall not yet enough research to draw definitive conclusions. Eichenberg says specialist therapeutic chatbots may be particularly useful for bridging waiting times or to complement traditional therapy, and that they can support self-management, serve as a training ground for role-play for example, or provide valuable real-time support in acute stressful situations. She underlines that the bots are no substitute for psychotherapy.

stories.Headline: Netflix builds knowledge graph for AI-driven observability
stories.Summary:
Netflix is developing an ontology-driven knowledge graph to accelerate production investigations and give AI agents a shared understanding of its operational environment, TechGig reported on November 13, 2026. The platform connects information about applications, incidents, deployments, alerts, and infrastructure dependencies across Netflix's systems. Engineers investigating a typical application regression can spend around four hours piecing together scattered information. Much of that time goes to reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing data. Netflix's solution makes these relationships explicit through an operational ontology and knowledge graph.

The Observability Ontology defines operational entities, their properties, and their relationships, using standards including RDF, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL. The knowledge graph is stored in QuipuDB, Netflix's distributed RDF database built on Rust's redb storage engine. A pipeline of components called enrichers populates the graph by consuming information from operational systems and transforming it into subject-predicate-object triples. Some enrichment is deterministic, while other stages use LLMs and probabilistic techniques to interpret less structured information. Netflix constrains these outputs through strict validation rules, including consistent entity types, URI naming conventions, and checks against its software catalogue.

Netflix identified a missing capability: a consistent way to describe how components relate to one another, and its Observability Ontology provides that common model. The company also captures information from incident discussions, including hypotheses, rejected explanations, and mitigation decisions, so human reasoning becomes part of the operational knowledge base. Its correlation engine examines 13 types of signals, including log errors, metric anomalies, traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, configuration changes, experiments, and code changes. The engine searches for potential causal relationships and evaluates evidence like temporal proximity and severity, producing ranked hypotheses. The knowledge graph underpins AutoRCA, Netflix's internal agentic AI system for root-cause analysis.

Agents analysing traces, logs, or deployments use the ontology as a common interface, contributing information about operational entities without understanding each other's internal implementations. Netflix already collects metrics, events, logs, and traces across its applications and infrastructure, but these signals are spread across alerting, incident management, deployment tooling, and engineering communication platforms. An application regression might originate from a client release, an experiment, infrastructure load shedding, or a downstream service, and engineers often connect this evidence manually. Netflix intends to use this foundation to produce ranked, evidence-backed explanations for incidents. The system aims to reduce the four-hour investigation times for application regressions and support automated root-cause analysis and self-healing infrastructure.

QCon AI New York 2026 has published its full schedule for December 15, 16, where engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, and other organizations will examine production AI systems. Fan Yang, Staff Software Engineer building Netflix's AI serving platform, and Rajat Shah, who leads technical architecture for ML model serving, explain how Netflix serves ML and GenAI from one platform. That platform handles about 1 million inference requests per second across 300+ models, after five years of consolidation. Ronak Nathani, Principal Staff Software Engineer in Compute Infrastructure at LinkedIn, presents LinkedIn's Kubernetes ops agent, which works across 500,000+ nodes and 5M+ pods. Its guardrails sit on the server, including rate limits, delete protection, and peer approval for production changes.

Pratik Agarwal, Distributed Systems Engineer on Figma's sandbox and caching platforms, explains how Figma provisions and secures production agents, with warm pools cutting provisioning latency by 90% and availability rising from 99% to 99.95%. Fabio Flores, Software Engineer at DoorDash who leads foundation development for its agentic ordering system, explains the eval loop behind it, where every change is checked before launch by an LLM judge calibrated against human reviewers. Min Chen, Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, presents LinkedIn's AI code review system, which reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across about 10,000 repositories, with more than 60% of sampled suggestions accepted. Liz Fong-Jones, Technical Fellow at Honeycomb, and Rebecca Murphey, Principal for AI Ops at Honeycomb, reflect on Honeycomb's 2x initiative, where peak weekday PR merges to its main monorepo rose from about 30 to about 74 between early 2025 and April 2026. Group registration for teams of three or more closes on November 27, 2026, with savings of $50 to $125 per ticket, and individual tickets are $1,790 until December 8.

stories.Headline: Meta expands AI age estimation on Instagram to apply teen safety settings globally
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms said in a Nov. 9 statement that it is expanding age estimation technology powered by artificial intelligence on Instagram. The system identifies users suspected of being teenagers even if they registered with an adult birth date. It automatically applies stricter safety settings to those accounts. The announcement places Meta's age-assurance system at the center of a widening debate over how platforms determine who is a minor online. The company said the system is designed to catch users who misrepresent their age at sign-up.

ConnectSafely CEO Larry Magid expounded on the technology in a Nov. 6 post on Meta's website. He denied that the technology is facial recognition, saying it looks for general visual characteristics that suggest someone underage. Magid wrote that the visual analysis is not intended to identify the person. Meta deactivates suspected under-13 accounts and requires proof of age to prevent deletion, he added. The feature is being applied on Instagram, Meta is continuing to roll it out on Facebook, and later this year it will reach Threads.

Meta said it has started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia as an additional method to help determine users' ages. When a parent sets up a smartphone for a teen, the app store can confirm the age of the person using the device and assign an age range, the company said. The expansion is global in scope, with the company describing the change as applying its age-estimation technology worldwide. The new technology follows a billion-dollar settlement between Meta and multiple U.S. jurisdictions in August over allegations that the company endangered children. Reporting on the settlement described a court-supervised identity system for Facebook and Instagram users under the teen safety provisions.

A separate analysis noted that the agreement included a provision in which states agreed not to sue Meta under existing child safety laws over its retention and use of children's data, for the limited purpose of training and testing Meta's age-assurance model. The Epoch Times reported that Meta recently filed a lawsuit seeking to block California from enforcing Assembly Bill 1709. The proposal bans online platforms from offering underage children features deemed psychologically exploitative that could result in compulsive use. Under AB 1709, accounts of children with such features must be deleted. Despite Meta's opposition, the Electronic Privacy Information Center welcomed the bill in a September statement.

Megan Iorio, director of EPIC's platform governance and accountability program, said California takes the right approach to protecting kids online with AB 1709. Google is entering the AI glasses market with privacy protections designed to address controversies surrounding Meta's smart eyewear. Google's new intelligent eyewear, developed with Warby Parker, Gentle Monster, and Samsung, became available for preorder Thursday, with retail availability scheduled for December 10. Google's privacy measures include automatic redaction of bystanders' faces before imagery reaches Gemini. Google says it does not save those visuals in Gemini History, use them for AI training, or use them for targeted advertising.

Google told 9to5Google that redaction occurs locally on the paired smartphone and that Gemini images are deleted immediately after processing. The glasses require separate camera and microphone permissions, feature an outward-facing recording indicator with tamper detection, and limit conventional video recordings to 90 seconds. Google also plans to extend its Private AI Compute technology to the devices. Its Android XR policies prohibit facial recognition, biometric identification, surveillance, real-time bystander identification, persistent eavesdropping, and voice identification. The restrictions place Google's platform in a different position from Meta, which has explored adding facial recognition to its smart glasses.

Google's Android XR hardware documentation explains how authorized third-party applications can access the glasses' camera through a companion smartphone using standard Android CameraX interfaces, including ImageAnalysis. Applications must obtain separate permission to access the glasses' camera, but permission controls and restrictions on subsequent biometric analysis are different mechanisms. Google prohibits facial identification, yet its documentation does not identify a universal operating system control that automatically prevents an authorized application from analyzing camera imagery to identify someone. Nor does it establish that Gemini's facial redaction applies to third-party applications. The published camera interfaces concern Android companion devices, and equivalent third-party access through an iPhone has not been established.

stories.Headline: Apple confirms a December update will let Siri AI unlock doors by voice for recognized users
stories.Summary:
Apple HomeView Siri AI currently refuses to unlock front doors or open garage doors by voice, according to reports from November 14, 2026. Reviewer Joanna Stern found that the assistant would not grant entry and once claimed it had no camera to see her. Apple confirmed that a software update arriving in December 2026 will extend voice control to these security accessories for recognized users. This fix addresses an authorization issue rather than a simple bug, as the system must trust the user before unlocking. Until then, users must use the Home app or the device touchscreen to manage their locks and garage doors.

The HomeView device costs 299 dollars and features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display with dual speakers and a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. It uses an A18 chip to lock camera and microphone data and can recognize up to six family members by face. HomeView ships with software version 26.5, but it prompts users during the setup process to update to version 27.2. Apple released version 27.2, build 24V526 on November 12 to fix nine security vulnerabilities, though it does not include the voice unlock. The December update has no specific release day or version number, but it will allow recognized users to unlock doors.

An Apple spokesperson told Stern that recognized users can already unlock doors on-screen, and the update will bring this to Siri AI. Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home, said Siri AI allows HomeView to deliver a previously impossible user experience. Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, described the new Siri AI as being much more capable than before. These executives believe the AI integration is why the HomeView product could launch now to compete with other smart displays. They maintain that the device is designed to manage everyday tasks and control smart home devices through this advanced AI.

Some users on X called the device the worst piece of tech they ever bought, citing a glitchy and inferior AI. These customers reported that Siri has multiple voices, cannot open apps by voice, and fails to play music directly via Apple Music. One user shared a video of the device glitching during music playback and noted that the 299 dollar product should just work. Other buyers experienced issues with pictures and reported that restarting the device sometimes resulted in seeing the Apple logo for 20 minutes. These affected users feel the product is missing features and is plagued by technical issues that Apple support cannot solve.

The HomeView is Apple's answer to the Google Nest Hub and Amazon Echo Show, serving as an entertainment system and AI assistant. It can make calls, send messages, and allow each recognized person to set their own calendar events and personal reminders. For personal content like Messages, Apple currently requires both a recognized face and a recently unlocked paired iPhone or iPad device. Research from the University of Michigan and University of Electro-Communications in Tokyo showed that light could inject commands into older Siri devices. This research found that attackers could potentially brute-force smart lock PINs or open garage doors using these injected voice commands.

Apple will release the voice unlock update in December, but the company has not specified the exact requirements for the check. It remains open whether a recognized voice alone is enough or if a paired device must also vouch for the person. Users are advised to keep their software updated and treat the upcoming voice unlock feature as an optional security tool. The company has not yet clarified if the system will require a recognized face, a recognized voice, or both factors. Future release notes will determine if Apple treats a recognized voice as a sufficient credential for opening a secure entry.

stories.Headline: Malaysia probes Megaspeed unit over possible illegal re-export of AI chips
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's trade ministry announced on 13 November 2026 that it is probing a company called Speedmatrix regarding the movement of AI chips. This company is the Malaysian unit of Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, and is currently under official investigation. The ministry is checking if advanced AI chips imported by the unit were later re-exported to other countries illegally. This probe is being conducted together with the customs department to see if the shipments complied with Malaysian law. The investigation follows reports that high performance chips linked to an Nvidia case may have been diverted from Malaysia.

Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and can bring AI chips into the country without a permit. However, since July 2025, any entity that wants to export, re-export, transship, or transit US AI chips must obtain permits. Giving customs false information about these items is a serious offence, and the ministry is checking for such violations. The ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, is working closely with authorities in Singapore and the US. MITI is also considering stronger controls where necessary to prevent the illegal movement of these high performance semiconductor chips.

MITI stated that Speedmatrix has never been cleared of wrongdoing and that official visits to its facilities were regular monitoring. The ministry said it is working with the customs department to establish if any chips were re-exported to other countries. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there is no indication that AI chips linked to Megaspeed were shipped out of Malaysia. He added that Malaysia has received no request for assistance from Singapore or the US but will collaborate on probes. Ibrahim stated that the government wants to make sure the rules are being followed regarding the movement of these chips.

Singapore is also investigating Megaspeed because servers containing chips were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but suspected of going elsewhere. Singaporean authorities barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her Megaspeed role. A US senator alleged that the firm may have been used to get around US controls on advanced semiconductor chips. The US alleges that Alice Huang spied for China, although China denies this and Singapore says she was not investigated. The Nvidia scandal has reportedly wiped almost half a trillion dollars off the market capitalization of the American chip giant.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny over ties between former executive Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who was the chief executive of Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned over an affair with Alice Huang, who is a Chinese national and a suspected spy for China. Megaspeed is accused of steering Nvidia AI chips to China despite US export rules designed to slow Beijing's AI development. The reports describe the chips generally as advanced or high performance, but they do not identify the specific chip model. None of the reports states that a re-export from Malaysia has been established, as the checking is still underway.

Megaspeed stated on its website that it takes its US compliance obligations extremely seriously but did not comment on the MITI statement. The next confirmable developments include the outcome of the customs check and any official assistance requests from Singapore or the US. It remains open whether the US Commerce Department will release official text regarding remote access through third country data centres. The articles leave open whether Malaysia will actually announce a change to its permit regime to strengthen its current controls. No statement has been provided by Nvidia regarding the probe into the re-export of chips through the Speedmatrix unit.

stories.Headline: Google open-sources AQuA to diagnose production AI agent failures
stories.Summary:
Google open-sourced its Ambient Quality Agent, known as AQuA, a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. Google did this, and TechGig published its report on Nov 14, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST, while InfoQ published Leela Kumili's report on Nov 13, 2026. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters and tracking issues.

Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics, and AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand. For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment, and its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs or retrieved data, but AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically. Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, and the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation, and after developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13.

The Google blog post states that an insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score, and that findings link to supporting traces, with proposed root causes required to reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation, and AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code. Google's open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows, according to the articles. The Google blog post describes the citations as the insight rather than a self-reported confidence score.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote that agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early. AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces, and cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. The articles state that these results came from controlled replay, not production traffic, and that sampling can miss rare failures while replay may not reproduce external state. The tool is affected by these constraints, and teams integrating production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows are the users the open-source implementation serves. The articles do not name further individuals beyond Dmytro Aprelenko of Redcore and author Leela Kumili of InfoQ.

The articles give as background that AQuA is a reference implementation designed to analyze production AI agent sessions, verify recurring failure patterns and investigate root causes against deployed source revisions. They state that the tool targets silent quality regressions conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. They describe AQuA operating alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, drawing telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. They note that Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, with six issues confirmed after verification. They add that the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster.

The articles state that AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand, and that developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria using a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. They say AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and that Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. They note that Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. They state that AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically, and that its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows. The articles leave open how AQuA performs beyond the controlled replay of 32 sessions and how the sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state affect diagnosis in production traffic.
