stories.Headline: Bain estimates $6.5tn spending needed for 150GW of AI data centre capacity by 2030
stories.Summary:
Data centre construction stocks lost $4.2tn as the boom in the AI trade unravelled, according to the Financial Times on 15 November 2026. The report put the figure in its headline, and the article itself sits behind a paywall, so the details of which companies fell and by how much are not available in the text. The same day, Data Centre Magazine published statistics from Bain & Company describing the scale of the AI data centre boom that had been driving the trade. Bain estimated that up to $6.5tn of spending would be needed to build nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030.

Bain's figures set out what the build-out requires, including expected growth of 20 to 30 per cent in data centre critical capacity over the next five years. Hyperscalers' data centre capital expenditure could top $1tn by 2028, and global data centre electricity demand is estimated to more than double from 589TWh in 2026 to 1,228TWh in 2030. The number of semiconductor companies manufacturing the most advanced logic node has fallen from 25 in 2002 to 2003 to just four from 2020 to 2026, a decline of 84 per cent. North America's virtual power plant market grew by 13.7 per cent last year to 37.5GW.

Bain & Company is responsible for the statistics, which come from its latest technology report and were drawn from the December Week 1 edition of Data Centre Magazine. The report says building AI-ready data centres is proving as much a test of supply chains and power infrastructure as it is of capital. Taken together, the figures show an industry expanding on several fronts at once, with capital, capacity, power and chip supply all being stretched. The pressure is unlikely to ease before 2030, and for operators, planning around the grid and the supply chain will matter as much as securing funding.

The context is an industry whose growth depends on spending, electricity and a shrinking pool of advanced chip manufacturers, all of which the Bain figures show under strain. The Financial Times report indicates that the stock market's confidence in that boom has faltered, with $4.2tn wiped from data centre construction stocks. Neither article says what happens next beyond 2030, and the Financial Times article gives no further detail beyond its headline because of the paywall. Data Centre Magazine points readers to the full Bain article for more.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind and University of Chicago researchers test AI agents to scale public policy consultation
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Chicago published a preprint on arXiv about pluralistic AI agents. This study evaluated how autonomous software representatives could represent citizens during deliberations regarding artificial intelligence governance to scale public consultation. The team tested these agents to see if they could capture diverse public input while identifying various operational risks. This research aimed to address low civic engagement and technical barriers that often hinder traditional public consultation on AI regulation. The final results were published by the CASRAI Editorial Board on November 15, 2026, as a four minute read.

The system requires three stages starting with an agent interviewing a person or persona to capture qualitative values and core priorities. Next, agents participate in structured multi-agent discussions using anonymized aliases, and finally, a policy-writing agent synthesizes the consensus into rules. The team, including Jacy Reese Anthis, Ken Burke, David Madras, Crystal Qian, Meredith Ringel Morris, Logan Cross, Caroline Pantofaru, and Utsav Prabhu, tested this. They used models like Claude-Opus-5, GPT-5.6-Sol, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K3, Mistral-Large, and Gemini-3.6-Flash across 5,947 deliberations using conjoint analysis. The study also involved 746 verified human participants recruited through Prolific across six different AI safety topics.

The investigators stated that pluralistic agents should function as amplifiers of public engagement rather than autonomous replacements for democratic institutions. They noted that prompt phrasing functions as de facto procedural rulemaking because verbosity and cooperativeness dictate the final policy outcomes. The authors emphasized that institutional researchers must implement safeguards against prompt manipulation and establish clear audit trails for agent interviews. They also argued that human stakeholders must retain ultimate ratification authority over any policies created through algorithmic consensus. The researchers highlighted that without transparent moderation algorithms, consultations risk skewing outcomes toward the most assertive delegates.

Human participants reported concerns regarding personal agency, noting that delegating deliberation prevented them from engaging in direct social learning. These participants felt that using proxies stopped them from updating their own viewpoints during the debate process. The study affected research administrators, ethics boards, and policy researchers by providing empirical benchmarks on how autonomous proxies deliberate. While participants preferred direct personal participation, pluralistic agents recovered 82 percent of the procedural justice gap against a baseline. When choosing between pluralistic agent proxies and direct deliberation with other humans, the participants split evenly at 50-50.

Traditional consultation mechanisms struggle to keep pace with rapid deployment cycles as universities and funding agencies navigate frontier AI safety. Public consultation often fails because institutions cannot disclose confidential technical details to broad audiences and citizens lack specialized engineering jargon. The researchers found that in 1,000 deliberations with 368 personas, agents matched desired priorities in 90 percent of cases. Direct human participation achieved an average attitude shift of 15.4 percentage points, while pluralistic agents produced a 13.9 point shift. This background shows that agents can solicit granular input on technical choices like computational safety thresholds and laboratory boundaries.

Next, university Research Ethics Boards must recognize the ethical nuances of algorithmic proxy representation when reviewing participatory research protocols. Institutions may adopt these multi-agent tools to improve democratic throughput while maintaining human oversight of the final policy decisions. The articles leave open how to standardize prompt calibration to prevent assertive agents from dominating the deliberative process. There is no mentioned solution for the loss of social learning that humans experience when using AI proxies. The text does not specify which specific AI safety topics were used for the 746 human participants.

stories.Headline: Applied Materials guides next-quarter revenue to $11.1 billion on strong AI demand
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials reported results for its calendar third quarter of 2026, which is its fiscal fourth quarter, on November 12, 2026. Sales rose 53.1% from a year earlier to $10.41 billion, above the $10.33 billion analysts expected. Non-GAAP profit was $4.16 per share, 2.6% above the $4.05 consensus. Adjusted operating income was $3.68 billion, a 35.3% margin, and operating margin was 35.1%, up from 25.2% a year earlier. Inventory days outstanding fell to 122 from 132 in the prior quarter, and market capitalization stood at $302.3 billion.

For the next quarter, the company guided revenue to $11.1 billion at the midpoint, above the $10.87 billion analysts estimated, and adjusted earnings per share to $4.35 at the midpoint, above the $4.23 consensus. Advanced packaging revenue grew about 90% for the year, and the eBeam and optical process control businesses grew more than 50%. The connected installed base passed 37,000 chambers, with service and spares revenue up 26% year over year. Customer roadmaps now extend through 2030, and more than 10 new major fab projects were recently added to its tracker.

CEO Gary Dickerson credited leadership in foundry logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, where he said customer demand was strong because of AI computing investments. Management said record revenue and profitability came from operational execution and supply chain collaboration. CFO Brice Hill said the company is investing so it can double systems output by 2028, and he described AI-driven demand as a multi-year opportunity for revenue and margins. The company also cited rolling eight-quarter customer forecasts and earlier orders.

Applied Materials plans to more than double manufacturing and lab capacity by 2030. Management said growth depends on scaling the whole semiconductor ecosystem, including clean room availability and supplier capacity, and that delays there could be headwinds. The stock traded at $383.72, roughly in line with $380.96 just before the earnings. Analysts will watch whether advanced packaging and process control momentum holds, how fast capacity expands, and progress on doubling output and growing service revenue.

stories.Headline: MeitY seeks data collection details from Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp over physical AI training
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology sought details from home services platforms about their collection of first-person video and sensor data from gig workers. The ministry asked Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp for information on data used to train physical AI models. A meeting chaired by MeitY secretary S Krishnan brought together senior executives from quick home services platforms and other technology and robotics companies. The meeting discussed concerns around workers' consent, consumer privacy and data sovereignty, according to a report by ET. Officials are concerned that recordings of everyday household activities could infringe workers' rights, compromise consumer privacy and pose risks to national data security.

The ministry sought details on the standard operating procedures companies follow for collecting, processing and storing such data. It also sought information on safeguards for obtaining workers' consent and protecting the privacy of other individuals captured in the recordings. MeitY further sought clarity on whether companies were selling, sharing or transferring the collected data to physical AI developers outside India. It asked Pronto to submit details of its data collection practices and the SOPs it follows, ET reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. Pronto confirmed it was running an opt-in pilot involving first-person video recordings of household chores, initially available only to customers who actively opted in during booking and limited to less than 0.01% of its users.

Pronto said it participated in the meeting as part of a broader industry consultation involving home services platforms, robotics companies and other stakeholders. A spokesperson said the consultation gave the ministry and industry participants an opportunity to exchange perspectives, share existing practices and discuss opportunities and challenges emerging from the evolving AI landscape. The spokesperson said Pronto shared its current practices as part of this exchange and looks forward to continued engagement with MeitY and other industry stakeholders. Pronto stated that raw footage was deleted immediately after work completion, while an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording remained accessible only to customers for 48 hours. Pronto said this anonymised footage was subsequently used for AI training, as outlined in its terms.

Snabbit clarified that it had conducted a limited assessment of the technology in a controlled training-centre environment but decided against proceeding with the proposal. Urban Company founder Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the company neither records inside customers' homes nor plans to do so. Inc42 has reached out to Snabbit and Urban Company for their comments on the development, and the story will be updated upon receiving responses. Concerns were also reportedly raised about India becoming a source of cheap training data for foreign AI companies. Executives suggested that the country should focus on developing its own physical AI capabilities rather than merely supplying data to overseas developers.

The development comes shortly after Pronto faced scrutiny over a pilot programme to record household chores using cameras worn by service professionals to generate training data for robotics systems. The controversy also brought Snabbit and Urban Company under scrutiny over their potential involvement in this. In July, Pronto formalised its data collection experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which professionals wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. Last month, Pronto founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based physical AI venture that will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. Provision Labs also announced the acquisition of Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a startup focused on perception technologies, and Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision's hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models.

The relationship between Pronto's household data collection and Provision Labs' operations remains unclear. Inc42 said the story will be updated upon receiving responses from Snabbit and Urban Company. The articles do not say what action MeitY will take after reviewing the details submitted by the platforms. The articles do not say whether the ministry set any deadline for the companies to respond. The articles do not say whether other home services platforms beyond Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp were asked for details.

stories.Headline: Sonic Intelligence Academy hosts first AI Music Awards in Los Angeles to normalize tech-assisted tunes
stories.Summary:
The Sonic Intelligence Academy hosted the first AI Music Awards on a Friday afternoon in Downtown Los Angeles. This inaugural event took place at the Mayan Theater, which is a century-old theater turned nightclub. The organization created these awards to normalize tech-assisted tunes and counter the music industry's aversion to AI. The event suffered from various technical glitches and a delayed start time of 6:15 p.m. Several independent media ventures attended the red carpet to interview the various nominees and VIPs.

Artists had to register tracks to the Verified Registry to show if songs were fully AI-generated or human hybrids. There were 25 categories, including Best AI Pop Song, Best AI Comedic Song, and AI Song of the Year. Xania Monet, the AI persona of Telisha Nikki Jones, won both artist and song of the year. DJ Shawn Q. won producer of the year, while Jones had previously won AI Album of the Year. The event was sponsored by Deepgram, an AI startup that specializes in text-to-speech agents.

Software engineer Timirah TJ James and her sister Mia James are the founders of the Sonic Intelligence Academy. They believe that infrastructure must support those using AI rather than dismissing the existence of the technology. The group wants to be an AI counterpart to the Recording Academy that governs the Grammy Awards. They advocate for artists to publicly associate themselves with their AI-powered work to highlight the human creators. The organization also launched its own AI music charts in January to challenge Billboard's industry standards.

Fredro Starr of the rap group Onyx claimed that humans cannot be replaced by AI technology. He touted the human vocals on his record, It All Started in Brooklyn, which he called the first AI vinyl. Telisha Nikki Jones stated that AI is just a tool that emphasizes what artists do. Kehlani previously slammed a three million dollar record deal that Jones received after hitting Billboard genre charts. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a flight ground-stop at 12:30 p.m. PT, preventing some media from attending.

The AI music space is currently facing thorny legal questions and copyright infringement lawsuits from artists and record labels. Generators such as Suno and Udio have been targeted by these legal actions over the use of copyrighted material. The AI Music Awards attempted to move past these issues to find relevance within various music genres. The event featured a commercial for Trinity Social that used the Rockstar Games logo without confirmed authorization. This use of copyrighted material reflects the same concerns that have rankled the mainstream music industry.

The evening ended with various technical failures, including a malfunctioning teleprompter and a broken AI voice introduction. Host Giovanni Wilson joked that the prompter had Tourette's while trying to maintain decorum during the chaos. A trailer for the film A Good Hand Wasted failed to play correctly during the ceremony. The event showed that new technology often comes with kinks that need to be worked out. The articles leave open whether Rockstar Games authorized the use of its logo in the Trinity Social ad.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives says Nvidia turmoil strengthens Big Tech as CoreWeave shares fall 10.19%
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives said on CNBC's ETF Edge show that Nvidia's turmoil could strengthen Big Tech, and he dismissed the market's reaction to the Democrats' congressional election gains as an overreaction he called a "blue tidal wave." Ives is a partner at Yorkville and a tech bull who argued the market may be underestimating AI demand and the advantage of companies with significant computing capacity. CoreWeave shares fell 10.19% to $50.83 as of 10:05 a.m. ET in Friday's regular session on November 13, extending Thursday's 6.86% drop as the Nvidia leadership shock hit Nvidia-linked names. Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January 2026. Huang's resignation followed reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International.

Ives said data centers probably 10% on the low end don't happen, maybe 15-20% on the high end don't happen, and still demand and supply is four to one. He said the compute of the hyperscalers is that much more valuable in capacity today than it was a week ago. He said the game is going to change for Big Tech, it will slow it down, but there are no overbuild and no bubble concerns, and he views that as actually a positive thing. CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue rose 168% to $3.7 billion, above the top of guidance, and CoreWeave raised 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion. Backlog stood at about $133 billion, and the shares jumped 24.7% on November 11, then gave it all back.

Ives said political headwinds could slow data center development but underlying AI infrastructure demand remains considerably stronger than available supply. Jensen Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. A petition urging NVDA to reinstate Huang as CEO has garnered over 135,000 signatures. Tesla CEO Elon Musk shared on X that he is also signing the petition. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan shared that he has signed the petition as Huang deserves "due process."

Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza said the latest market turbulence could benefit hyperscalers at the expense of smaller players in the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Mazza pointed to investor flows into Roundhill's Magnificent Seven ETF, BATS:MAGS, and the Roundhill Necloud ETF, NASDAQ:NCLD, highlighting different market dynamics in the two segments. He noted the Magnificent Seven had been "sort of left for dead for most of 2026" before a strong comeback in September, partly because of defensive characteristics and ability to generate substantial cash. Mazza said hyperscalers may continue to benefit because they have the compute available, which is going to be more valuable if the demand is there. He said some companies Nvidia has been fostering on the neo-cloud build-out are getting hammered worse, and that net-net Big Tech may end up as the winner once again.

ARK Invest bought 283,022 CoreWeave shares, worth about $16 million, on Thursday. CoreWeave's corporate debt is about $41.6 billion, and 2026 capex guidance is $37 billion to $39 billion. CoreWeave's model works only while lenders and customers keep funding the build-out, so sentiment shocks hit it harder than cash-rich hyperscalers. Friday's price is close to the 52-week closing low of $43.66 set on November 5. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of just 14/100, reflecting a heavily leveraged balance sheet and thin profitability.

The next test is Nvidia's November 17 report and any sign of change in Nvidia's support for its cloud partners. Investors have increasingly questioned whether Big Tech's enormous capital expenditure commitments are generating sufficient returns and whether the infrastructure build-out will need to be financed with debt. The articles leave open what Nvidia's November 17 report will show and whether Nvidia's support for its cloud partners will change.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid scandal and a threatened 500 billion dollar AI financing plan
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive, president, and board member of Nvidia on December 12 local time. He stepped down following a scandal involving multiple affairs and allegations of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. This sudden departure has caused the company stock to drop by 4.34 percent. Citizens expressed their reactions by laying flowers in front of the Nvidia headquarters located in California. The exit has created significant uncertainty for the broader artificial intelligence industry and global markets.

The resignation disrupts a 500 billion dollar AI financing plan that Huang announced in August to supply computing infrastructure. This initiative involved six firms, including Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs, and KKR. Nvidia planned to provide residual value guarantees covering 25 percent of each transaction, but financial firms pushed for more. No loans have been made under this plan, and the first deal may not occur until January at earliest. The plan aimed to help AI companies raise money to buy expensive Nvidia chips and computing equipment.

CFO Colette Kress was appointed as the interim CEO while the board considers new candidates for the role. Harvey C. Jones was appointed as the first ever chair of the board to lead the company. Kress and Jones wrote internal memos to rally Nvidia staff during this period of leadership crisis and transition. Huang had personally lobbied the heads of financial firms, including Goldman Sachs Chief Executive David Solomon, to form the consortium. Some executives at the participating firms stated they had not been fully briefed on the financing plan.

Michael Edwards of Forum Markets said Nvidia is the central bank of the AI industry, like a Federal Reserve without a chairman. Other observers argue that Nvidia's influence will not weaken because of its financial firepower and dominance in AI chips. Wall Street banks and asset managers are concerned because they earned billions in fees from Huang's large scale investments. The Trump administration has maintained a regulatory stance favorable to the AI industry despite the current leadership scandal. Some tech leaders reacted to the resignation by calling the situation a mistake for the company.

Huang had driven aggressive investment and fundraising across the AI industry by taking stakes in companies like CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN. He led the company for three decades after co-founding it and moving into acquisitions of AI chips and related technology. The New York Times reported that the financing initiative is now in doubt based on sources familiar with the matter. Bloomberg reported that Nvidia faced pressure from customers and Wall Street firms to expand its financial guarantees. The scandal has raised national security concerns due to the alleged ties to a Chinese spy.

The board of directors is currently searching for a permanent replacement to lead the company after the interim appointment. It remains unclear if the 500 billion dollar financing program will be derailed or if individual contracts will survive. At least one of the six participating financial institutions has discussed withdrawing from the project following the CEO's exit. The articles leave open whether the first transaction will be announced in January or be delayed further. There are unanswered questions regarding the full extent of the drama and the future of Nvidia's leadership.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Home Shopping launches AI-REAL to produce full broadcasts without hosts or camera crews
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Home Shopping of South Korea is introducing a broadcast production system called AI-REAL, in which AI generates both voice and video without show hosts or camera crews. The company announced the system on November 15, 2026, for its data home shopping channel, Hyundai Home Shopping Plus Shop. The first regular application will be a November 16 broadcast at 3:20 p.m. selling Jeju Heart Gold Kiwi. Hyundai Home Shopping says this is the industry's first fully AI-produced broadcast from start to finish.

The company said it will introduce AI-REAL on its data home shopping channel, also called Hyundai Home Shopping PLUS#. AI-REAL generates on its own the voice and video needed for a broadcast, without a presenter or camera crew. The system reproduces as video everything from the cultivation environment and soil conditions of agricultural products to their distribution channels. In a pilot broadcast, partner company costs for preparing product samples and producing broadcast video fell more than 80% compared with before. Sales in the pilot reached 120% of the initial target.

Hyundai Home Shopping plans to schedule AI broadcasts at least once a month, starting with agricultural, livestock and fishery products, and later expand to processed foods and household goods. Lim Hyun-tae, head of Hyundai Home Shopping's Channel Strategy Division, said the company developed the AI broadcast system to achieve shared growth with small and mid-sized partners and to differentiate the customer shopping experience. He said the company will continue to apply AI technology to a variety of tasks to accelerate AI transformation. Lim Soo-jin, head of broadcast production at Hyundai Home Shopping, said viewers told the company the broadcast felt as natural as one with a human host. She said viewers said information such as growing conditions and cooking examples helped them decide whether to buy.

A company official said viewers responded that the AI-produced broadcast felt as natural as one hosted by an actual show host. Lotte Home Shopping is running fashion broadcasts featuring the virtual human Lucy. GS Shop has introduced an AI Studio that creates virtual broadcast spaces with generative AI and, as of September this year, had applied it to 62% of all its broadcasts. CJ OnStyle is using its AI chatbot AiON to respond in real time to customer inquiries during mobile live broadcasts.

Small and mid-sized partners will be able to introduce products without expensive production infrastructure. A reduction in the roles of broadcast production staff and show hosts is expected to be unavoidable, so changes in the industry's workforce management are also drawing attention. Previously, introducing a producing region or the production process required dedicated filming and editing staff. Until now, home shopping broadcasts were structured so that a show host's presenting ability and the quality of on-location filming determined sales performance.

The company explained that while there have been cases in the industry of using AI show hosts or producing only some video with AI, this is the first time an entire broadcast has been realized with AI. Previous uses of AI in home shopping replaced individual scenes or presenters, the company said. This case is seen as a signal that production methods in the home shopping industry are shifting from labor-centric to system-centric. Hyundai Home Shopping plans to air at least one AI-generated program a month, starting with produce, meat and seafood.

It plans to expand gradually into categories such as processed foods and household goods, where smaller suppliers have shown strong interest in selling through the retailer. Lim Hyun-tae said Hyundai Home Shopping plans to expand the use of AI across its operations. The company says it will continue to apply AI technology to a variety of tasks. The articles do not say when the expansion to processed foods and household goods will begin.

stories.Headline: Vertiv launches ecosystem with Dow and Solenis to manage AI liquid cooling
stories.Summary:
Vertiv launched a global ecosystem initiative to help data centre operators manage and optimise liquid cooling infrastructure for artificial intelligence workloads, the company announced on November 12, 2026. The offering combines an expanded collaboration with materials science company Dow and a new partnership with specialty chemicals and water treatment solutions provider Solenis. Together the partnerships will deliver end-to-end thermal and fluid management services, Vertiv said. The announcement comes as rapid growth of AI workloads drives higher computing densities in data centres, increasing the need for advanced liquid cooling systems. Vertiv said the ecosystem brings together its infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities with expertise in coolant technologies, fluid chemistry and water treatment.

The ecosystem integrates infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities, according to Vertiv. Dipti Singh's sponsored DataCenterDynamics piece, dated November 13, 2026, says the primary facility water system serves as the heat-rejection backbone for the coolant distribution units that protect the racks. A heat exchanger inside the CDU sits between the technology cooling system and the facility water system, so facility water never enters the servers. Singh puts the heat-transfer relation as Q = UAΔT, where heat moved equals how readily heat crosses the exchanger surface times the surface area times the temperature difference. ASHRAE's integrated design guidance, part of its AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework, says rack densities have climbed from roughly 120 kW to several hundred kilowatts, with megawatt-class racks expected in the near term.

Ron Bednar, Senior Vice President of Global and Americas Services at Vertiv, said AI is changing liquid cooling from an equipment decision into a system-management imperative. He added that operators need to manage thermal infrastructure, fluid health, monitoring and lifecycle service as one interconnected discipline. Bednar believes managing these complex interdependencies and fluid chemistry together will help operators improve system efficiency and uptime, reduce risk and extend equipment life. Singh argues that operators should stop treating the system as a building utility inspected on a schedule and should manage it continuously as an engineered thermal system. She writes that primary-side fouling, low flow, unstable temperature, biological growth and corrosion debris each eat into the CDU's thermal margin.

Singh says the facility and technology loops need separate chemistry specifications, and the parameters monitored on the facility side should look much like those on the technology loop. Her list includes pH and conductivity, chloride, hardness, alkalinity and silica, dissolved oxygen where relevant, inhibitor residual and glycol concentration, suspended solids and corrosion metals, and microbial indicators. She tells engineers to drop the assumption that deionized water is safe by default, because without buffering and inhibitors it can aggressively pick up ions from the metals and other materials it touches. Steven Lucente, a business development manager for Xylem's Applied Water business who leads its data center business development, wrote in an October 5, 2026 article in Data Center Knowledge sponsored by Xylem's Bell & Gossett that the power a data center draws can bring a water footprint of its own. Manfreid Chua, ZutaCore's VP of Business Development, AI and Sustainability, cites IEA figures in an Enterprise Viewpoint piece and argues the challenge of supporting much higher computational density while using energy and resources responsibly starts at the chip.

Singh says specifications should spell out capped storage for pipe, clean methods of assembly and the use of temporary strainers, and should set flushing velocity, turnover volume, passivation criteria, acceptance limits for differential pressure across filters, endpoints for particles or turbidity, and rules for preserving branches that stay idle until a later phase. She recommends checking headers, branches and CDU connections against both the initial and the expanded loads, and says design reviews should map which racks lose cooling in each failure. Commissioning should record clean-system performance at representative loads and test how controls respond to failures, she says. She also covers the tradeoff behind every choice of heat rejection: evaporative systems use more water but less power, a closed loop recirculates its coolant and uses little water itself but isn't zero-water, and dry cooling avoids evaporation but runs more compressor and fan power, which pushes power usage effectiveness up. Her rule of thumb is that water-stressed sites with plenty of power may accept that penalty, while power-constrained sites with plenty of water may favor evaporative cooling.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2025 update says data centers could account for 9.5 to 15.3% of US electricity by 2030, and the IEA estimates data centers worldwide consumed about 415 TWh in 2024 and projects use could reach about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI a major driver. ASHRAE says integrated liquid-cooled facilities can achieve a PUE of about 1.10 versus about 1.4 to 1.6 for traditional designs, and its framework says warm-water, chiller-less cooling enables near-zero water use in many climates. Singh notes that water usage effectiveness counts water per kWh of IT energy and leaves out the water used to generate the electricity. Lucente suggests project teams begin with the full water cycle: the source of the water, the quality it needs, how it is treated and moved, how much can be reused, how heat is rejected and what happens before discharge. ASHRAE says that when integrated design is not applied effectively, facilities risk stranded capacity, operational instability and costly retrofits.

stories.Headline: Shufti launches patented on-device AI age verification that keeps facial images on the user's device
stories.Summary:
Shufti launched its Privacy-Preserving Age Verification Solution, incorporating patented on-device AI technology, on Nov. 13, 2026, in London, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The company described itself as a Glocal identity verification, Anti-Money Laundering and fraud prevention platform. The solution lets businesses confirm users' age eligibility without the facial image or any other higher-assurance proof of age leaving the user's device. The technology is protected by US Patent No. 12,749,342 B1, titled AGE VERIFICATION, issued by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The patent covers an AI-based system combining on-device facial analysis, split inference and encrypted One-Time Age Tokens.

The solution uses patented split-inference technology to divide AI processing between the user's device and a secure verification server. AI models analyse facial characteristics to estimate age and assess liveness locally, helping identify spoofing attempts involving photographs, masks, screen replays and manipulated images. The device generates an encrypted One-Time Age Token containing intermediate AI outputs rather than transmitting the original facial image. The verification server validates the token, completes the remaining AI processing and determines whether the user meets the required threshold, such as 18 or 21. Tokens are time-limited, can be marked as used after verification and may be restricted to a specific merchant to prevent unauthorised reuse or sharing across platforms.

Shufti's wider Age Verification Solution lets businesses select the level of assurance appropriate to their risk exposure, users and regulatory requirements while minimising collection and exposure of personally identifiable information. It offers docless age checks through facial age estimation or eIDV, configurable age thresholds and confidence-based escalation, risk-based verification, document verification or authoritative database checks, and biometric liveness detection supported by iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance. Shahid Hanif, CEO of Shufti, said a business should not have to collect someone's full identity simply to confirm whether they are old enough to access a service. He said the company developed the solution to help businesses prevent underage access without requiring every legitimate user to provide higher-assurance proof of age. He said the patented on-device approach keeps facial information on the user's device while securely confirming age eligibility, and called the US patent an important milestone.

The articles said a self-declared "I am over 18" click offers little assurance, while an ID upload and selfie can provide stronger evidence but many users are reluctant to share such personal information, particularly for sensitive services. Businesses collecting these records must also manage their security, retention and deletion. In the UK, Ofcom does not recognise self-declaration as a highly effective age assurance method under the UK Online Safety Act. The European Commission is advancing privacy-preserving proof-of-age tools that allow users to establish age eligibility without revealing their identity. The solution supports adult entertainment platforms checking age before content access, social media services applying minimum-age policies, gaming and gambling operators verifying eligibility at registration, and e-commerce businesses checking age before restricted purchases.

Shufti said dividing the final AI model between the device and server reduces exposure of the complete model, making it harder to reverse-engineer the verification process or manipulate locally generated results. The articles said an adult entertainment platform may need to confirm a visitor is over 18, while a regulated gambling operator may also require documentary proof of identity. Shufti's Glocal Trust OS unifies KYC, KYB, eIDV, age assurance, AML screening, agentic transaction monitoring, Know Your Agent and fraud prevention. Shufti's biometric liveness technology holds iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance under ISO/IEC 30107-3. Shufti is recognised as a Leading vendor in Liminal's 2026 Age Verification and Age Estimation Indexes, receiving the highest-tier Exceptional rating for Market Presence in both categories.

Shufti invited businesses to book a personalised demo of the patented Age Verification Solution. The articles listed Aroosa Virk, Brand and Communications Manager at Shufti, as media contact at partnership@shuftipro.com. A photo accompanying the announcement was available at a GlobeNewswire attachment link. The articles did not say when the solution would become generally available or how it would be priced. The articles did not name any business that has adopted the solution.

stories.Headline: Google lets US Gemini users link Google Wallet for read-only spending insights
stories.Summary:
Google launched a Gemini app feature connecting to Google Wallet, announced in a blog post, rolling out today for all Gemini users in the U.S. The feature lets users receive personalized financial insights drawn from their spending habits. It is initially rolling out to users in the US on Android, iOS, and the web. Small Business Trends published its report on Nov 13, 2026, by David Wilson. How-To Geek published its report on Nov 13, 2026, at 4:57 PM EST, by Jefferson Mangubat. Users can link Google Wallet via Gemini’s Connected Apps settings and mention @Google Wallet when asking questions about their finances.

Google also allows users to link bank accounts and credit cards to Wallet through Plaid, a financial technology company that helps connect financial institutions to third-party services. The integration is part of Google's Personal Intelligence initiative, which already connects Gemini with Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search. Google is also rolling out an update to its Memory Summary feature that will enable users to review, edit, and delete what Gemini remembers about their preferences and ongoing goals. Google says the integration is read-only, so Gemini can see linked account information but can’t move money, manage accounts, make purchases, or invest for you. Google says connecting Wallet is entirely optional, and users can revoke access at any time.

Google provides several practical suggestions for using the service, such as asking Gemini to look at spending over the last quarter and come up with a plan to save $1,000 over the next three months. Google says the integration is fully opt-in, so privacy-conscious users can keep it switched off. How-To Geek says it still takes a giant leap of faith to give an AI the keys to your transaction history, particularly when chatbots are still prone to the occasional math error and hallucination. Small Business Trends says business owners will need to dedicate time to learn how to fully leverage the capabilities of the Gemini app. Small Business Trends says they must also consider the security implications of linking financial accounts, as this might raise concerns about data privacy and vulnerability.

Small Business Trends says small business owners often face the dual challenge of limited resources and high competition, making financial efficiency crucial. Gemini has evolved from a general-purpose chatbot to a more personal AI assistant by integrating with services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search to give it more context about users’ lives. Many small business owners already use a range of Google services, such as Gmail and Google Search. The Gemini app leverages Personal Intelligence to provide tailored responses.

With Google Wallet in Gemini rolling out across both web and mobile platforms, small business owners now have access to a robust suite of tools, backed by the reliability of Google services. Users can ask the app specific questions like, “Can we review my spending from last quarter so I can save $1,000 over the next three months?” With this request, Gemini generates dynamic charts that illustrate cash flow, asset allocation, and budget outlines directly within the chat interface. The question, “What subscriptions am I still paying for, and did any of them go up in price this year?”

can prompt Gemini to search through linked accounts, highlighting recurring charges and alerting users to any price hikes. Users can ask “How much did I spend on gifts and travel last year? Use that to help me set a holiday budget for this year.” Gemini will sift through past transactions and suggest budgets customized to individual spending behavior.

stories.Headline: China mandates labels and filings for AI generated short dramas
stories.Summary:
The National Radio and Television Administration introduced landmark rules for AI generated short dramas on September 1 to improve overall output quality. These new policy measures bring synthetic digital entertainment under unified national oversight for the first time alongside traditional live action short dramas. The regulatory crackdown follows an explosive surge in production volume and widespread viewer backlash to a market plagued by disorder. Regulators now require mandatory pre release filings, episode by episode AI labels, and strict tiered administrative reviews for these titles. This move formalizes an ecosystem that previously hovered in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full scale series.

High budget AI productions of 800,000 yuan or more, or those covering politics, national security, military, or religion, face national NRTA pre filing. Mid tier productions with budgets between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan are subject to review and registration by provincial level broadcast authorities. Low cost productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. Every episode of an AI generated micro drama must display a clear, prominent prompt informing viewers of its synthetic origin. These budget triggers are lower than the 2 million to 3 million yuan required for traditional live action micro dramas.

He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, stated that standardized governance is key to ensuring content quality. He emphasized that regulating AI short dramas means stabilizing volume and improving quality while holding the copyright and ethical bottom lines. Lin Qiwen, vice president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI dramas a clear identity. He noted that clear labeling protects the right of viewers to know and reduces the risk of being misled by false content. Lin added that these rules provide a foundation for the industry to move toward quality driven development.

Viewers complained of repetitive tropes like domineering executive romances, time travel themes, instant revenge stories, clickbait, copyright theft, and unauthorized digital clones. Model Qi Hai found that the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app used her image without consent, garnering 40 million views. The legal team for actor Luo Yunxi objected to a near identical digital replica of his likeness in another high profile production. Professor Zhang Lanshan said humans must guard the soul of narrative while AI expands the boundaries of creation. She argued that AI will force human creators to shift from competing in efficiency to competing in value.

Data from the China Network Audiovisual Association shows platforms released over 367,000 micro short dramas in the first half of 2026. AI generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, with over 1,500 new AI series published daily. DataEye reported the user base for AI assisted short series grew from 120 million in 2025 to over 600 million in 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI drama series were published in the first half of the year, but only 1,055 exceeded 100 million views. In the first nine months of 2026, 490,000 micro dramas were released, which is 13 times more than in 2025.

On November 6, the NRTA launched a two month enforcement campaign targeting low brow themes, copyright violations, and technical loopholes. Regulators are still refining operational definitions, such as the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers the mandatory labeling requirement. They are also working to unify self review standards across competing streaming platforms and eliminate disclaimers shrunk into screen corners. The success of the AI drama Armed Into the Song Dynasty shows a shift toward higher production values and historical accuracy. The articles leave open how the NRTA will handle the specific percentage of AI assets required for labeling.

stories.Headline: ReNew plans ₹80,000 crore Andhra Pradesh investment for green data centre and silicon manufacturing
stories.Summary:
ReNew Energy Global announced in November 2026 that it plans to invest about ₹80,000 crore in Andhra Pradesh for data centre infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing. The plan includes a 1 GW green hyperscale data centre in Anakapalli that is designed to run on renewable energy. The company has allocated ₹67,000 crore for the data centre and ₹11,000 crore for polysilicon and metallurgical silicon facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore. It also plans to invest ₹1,500 crore in a permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli, with commissioning expected by March 2029.

Separately, ReNew will set up the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence in Visakhapatnam under the PM SETU Scheme. The centre will develop a cluster of five industrial training institutes in Gajuwaka. ReNew already makes solar cells and modules and is developing a 6.5 GW ingot and wafer facility in Anakapalli, expected to be commissioned by March 2028. The new facilities will add polysilicon and metallurgical silicon production to its existing operations.

The investment comes as India expands its data centre capacity to support artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Installed capacity grew from about 375 MW in 2020 to 1.57 GW by August 2026 and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030. The articles say power availability, water consumption and project approval timelines remain challenges for the sector. Google announced in October 2025 that it would invest about $15 billion, or ₹1.3 lakh crore, in an AI infrastructure hub in Visakhapatnam between 2026 and 2030.

Clean Max Enviro Energy Solutions also signed a preliminary agreement with the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board for an investment of about ₹50,000 crore. Its proposal includes 3 GW of combined wind and solar capacity and 1 GW of pumped hydro storage. These would supply a 2 GW green compute factory in Kurnool, developed with Neysa. Neysa, an AI cloud provider, will anchor 1 GW of the facility's IT load.

stories.Headline: Anthropic publishes recommendations for more reliable AI safety evaluations
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published recommendations for building more reliable AI safety evaluations in a research post on Friday, November 13, 2026. The company warned that safety scores can be misleading when tests are easy to game, poorly documented or measure the wrong behavior. Anthropic is a leading developer of large language models. The recommendations cover evaluation design, testing environments, grading and the reporting of results. Anthropic said decisions about whether a system is ready to ship, what guardrails it needs and where future safety work should focus all rest on the quality of the evaluations behind them.

Anthropic said evaluations should assess whether responses raise or lower the likelihood of harm rather than what a model can do. It argued that refusal rates alone are a poor gauge, since declining to engage with a user in crisis is itself a failure. The company called for multidisciplinary evaluation teams, sandboxed testing without internet access, multi-turn conversation tests, human validation of AI graders and published statistical uncertainty. It said it had hardened its own testing environments after incidents, temporarily halted many evaluations that grant models internet access and added real-time monitoring for web-search tests that still need connectivity. Anthropic narrowed its advice to three priorities: define what is being measured before testing begins, validate AI-based grading against human expert judgment, and report statistical uncertainty so readers can tell a real improvement from noise.

Anthropic wrote that when it says a model is safer than its predecessor, it means the model scored better on a set of evals someone built. The company wrote that a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. It wrote that when a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure. Anthropic wrote that in recent months, in response to its own incidents, it had hardened its evaluation environments. It wrote that humans extract harmful information from a model through gradual escalation, so a model that handles the first message well may respond inappropriately by the fifth.

Anthropic said an appropriate response in biology and cybersecurity is rarely a flat refusal, and models should engage with legitimate requests while withholding operational details that could enable misuse. The company said evaluations need to capture both a model's willingness to comply with harmful requests and its tendency to reject harmless ones. It said results can shift on seemingly minor design choices, such as whether a question is multiple-choice or open-ended, or how the answer options are ordered. Anthropic said it runs multi-turn evaluations that grade an entire conversation against rubrics written by domain experts, with a single failure sinking the whole interaction. The recommendations arrive as regulators and enterprise buyers increasingly ask vendors to substantiate safety claims, and as model releases are marketed partly on benchmark performance.

Anthropic distinguished observational designs, suited to understanding how a model behaves, from causal designs, needed to test whether a specific intervention changes outcomes. It called for measurement specialists to decide how responses are sampled and scored, and subject-matter experts to identify realistic risks and define what a sound answer looks like. The company likened the state of the field to psychology a decade ago, when similar problems with measurement were addressed through reforms such as preregistration and better methodology. Anthropic said some evaluations run with standard safeguards switched off so that a model's baseline behavior can be observed, which can let a system reach beyond its intended testing environment. It urged developers to document testing configurations so that independent teams can reproduce results.

Anthropic said that if scores can move with the format of a question, comparisons across models and versions become difficult to defend, weakening the case for evaluation results as a procurement or compliance signal. For AI developers, the practical burden is heavier than running a standard benchmark, since expert-designed rubrics, human validation of automated graders, longer conversational tests and published uncertainty ranges all add cost and time to the release cycle. Anthropic's own account suggests the payoff is a clearer picture of what a model will actually do once deployed, rather than a number that may not mean what it appears to. The articles do not say when Anthropic will publish further recommendations or whether regulators will adopt them. The articles do not say how many incidents prompted Anthropic to harden its testing environments.

stories.Headline: UVA Darden professors propose AI firms release model weights annually if using unlicensed training data
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed to go public on October 26, and reports put its valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion. Three days later, Alphabet lost nearly 13% of its value in a single day, about $500 billion, on worries about whether its AI spending will pay off. UVA Darden professors Mike Lenox and Alex Cowan argue that AI companies using unlicensed training material should release their model weights to the public once a year. They say the time to adopt their proposal is before AI companies go public.

The proposal requires any firm that trains AI models on material it hasn't licensed, or builds on a model that used unlicensed data, to release the weights of those models to the public once a year. Firms keep a lead of six to 18 months, or about a year on average. The IPOs still happen, and the value just spreads out. The authors say the rule should be given two or three release cycles, 24 to 36 months since releases happen once a year, then market concentration and prices should be checked.

Lenox and Cowan say nobody feels great about AI right now, that the people running the frontier labs say in public they're worried about what they're building, and that the incumbents say the same. They say young people are worried about jobs, the public is worried about safety, and governments aren't sure what to do. They describe two current approaches to govern AI: the status quo of patchy rules like the EU AI Act and California's SB 53, with safety left to a few firms policing themselves and creators paid one lawsuit at a time, and heavy government involvement through licensing, a new regulatory agency, steep taxes or a government stake. They call their proposal a third way that's simpler than either and much better tested.

In a survey of 2,778 AI researchers, the median respondent put the chance that AI leads to human extinction, or something similarly permanent, at 5%, and between 38% and 51% put the chance of a generally bad outcome at 10% or more. In March, a record 59% of voters told NBC News that the economic and political systems are stacked against people like them. Economists Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo estimate that automation accounts for 50, 70% of the change in the U.S. wage structure over the last four decades. In 2024, a federal judge ruled that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search, while nobody owns the protocols that move data across the internet, or Linux, which runs most of the world's websites.

Since 1980, average price markups in the U.S. have risen from 18% above marginal cost to 67% now. Antitrust expert Tim Wu warns in "The Curse of Bigness" about a few megafirms that outspend the public interest on lobbying. In the early 2000s, software vendors sat on reported vulnerabilities for a year or more, sometimes never disclosing them, and today the standard is coordinated disclosure, with Google's Project Zero settling on a 90-day deadline. By 2019, Project Zero reported that 97.7% of the issues it found were fixed inside that window, and a patent gives an inventor about 20 years of exclusivity in exchange for publishing how the invention works.

In five national polls this year, between 55% and 77% of Americans said AI is moving too fast or should slow down, and in the AP-NORC poll just 8% said it's moving too slowly. Under Nasdaq's new fast-entry rules, a newly public company of significant size can join the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days, and from there it lands in index funds, pensions and the retirement accounts of the 62% of Americans who own stock. The authors say that once that happens, every rule that touches AI's value has tens of millions of people on the other side of it, and acting then will be a lot harder than acting now. They say the most important part of the process is robust, transparent debate, and that if market concentration and prices haven't moved after two or three release cycles, the public should ask for more and they'd be the first to say so.

stories.Headline: Ontario court lets Canadian news publishers pursue copyright case against OpenAI
stories.Summary:
The Ontario Court of Appeal allowed a copyright lawsuit against OpenAI to proceed on Friday, November 13, 2026, after dismissing a company appeal. A coalition of Canadian news publishers filed this legal action two years ago to address the use of their content for AI. The publishers claim that OpenAI used their news articles to train ChatGPT, which they argue is a breach of copyright laws. These news organizations allege that the company is profiting from their intellectual property without providing any permission or financial compensation. This specific legal battle is the first Canadian case to address the practice of using copyrighted content to train generative AI.

The case involves a coalition including The Canadian Press, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, Postmedia, and the public broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada. OpenAI argued that the case should be heard in a United States courtroom instead of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. The court rejected this jurisdictional challenge, ruling that the legal proceedings will remain in the province of Ontario for now. The decision noted that OpenAI failed to provide evidence that a Canadian judgment would conflict with any existing laws in America. The court also stated that the efficient working of the Canadian legal system favors authors bringing claims against foreign companies.

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice is responsible for hearing the case after the higher court dismissed the appeal from OpenAI. The court stated that allowing Canadian authors to sue foreign companies for breaches of Canadian laws supports the fair legal system. Judges found that there was no evidence that enforcement of a Canadian ruling would be complicated by laws in the United States. The court determined that it does have the proper jurisdiction to hear the claims brought by the news publishers. These legal rulings ensure that the merits of the copyright claims can be argued within the Canadian judicial system.

The news publishers are affected by the alleged scraping of their articles from the internet to train the generative AI system. Other publishers, including Condé Nast and McClatchy, are involved in a separate United States case against the Canadian AI company Cohere. News and cultural industry groups have called on the federal government to take a stand on how AI uses copyrighted content. These groups want the government to clarify the rules regarding the use of intellectual property by artificial intelligence companies. The publishers argue that the current practice of using their content without payment is an unfair use of their work.

The lawsuit against OpenAI has dragged on since 2024, following the rise of generative AI systems like the one powering ChatGPT. Earlier this year, Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, and The Canadian Press launched another separate lawsuit against the company Anthropic. Multiple lawsuits dealing with AI systems and copyright have been underway in the United States since as early as 2023. These cases highlight a growing global conflict between traditional media publishers and the developers of new artificial intelligence technologies. The legal landscape is evolving as courts decide if training AI on existing data constitutes a copyright violation.

The lawsuit will now move forward in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to determine if OpenAI breached Canadian copyright laws. The articles leave open whether the federal government will ever update the Copyright Act to address these specific AI concerns. It remains unclear if Ottawa will eventually take a formal stand on how AI systems should use copyrighted news content. The outcome of the case against OpenAI may influence other pending legal battles involving AI companies and media publishers. Future rulings will likely define the boundaries of fair use for training generative AI systems within the Canadian legal framework.

stories.Headline: Senate passes BAAJA draft to let AI companies build power plants
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, the United States Senate approved a preliminary version of the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act, which is called BAAJA. This legislative action was taken by a large Senate majority to provide a roadmap for new power generation at various AI data centers. The bill was advanced through a procedural vote of 73 to 25 that took place on November 9, 2026. This move allows large AI companies to build power facilities regardless of existing legal constraints or environmental rules. The authors describe these influential AI giants as apex predators or T-Rexes because of their enormous size and political clout.

The BAAJA bill requires a rapid build-out of gas pipelines and electric power transmission to serve these new and massive AI facilities. It changes the law by limiting the ability of tribal authorities and state attorneys general to stop the construction of new lines. The legislation allows companies to ignore existing environmental regulations regarding water and air pollution to facilitate the rapid data center build-out. It asserts that it will increase transmission, increase generation supply, improve grid capacity use, and connect consumers to cheaper generation. These changes could add 40 to 50 gigawatts of gas-fired generation at the proposed facilities across the United States.

Analysts Leonard Hyman and William Tilles are responsible for the report and they argue that BAAJA gives AI giants a legal roadmap. They stated that these companies will use small, inefficient, and highly polluting gas combustion turbines to power their new facilities. The authors believe that the political influence of these companies allows them to stomp on relatively puny electric utilities. They compared the situation to a Broadway song, suggesting that these AI giants will get whatever they want from the government. The analysts claim that the search for incremental electric power has resulted in a desperate grab for gas.

Critics warn that this permitting bill is a massive giveaway to the AI data center industry and divides green energy environmentalists. The bill affects electric utilities, which may see their profitability squeezed if consumers gain access to cheaper power sources. In Texas, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas published an update in September listing 158 gigawatts of solar requesting interconnection. This queue also includes 49 gigawatts of wind and 166 gigawatts of batteries, though some of these requests are duplicative. Currently, there are only 38 gigawatts of installed utility-scale solar in Texas compared to the massive amount of pending requests.

The background provided shows that Anthropic announced a multi-billion-dollar purchase of gas combustion turbines to power a new facility in Texas. The authors previously published a report titled The AI Power Grab That Could Upend America's Utility Industry to explain their thesis. They note that data centers might buy power directly from a utility at full wholesale rates to improve grid capacity. However, they believe this interaction will be a minor part of the future relationship between utilities and the AI data centers. The current trend suggests that AI companies will prioritize their own power generation over relying on the existing utility grid.

A final vote on the BAAJA bill could occur during the week of November 16, 2026, following the preliminary approval. The bill is an early draft that will likely be revised several times before it reaches a final legislative version. It may still die in a newly reconstituted House of Representatives after the election that took place in November 2026. The articles leave open whether the proposed 40 to 50 gigawatts of gas generation will actually be funded and built. It remains uncertain if the overall grid impact will be positive given the uncompetitive prices of gas combustion turbines.

stories.Headline: AI interviews raise job offers and retention, Brian Jabarian finds
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon’s Brian Jabarian, a former principal researcher at Chicago Booth, and his coauthor partnered with a recruiting firm hiring for customer service positions, and 70,000 candidates were randomly assigned to interview with an AI agent or a human recruiter. Candidates knew when they were speaking with AI, and final hiring decisions were always made by human recruiters reviewing the interview transcripts and audio. The researchers found that candidates who got a job interview with an AI were more likely to receive a job offer, more likely to start the job, and more likely to stay in the position after 30 days and up to four months. The retention rate was much better for the AI-interviewed group, and this retention did not come at the cost of productivity loss. Comparing employees interviewed by an AI and employees interviewed by a human, the researchers saw no difference in productivity metrics and no difference in separation after 30 days.

Both human and AI recruiters were required to cover 14 interview topics, but humans naturally vary in how consistently they conduct interviews, and fatigue, time pressure, and conversational drift can all change how questions are asked. AI is more consistent than human recruiters at covering more topics, with less variation in follow-ups and in the flow of the interview, and it more consistently applies a higher language across interviews. In response to this consistency, candidates are more likely to reveal their true type in a job interview conducted by an AI than in one conducted by a human. Candidates who got a job interview with an AI are more likely to display interactivity as a signal during a job interview and less likely to display other cues. Forty percent of people left voluntarily in both cases, and the researchers saw no deterioration in productivity downstream.

Jabarian said the overall takeaway of the research is not that you should replace all the time humans by AI, calling it more subtle and more complicated. He said AI adoption shouldn’t be seen as a task-by-task decision but more about organizational design as a whole, and about thinking how to combine AI agents working together with human agents in the workplace. He said AI is not so magic, and that it is an interesting tool to more consistently perform different interviewing tasks, such as covering a certain set of topics, having a certain order, and having a certain language. He said that when you are a human interviewer, sometimes you start the job interview in the morning and perform really well at your task, but for reasons of fatigue you might be less consistent. He said that if we were in a world where AI was artificially inflating your value during a job interview, you would see deterioration in terms of productivity downstream, but we don’t see this here.

Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company, said human eyes may not be the first to look at a job application these days. He said most of the companies he deals with run applications through that, and then they have also a human or HR professional. He said the practice picked up in the last two years, with technology scanning resumes for buzzwords pulled from the posted job description. He cautioned against copying a posting outright, saying you want to tailor it to the job description when you are applying, but you don’t want it to read word for word, which indicates a red flag to an employer. He recommends people use AI to help organize and format a resume, and not use it to embellish skills they do not have, and he said Microsoft and Claude work well.

Pasola said he “absolutely” believes some qualified candidates are slipping through the cracks or not getting hired because they are not using AI tools. He said this is because they have skills that they can put to the forefront in front of the employer that they are not showing. As Texas prepares for its first new governor in 12 years, Gina Hinojosa is searching for her team using a digital portal rather than a stack of paper resumes. That mirrors a hiring shift playing out across the job market, according to Pasola. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these accounts.

The articles leave open what happens next, and they do not give further background beyond the experiment and the staffing company’s observations. The Chicago Booth article was published November 13, 2026, and the KSAT article was published November 11, 2026. The KSAT article was reported by Olivia Dague, who joined KSAT 12 in July 2026 after spending three years reporting in Knoxville, Tennessee, at WBIR. Dague is from Arlington, Texas, and is a graduate of the University of Oklahoma. The articles do not state any additional plans or follow-up studies.

stories.Headline: University of Michigan researchers find generative AI consumes more energy for non-English text
stories.Summary:
Researchers from University of Michigan Engineering discovered that generative AI consumes significantly more energy when processing non-English text. This study was presented at the Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics. The team analyzed three open-source models, including Meta's Llama 3.1, Google's Gemma 3, and Alibaba's Qwen 3. They found that these models often produce lower-quality output while using more power.

The energy cost for non-English text ranges from 1.4 to 180 times that of English. Bengali requires 15.3 times more energy, while Hindi needs 7.9 times more. Most Western European languages use twice as much energy or less. These disparities affect roughly 5.2 billion people who must pay more or switch languages. This occurs because non-Latin scripts require more tokens, which consumes more memory and power.

Naihao Deng, a doctoral student and first author, stated that the most energy-intensive languages often have lower accuracy. He warned that this double penalty could price some people out of using AI. Rada Mihalcea, the U-M AI Lab director, urged developers to create more resources for these languages. She suggested using crowdsourced native speakers to improve training data and efficiency.

The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation and DARPA, with support from OpenAI and Ford. To fix these issues, the team recommends that companies use translation pipelines or models tailored to specific languages. They also suggest routing queries to specialized models to reduce costs. These changes would help prevent global inequalities in AI access.

stories.Headline: Simons Foundation renews $6m grant for Lauda-led topology collaboration studying knots, quantum computing and AI
stories.Summary:
The Simons Foundation renewed a $6 million grant for an international research collaboration led by Aaron Lauda, a mathematician and divisional dean at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. The collaboration, called the Simons Collaboration on New Structures in Low-Dimensional Topology, was established in 2023 and brings together 11 institutions worldwide. The new award raises the foundation's total investment in the project to $14 million, and USC will receive more than $2 million of the new funding. The renewal supports the work for another three years.

The research explores connections between knot mathematics, quantum computing and artificial intelligence. One focus is anyons, particle-like phenomena first observed in 2020, whose movements form braids that could help quantum computers keep information nearly error-free. In a 2025 Nature Communications paper, Lauda and collaborators Filippo Iulianelli, Sung Kim and Joshua Sussan added a new type of anyon, called a "neglecton," to an expanded model and showed the full range of quantum computations could be done through braiding alone. The breakthrough remains theoretical, and researchers still need to find a physical system to put it into practice.

Lauda said the team began with fundamental questions about knots and the possible shapes of three- and four-dimensional spaces, including those used to describe spacetime. He said following those questions led to new ways of thinking about quantum computation and machine learning. Cris Negron, an associate professor of mathematics at USC Dornsife, said the team wants to turn insights from physics into precise mathematical tools that offer new methods for analyzing and distinguishing knots and spaces. Negron also said working with people who approach problems differently helps young researchers refine their questions and can have a lasting positive impact on their careers.

The collaboration also studied how AI learns through trial and error when rewards are rare, using the Andrews, Curtis conjecture, a puzzle that has stymied researchers for more than 60 years. Caltech collaborator Sergei Gukov and colleagues showed that several suspected exceptions to the conjecture were not exceptions after all, and the work points toward ways to improve AI's search methods. Researchers Qiuyu Ren of Stanford University and Michael Willis of Texas A&M University used knot mathematics to distinguish some four-dimensional spaces beyond spacetime. In June, Negron co-organized a workshop at the American Institute of Mathematics in Pasadena, California, for graduate students and recent PhD recipients. With the renewed funding, Lauda said the team can develop ideas from the first phase together, giving the mathematics time to mature while pursuing connections to quantum computing and AI.
