stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy joins federal StabilityMax program to test fuel cells for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy, a fuel cell company headquartered on Great Pasture Road in Danbury near the Bethel border, will take part in a three-year federally funded program to test whether fuel cells can provide electricity to data centers where there are rapid fluctuations in power consumption. The company announced the project in a release dated Nov 13, 2026, reported by staff writer Rob Ryser. The program is known as StabilityMax. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Danbury, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The federal government wants to know whether fuel cells, which already power commercial and industrial facilities, can handle the heavy demands of artificial intelligence data centers.

The project runs three years and is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratories of the Rockies. FuelCell Energy reported 425 employees worldwide last year, most of them at the company's Danbury headquarters and its Torrington manufacturing plant. FuelCell planned to keep its staffing levels the same. Details about the StabilityMax grant program, such as how much federal money is involved, were not disclosed. The pairing of fuel cells with data centers made news in October when a developer proposed to reinvigorate a 1.3-million-square-foot office structure in Danbury by bringing in a data center and using fuel cells to power it.

Mayor Roberto Alves said Thursday that FuelCell Energy's participation in the national research effort is a strong example of the innovation and expertise rooted in Danbury. Alves said he was pleased to see a Danbury company working with leading national labs on the challenge and looked forward to learning what the project demonstrates about performance, cost and the effects on the electric grid. Kathleen Blomquist, the company's director of communications, said the project isn't about testing whether fuel cells can power data centers because they can. Blomquist said the question is how to optimize a fuel cell-based power system for the rapidly changing demands of AI infrastructure, including how fuel cells, batteries, power electronics and advanced controls work together as computing loads fluctuate. Zhiwen Ma, a principal investigator at the National Laboratories of the Rockies, said fuel cells combined with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure.

Ma said that through the project, NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers. Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell, said the insights gained through the work will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions, and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. The company's release said that as AI adoption accelerates, data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and creating rapid fluctuations in power consumption. A data center is an umbrella term for computer processing plants that support all the ways artificial intelligence is used today. Public concern about energy usage by data centers has made headlines across Connecticut and the region.

A fuel cell makes electricity from fuel and air, eliminating the need to burn fuel. The company's headquarters sits on the city's east end. A FuelCell Energy power plant stands on Triangle Street in Danbury. The three-year project isn't as much about testing whether fuel cells work but about applying the technology to the next level. The federal government also wants the work to limit impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

The articles do not say when the three-year project begins or ends. The articles do not disclose how much federal money is involved in the StabilityMax grant program. The articles do not say what results the test facility is expected to produce or when. The articles do not say whether the October proposal for the 1.3-million-square-foot Danbury office structure is connected to the StabilityMax project. The articles do not say what the national laboratory-supported testbed will cost or who beyond FuelCell Energy will run it.

stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang says Muse now calls US businesses for paying subscribers
stories.Summary:
Meta's AI agent Muse can now place outbound phone calls to businesses in the United States on behalf of its users. This feature was tested in September and is now available to all paying Muse subscribers located within the US. The agent launched on September 8 and later received a Mac app on September 17 to expand its reach. Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang announced that the agent now handles tedious calls to restaurants, cable companies, and the DMV. This capability turns a feature once demoed by Google Duplex in 2018 into a standard tool for always-on AI agents.

The calling feature is limited to subscribers on monthly plans costing twenty dollars or one hundred dollars for various token amounts. The twenty dollar plan provides 500 million tokens a week, while the one hundred dollar plan offers 3 billion tokens. Muse has passed 10 million users, though it offers a free tier that does not include the phone calling feature. The service is currently restricted to the United States, and it handles appointments, reservations, and waiting on hold for users. Meta also launched the Muse Charm keychain gadget and glasses updates during a six week blitz to reclaim its frontier spot.

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang pitched the tool as a way for users to avoid making calls they do not want. Spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reuters that the company would only roll out certain features when ready and with proper disclosures. A Meta executive later conceded that using human operators without clear disclosure was a mistake, leading to the feature being pulled. Meta communications reported that human-placed calls were expected to succeed 95 to 98 percent of the time during testing. These human agents were intended to take over requests to ensure a higher success rate than AI-only calling could manage.

Many businesses and receptionists hang up the moment they detect an AI agent is on the line during a call. Users are drawn to Muse because the AI will sit on hold indefinitely and work through complex phone menus without complaint. Some Meta staff warned internally that sensitive details could reach call-center contractors without anyone intending it during the human tests. Muse tells the person it is calling on someone's behalf and transcribing the conversation, though it is not always explicit. The feature affects paying subscribers who must decide if the time saved is worth the monthly subscription fee for the service.

Meta previously ran a Messenger assistant called M from 2015 to 2018 that used human staff and reached 30 percent automation. Google's Gemini and the startup Instinct already offer similar calling features, while xAI's Grok Bot can also place phone calls. In contrast, OpenAI's ChatGPT Dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet still cannot make calls, leaving Meta to compete with a few rivals. Google Duplex previously experienced a launch where one in four calls was handled by a human to ensure better success. Synthetic voices are becoming more realistic, which makes it increasingly difficult for businesses to detect that an AI is calling.

The Muse agent will soon receive a free email address to further expand its capabilities for the paying subscriber base. It remains unresolved whether paying customers can currently be routed to a human concierge for their outbound business phone calls. The articles leave open whether the twenty dollar plan alone unlocks calling or if the feature requires a higher tier. There are no public reports regarding specific call limits, per-call costs, or geographic limits beyond the current United States rollout. Meta continues to test the paywall to see if consumers will pay 240 dollars a year to run a consumer agent.

stories.Headline: Alice Huang allegedly diverts 7.5 billion dollars in Nvidia AI chips to China using personal ties to the CEO
stories.Summary:
A report published on November 10, 2026, alleges that Alice Huang used personal ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to divert advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. This operation reportedly moved approximately 240,000 high-performance chips, including H100, H200, and A100 models, worth roughly 11 trillion won or 7.5 billion dollars. Alice Huang allegedly built a complex corporate network involving her husband, Kang Wei, and her sister, Huang Yu, to bypass official scrutiny. This network spanned three countries and included the Chinese firm Shanghai Century Litong, the Singaporean company Megaspeed, and the Malaysian subsidiary SpeedMatrix.

The scheme required Shanghai Century Litong to obtain preferred cloud partner status in October 2023, only four months after its founding in June 2023. This status allowed the firm to provide restricted computing capacity to Tencent, Alibaba, and various Chinese AI research labs. Megaspeed acted as a central hub for moving hardware from Southeast Asia into China after Alice Huang acquired a subsidiary of 7Road in 2023. SpeedMatrix further supported the operation by pledging intellectual property and servers as collateral to a subsidiary of Alibaba known as Apex.

Nvidia stated that information shared with Asian cloud customers involved ordinary business data rather than trade secrets or national security concerns. Outside directors at the company appointed a former prosecutor to lead an internal investigation into the governance risks. Meanwhile, the FBI launched an inquiry to determine if Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency. President Donald Trump mentioned his belief that the CEO was unaware of any alleged espionage involving Alice Huang.

The U.S. Department of Commerce is scrutinizing the network after unusually large orders drew attention, though it reportedly delayed adding Megaspeed to the Entity List. Market capitalization for Nvidia dropped by approximately 432.12 billion dollars over two days, causing shares to fall 9.5 percent. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has briefed the president on the matter while Democrats seek legislation to tighten chip export restrictions. Taiwanese authorities monitored the movements of Alice Huang at the request of the United States government.

stories.Headline: Getty appeals to the Court of Appeal over whether AI models can be infringing copies
stories.Summary:
Getty Images is appealing to the Court of Appeal in its dispute with Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion image generator. The appeal is being heard over two days, Wednesday and Thursday, in the week of 11 November 2026. The High Court gave its first instance judgment in November 2025 and largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on only a small part of its trade mark claim, and its copyright claim failed. Getty's barrister told the court that Stability "doesn't think it should have to pay" for Getty's content.

The central question is whether an AI model can be an "infringing copy" under section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, even if the model never contained copies of the works. Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, so Getty dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial and kept only a secondary infringement case. That case argued that the model was an infringing copy imported into, and distributed in, the UK. The High Court accepted that an intangible AI model can be an "article", but held that an infringing copy must actually be a copy. Because the model weights had never stored Getty's images, the High Court ruled that the model could not be an infringing copy.

Getty says that "making" a model includes training it, which involves copying images, and that the finished model need not itself contain copies. In its view, if making the article in the UK would have infringed copyright, the article is an infringing copy whether or not it holds copies. Getty's barrister said Stability wants to separate what was done with the copyright works from the act of training, but can only do so by mischaracterising the facts. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed. It says Getty's approach would produce odd results, such as making it unlawful to import the model but lawful to copy it once it is in the UK.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited, known as BPI, represents the UK recorded music industry and has permission to intervene in support of Getty. It warns that the High Court's approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back into the UK, with significant consequences for the music and wider creative industries. BPI also notes that Getty accepted at trial that the versions of Stable Diffusion did not contain copies, and cites two recent German cases in which the Munich Court found that models had memorised works they were trained on. On that basis BPI says the Getty judgment has "no wider significance" on whether models contain copies, because the question depends on the facts of each model. Stability AI also argues that extending the law to models trained overseas is a matter for Parliament, not the courts, and it has cross-appealed two findings that went against it.

The High Court case was heard in June 2025, and Getty dropped one of its primary copyright infringement claims just two weeks into the trial. The claims that remained before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith were secondary infringement, trademark infringement and passing off. The court found that Getty succeeded in part on trademark infringement, but only for older models and on isolated examples. Getty had alleged that Stability copied and processed millions of copyrighted images to train Stable Diffusion in the US. Stability's directors include the filmmaker James Cameron, and Stability argues that the images were downloaded and stored in data centres outside the UK, so UK copyright law does not apply.

Stability AI is asking the Court of Appeal to overturn two findings that went against it at first instance: that an intangible model can be an "article", and that Stability itself imported or distributed the model in the UK. Getty disputes both points. If Getty succeeds, developers could face UK copyright claims over models trained abroad on unlicensed works, even where the imported model stores no copies. If Stability succeeds, where a model is trained and whether it stores copies will remain key to any claims. The judgment has not yet been handed down, and the Government continues to consider its approach to copyright and AI following its March 2026 report.

stories.Headline: Kansas education board requires school districts to adopt AI classroom policies
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education created an instructional technology policy earlier this week, the Kansas State Department of Education announced in a press release on Nov. 13, 2026, from Topeka. The policy requires Kansas public school districts and accredited nonpublic schools to develop policies outlining how technology is used in classrooms. The policy establishes statewide minimum requirements for instructional technology use while allowing local school boards to decide how those expectations will be implemented. Kansas Education Commissioner Dr. Jake Steel said the policy is intended to ensure technology strengthens teaching and learning rather than replaces meaningful interactions between teachers and students. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners.

Every district and accredited nonpublic school must adopt both an instructional technology policy and an implementation plan, and both must be approved by local school boards and reviewed annually. The plans must address the purpose and intended use of classroom technology, student access to school-issued devices, whether students can take school-issued devices home, digital citizenship and student well-being, the use of artificial intelligence by teachers and students, student privacy and cybersecurity protections, and technology expectations and violations. Schools will also be required to establish guidelines for how artificial intelligence tools, including chatbots and generative AI, are used. Districts and accredited nonpublic schools must make their policies and plans publicly available on their websites and submit their adopted plans to the Kansas State Department of Education by July 1, 2027. Beginning in the 2028-29 school year, parents or guardians must receive access to their school's technology-use plan and acknowledge it before students receive access to school-issued devices, and the policy will remain in effect until July 1, 2030 unless it is reauthorized, amended or extended.

Steel said the State Board has sent a clear message that technology only belongs in the classroom when it strengthens teaching and learning. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners. KSDE officials said it encourages schools to involve families and caregivers in developing their technology-use plans. It also recognizes that some students may need additional or different access to technology because of disabilities, medical needs, language needs or other educational requirements. The Kansas State Board of Education created the policy earlier this week, according to the KSDE press release.

Princeton University recently decided to offer access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro to its students and faculty through a new one-year pilot program, The Daily Princetonian wrote on Oct. 30. The Daily Princetonian later published an editorial about the program on Nov. 6, questioning how the implementation of AI in an academic environment will affect students' ability to learn and how it reflects on the university's fundamental mission of education. The Daily Princetonian's Editorial Board said it was not convinced that a sweeping ChatGPT pilot will suit the distinct learning methods across disciplines. Students at the College have had the ability to use several different AI tools at their full capacity for about a year now, after Vice President for Operations Sharon Blanton announced in an email to the College on Oct. 2 that students and faculty were granted secure access to Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Google NotebookLM, The Signal reported in 2025. Students can find an instructional article on the College's website titled "Getting Started with Gemini: Your AI Assistant for Campus Life."

Artificial intelligence has been developing at an exponential rate since ChatGPT was first introduced to the internet in 2022, and after about four years it has become an integral part of every app, including search engines like Google. The Daily Princetonian wrote that students will be able to request access to ChatGPT Plus before the start of next semester, and faculty and staff could request access beginning Wednesday. The tech giant Google recently announced that if schools ban use of their AI features, students will no longer be able to use Google Search, according to The Guardian. Students at the College were encouraged to use the tools responsibly and to follow course guidelines, which can differ for each instructor. Princeton's implementation of ChatGPT Plus and Pro, which one typically has to pay for, also brings up the question of how much money is being spent to give access to all students and faculty who request it.

The Kansas policy will remain in effect until July 1, 2030 unless it is reauthorized, amended or extended, and districts and accredited nonpublic schools must submit their adopted plans to the Kansas State Department of Education by July 1, 2027. Beginning in the 2028-29 school year, parents or guardians must receive access to their school's technology-use plan and acknowledge it before students receive access to school-issued devices. The Daily Princetonian's Editorial Board questioned how the implementation of AI in an academic environment will affect students' ability to learn and how it reflects on the university's fundamental mission of education. The Signal reported that it is important for colleges to consider whether aligning themselves with AI companies would truly be beneficial for all their students. The articles leave open how much money Princeton is spending on the pilot and how each Kansas district will implement its plan.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms use restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips despite US sanctions
stories.Summary:
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed that sanctioned Chinese entities obtained restricted Nvidia AI chips despite strict United States export controls. This discovery occurred as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation on Thursday following a scandal involving an alleged extramarital affair. The U.S. government is investigating Huang's ties to Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former Megaspeed executive. She is suspected of collecting intelligence for Beijing and helping Chinese clients acquire restricted chips through her connections. This situation has been described as an AI industry earthquake that has attracted intense attention from outside observers.

The National Supercomputing Center Jinan, also called Shandong Computing Center, won a bid for RTX 5090 and DGX Spark products. On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network announced Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd. won the bid. The winning bid price was RMB 148,500, which is approximately 22,000 US dollars, for one batch of AI equipment. The RTX 5090 uses Blackwell architecture with 32GB GDDR7 memory, while the DGX Spark uses the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. These products were solicited by the Jinan center as of June 2026 despite its status on the entity list.

The U.S. Department of Commerce is responsible for the entity list and stated that Jinan supported Chinese military modernization. Chris Tseng of the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said controls rely heavily on corporate self-compliance. He noted that licenses are required to transfer regulated items to controlled entities even through legitimate third-country distributors. Sylvia Chen of DSET stated that third-party enterprises bear legal liability if they illegally transfer controlled products within China. She explained that the Bureau of Industry and Security has only fifteen export control officers worldwide to verify end-users.

DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group are affected because their models show evidence of using restricted Blackwell GPUs. Unemployment Labs, led by Will Depue, found that these firms used B200, B300, GB200, and GB300 chips for training. The report analyzed six systems released since April, including DeepSeek V4-Flash, V4-Pro, Kimi K3, K3.1-Pro, MiniMax M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash. These companies may have skirted controls by renting compute in Southeast Asia or using smuggled chips via workaround routes. The report estimates that 12,000 Blackwell GPUs were deployed, with costs reaching roughly 500 million US dollars.

The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with the Qilu University of Technology in China. The U.S. Department of Commerce placed the center on the entity list in April 2021 for national security reasons. Broad export restrictions on advanced computing chips to China began in 2022, following the initial listing of the center. Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology was an Nvidia Elite Partner until it was sanctioned by the U.S. on April 11, 2024. The Trump administration allowed limited exports of H200 chips but did not approve exports of Blackwell or Rubin chips.

Nvidia must now investigate the sales and ultimate flow of products if Qiyuan Jiasu inherited Sitonholy's original business operations. The U.S. government continues to investigate the role of Alice Huang in smuggling advanced AI chips into China. It remains open whether the RTX 5090 cards purchased were the original version or the China special edition. Researchers cautioned that they did not verify the physical location of the chips or prove specific export law violations. The articles leave open whether Qiyuan Jiasu is simply a shell company used to bypass the Entity List.

stories.Headline: Romance novelist Coral Hart writes 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI since 2025
stories.Summary:
Coral Hart, a romance novelist who began with Mills & Boon, has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI since 2025, earning "high six figures," as reported by the Guardian on 14 November 2026. She self-published full-time from 2015 after three years of self-publishing dark romance. She sells her books on Kindle Unlimited, which pays only per pages read. She told the Guardian she can write 10,000 words a day by herself. She said she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace with the algorithm.

A study awaiting peer review, led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. In March, Hachette withdrew the romance novel Shy Girl over evidence that author Mia Ballard used AI. This year's Commonwealth short story prize winner, Jamir Nazir, was accused of using AI after readers ran his story through Pangram, a leading AI detection program. Pangram later concluded that since 2025, four regional winners were likely to have used AI. In July, agents for debut novelist Jerry Falade withdrew from a $2m (£1.5m) book deal after he was accused of using AI.

Hart said a bad writer or storyteller will not get a good book out of AI and that you still need to understand craft, structure and what a reader wants. She said AI is not taking the human out of the equation but taking the friction, time and business blocks out of the way. She said the minute someone discloses AI use they get death threats, get called names and are ousted. She advises other authors not to disclose AI use unless it becomes a legal requirement. After she talked to the New York Times earlier this year she was doxed and faced death threats.

Falade wrote an essay saying writing by non-native speakers or in "culturally unfamiliar" English is more often treated with suspicion and suggested the accusations against him may be tinged with racism. He wrote that he hasn't seen this kind of investigative zeal directed at white authors accused of using AI. Every writer at the centre of these AI scandals has been an author of colour. In May, Steven Rosenbaum, who is white, was found to have accidentally inserted fabricated quotes into his book The Future of Truth: How AI Reshapes Reality when he used AI, which he disclosed in the acknowledgements, and his book wasn't withdrawn. Hannah Bowman, chair of the Association of American Literary Agents' AI special committee, said it's a shame all of these things are getting addressed so publicly and that there needs to be a fair and thoughtful process.

Last year a class action lawsuit involving around 500,000 titles won a $1.5bn settlement from the AI firm Anthropic for alleged use of writers' work without consent, and other similar lawsuits are ongoing. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers, Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan, to promise they will "never release books that were created by a machine," and the publishers did not promise. Last month the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien's novel was struck off the Goncourt Academy longlist, France's most prestigious literary prize, after social media users ran his novel through AI detection software. He denied using AI to write his novel but admitted to plagiarism in some of his other writing, including a short story he wrote more than a decade ago, and his publishers Boréal dropped him in late October. Academic research estimates Pangram is at least 95% accurate at detecting AI-generated writing, with a near-0% rate of false positives.

Thad McIllroy, a publishing expert and author of The AI Book Revolution, said he was surprised when Shy Girl was cancelled and that the cancellation was partly his fault after he ran it through Pangram and approached the New York Times. He said he felt so stupid when Hachette cancelled it because it never occurred to him that would have been the response. He said publishers need to be "brave" and publish extensive AI policies outlining how they use the technology in-house and what authors are and aren't allowed to do. Liz Gately, a New York-based book scout, said many agents have started recommending their writers not send documents as PDFs and save multiple drafts in case they are subject to AI accusations. Falade has recently signed with a new agent.

stories.Headline: Five nonprofits sue Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX to halt all AI development
stories.Summary:
A coalition of five nonprofit online safety and advocacy groups filed suit in the San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, alleging that artificial intelligence systems are already autonomously breaking the law and causing harm. The suit demands an immediate injunction to halt all further development of AI, particularly ChatGPT, Grok, Muse, Gemini, and Claude. The plaintiffs allege that several Big Tech companies violated the Business and Professions Code of California's Unfair Competition Law, specifically the section prohibiting unlawful business practices. The plaintiffs allege that under the code AI is a public nuisance, defined as anything injurious to health or an obstruction to the free use of property that interferes with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by an entire community or neighborhood. The suit was filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and Future Tech Insights, doing business as The Alliance For Secure AI, and names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX.

The complaint quotes Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX and has invested heavily in AI, as saying AI has the potential of civilization destruction. The complaint also quotes Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, as saying AI developers do not understand how their own AI creations work. Amodei also said AI could enable a group to carry out a large-scale biological attack, which he called a grave threat to U.S. national security in a hearing before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee. In June, the mother of a Canadian child who died by suicide filed a suit against OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT encouraged the girl's suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in the same month, alleging ChatGPT harmed children by providing information to school shooters, advising children on self-harm, and intentionally addicting children.

Attorney Matthew Platkin, who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs, said in a press release from Public Citizen that it is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race. Platkin said they are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm. The plaintiffs wrote that no other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products, much less ones that could kill us all, as inevitable. A group of state attorneys general filed a similar suit in October. In July, Illinois passed legislation holding AI developers responsible for safety risks, including a requirement for audits of safety issues by independent third parties, with publication of the results.

The University of Missouri's Career Center directs students looking for work to Handshake, which describes itself as the career network for the AI economy and which Mizzou partnered with in 2017, guaranteeing students an account and access to the platform's job network. Handshake AI pays around $60 million monthly to students from over 1,600 institutions and connects other AI companies to Mizzou students for remote projects usually lasting between two weeks and six months. Handshake AI's entry-level positions offer hourly rates of $17 to $30, while positions requiring years of extensive experience can offer over $100 hourly, and last academic year Handshake AI paid out $117,174 to Mizzou students. According to Cynthia Singleton-Diaz, student coordinator I at the Career Center, 1,623 Mizzou students have submitted 2,710 applications to jobs posted by Handshake AI. Mizzou junior Prajit Rayaprolu was an AI trainer for seven months last school year, attracted by the work's simplicity, flexible hours and a friend's recommendation, and while he felt fairly compensated he eventually stopped seeing the job as sustainable for his well-being.

Amanda Nell, senior student services coordinator at the Career Center, said there are lots of networking opportunities and skill-building opportunities and that they invest and innovate the platform on a pretty regular basis. During his time as an AI trainer, Rayaprolu sorted online photos and evaluated AI-created images and videos for realism, and he was also tasked with writing lengthy prompts and having conversations with AI assistants to complete tasks. Researchers investigating this digital labor use the term human computation to describe human labor in tasks AI struggles with, including sorting data, labeling pictures and letting AI know when it makes a faulty or unfair association, and this labor was extensively used in the early development of AI models such as ChatGPT, Llama, Claude and Gemini. In the early development of AI models much of this training was done by workers paid below their local minimum wages, often contracted through middlemen who assigned digital labor as gig work, and the most popular subcontracting platform for human computation, Amazon Mechanical Turk, was discontinued Sept. 30, 2026, with workers paid per task as independent contractors at rates as low as 1 cent. Peter Mueser, an emeritus professor and specialist in labor markets, said this work was valuable to outsourced workers, as in any growing industry workers are attracted only when jobs pay higher wages than their alternatives.

Elizabeth Lucas, an AI fellow at the Missouri School of Journalism, said these are all things that are part of bigger systems that have really broad impacts and that it is incumbent upon us as humans to think about that and recognize that and see ourselves as one small piece of a very large system. Hayden Hawkins, an undergraduate student representative on the AI standing committee, said in an email that it is imperative that artificial intelligence companies ensure their workers receive fair pay, maintain worker safety and consider data privacy when sourcing their labor. The median wage on MTurk was significantly above the World Bank's $3-per-day international poverty line, though The Journal of Collaborative Computing and Work Practices reported that other crowdsourcing platforms pay around or below this line. Companies hoping to employ students at Mizzou for human computation are vetted by the Career Center before they can be connected with students, and the Career Center works with Mizzou's standing AI committee and UM System Associate Director of AI Justin Palozola to ensure operations on Handshake align with system policy. MU Career Services notifies potential users of Handshake that users are responsible for evaluating the safety, wages, working conditions and other aspects of job listings.

Rayaprolu said he stopped working for Handshake AI after it created a large Slack channel where it frequently posted new guidelines, limited the hours employees could work per day and started to require employees to complete quizzes before they could start working for the day. On Oct. 1, AI trainers working on Project Hedgehog, the project Rayaprolu had spent the majority of his time working on, were required to pass an assessment, and if they did not pass they risked being removed from the project. Rayaprolu also mentioned a four-level rating system for every output he submitted, with scores matching bad, acceptable, good or excellent outputs, and he said that if your scores dropped below two you weren't allowed to access any assessments. The process some social scientists call human computation was first used on a large scale by a Stanford professor, Fei-Fei Li, and as generative AI development progressed companies used this process to test their models and create training data, often sharing methodologies and employees. The extent to which human computation is currently being used in the training of AI systems is unclear, as many tech companies view pre-training strategy as a trade secret that provides them with a competitive advantage, and the future of human computation is unpredictable as AI is increasingly used to evaluate and learn from its own inputs.

stories.Headline: Insight launches an Agent Store with 15 AI solutions across 14 countries
stories.Summary:
Insight Enterprises announced the global launch of its online Agent Store on November 13, 2026, in Chandler, Arizona. This new catalog provides clients with proven AI solutions and integrated services to deliver measurable business outcomes. The company aims to help organizations move AI from isolated pilots into production to generate long-term value. These offerings allow companies to achieve value in as little as days or weeks rather than months. Insight deploys these solutions independently or as part of broader AI transformation initiatives using its managed services.

The store is available across 14 countries, including the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Insight added six new agentic offerings to its library, which now contains 15 total solutions after nine were introduced earlier this year. New tools include Quote Advisor for pricing and inventory, NDA Review Agent for legal policies, and Parts Order Assist for catalog search. Other solutions include TokenScope for managing AI spend and Insight AI Flight Academy for training and change management. These tools were first developed for internal use in security, finance, and legal departments to improve overall efficiency.

Jack Azagury, the president and CEO at Insight, stated that the company acted as Client Zero to build a repeatable approach. He noted that Insight has driven over 90 percent internal AI adoption and knows how to scale agentic AI responsibly. Azagury believes combining the Agent Store with consulting expertise empowers clients to move from hype to how with AI. He emphasized that this combination helps enterprises deliver measurable results and generate value across every industry. The CEO believes this approach helps organizations face the pressure to move AI into production.

Culligan International became the first external client to implement Flight Academy to build AI fluency across its global workforce. Laura Walsh, the global CIO at Culligan International, said that people, not technology, are what truly transform a company. She stated that it is the responsibility of the company to arm teams with the best tools for the future. Walsh noted that prioritizing AI education allows her teams to leverage AI productively and responsibly through a functional champions network. Culligan uses Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure, and Microsoft Fabric while incorporating governance for cost and responsibility.

Insight Enterprises is a global Fortune 500 technology company and a leading Solutions Integrator that has operated for more than 35 years. The company utilizes a network of over 6,000 partners and experts worldwide to provide end-to-end IT capabilities. It is listed on the NASDAQ as NSIT and is rated as a Forbes World’s Best Employer. The company is also recognized as a Great Place to Work and a Fortune World’s Best Workplace. Insight helps clients solve technology challenges by combining hardware, software, and services.

The Agent Store is now generally available to help clients automate core business processes and promote internal AI adoption. The company will continue to provide consulting, implementation, and managed services to support these AI transformation initiatives. The articles do not state how many more agents Insight plans to add to the library in the future. They leave open whether other external clients will follow Culligan International in using the Flight Academy platform. The text does not specify the exact pricing models for the various agents available in the store.

stories.Headline: Bank of America survey finds 72% of Americans plan to avoid AI for holiday shopping
stories.Summary:
A Bank of America survey released in November 2026 found that 72% of Americans do not plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025. The 23-percentage-point jump was reported by Fortune on November 14, 2026, in a story by Tatiana Sataua. Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop, and Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart, Meta's Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. The survey suggests a gap between the industry's ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it.

Among those who do not plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they do not trust AI recommendations. The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year. It also found that 63% said they base their spending strictly on their own budgets rather than what friends or family spend. The survey found that 17% plan to use AI to compare prices or deals, 14% for gift ideas or inspiration, and 7% to write messages or cards, and respondents could select more than one use. Bank of America said it asked the AI shopping question the same way in both years, though the survey only measures intentions, and the bank does not have data showing whether shoppers are actually using AI less.

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America, said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending. She told Fortune that some of last year's curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and that we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue. She said gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they are giving. She said that same budget-focused approach may be shaping how consumers use AI and social media to shop. Monfared's comments were reported by Fortune in its November 14, 2026 story.

Colleen Kirk, a professor of marketing and management at New York Institute of Technology, told Fortune that the hesitation may have less to do with what AI can do than what shoppers feel they lose by using it. She said gift giving is a very personal act, and gifts, especially to close family and friends, are given from the heart. In her research studying consumer psychology, she has found that consumers can feel guilty when they use AI to write heartfelt messages because the words no longer feel entirely their own. She said that effort creates what researchers call psychological ownership, or the feeling of having a personal stake in something, and that using AI can take away this sense of ownership. Kirk said AI may have a more natural place in the less personal parts of shopping, such as finding coupons, comparing prices, or buying groceries and household supplies, and she suggested consumers come up with their own ideas first, then turn to AI to help narrow their options.

Amazon.com Inc. is considering building a global product database to minimize buyers' use of Google and other websites, according to a Reuters-reviewed internal document reported by GuruFocus on November 13, 2026. The initiative, called World Product Graph, gathers data on internet-sold products, including items Amazon does not sell, so shoppers can compare goods, find newer models, and buy without leaving Amazon. The project would merge manufacturer and retail website data, Coke and Bayer are sharing product information, and Amazon is considering a Procter & Gamble experiment. Amazon's Alexa for Shopping, formerly Rufus, may benefit from the project, though the assistant's replies were wrong or partial and the service was pricey, according to an internal paper. Amazon refuted the paper, stating that its shopping assistant is 97% accurate worldwide, and the concept included an October 2027 start date that Amazon has not verified.

Amazon said the paper is preliminary and may not reflect its current goals, and retail sales and advertising income depend on Amazon's shopping traffic. The Reuters-reviewed document reflects competition from AI shopping bots that can compare and buy across sites. Fortune reported that it is an awkward moment for tech companies betting that shoppers will eventually trust AI to do more than recommend products, including making purchases on their behalf. Kirk said research has found that people feel more ownership over an outcome when they generate their own ideas before using AI. She said some consumers may decide that letting AI handle the less personal tasks is a worthwhile trade-off, and that consumers might just decide it is worth it to give up a little bit of ownership of the process in exchange for getting more time for those special emotional connections with the humans they love.

stories.Headline: Arizona judge releases DUI suspect after trooper uses AI in arrest report
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, an Arizona judge released Anthony Edward Rene Quidera, a DUI suspect, after the arresting officer used artificial intelligence in his arrest report. Maricopa Superior Court Judge Daniel Fenzel ordered the release during Quidera's initial court hearing. The police report about the October 29 arrest ended with a disclaimer that it was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. Quidera, 37, was accused of driving 100 miles per hour on Interstate 10 in Phoenix around 12:33 a.m. The unidentified Arizona Department of Public Safety trooper alleged he smelled an intoxicating beverage and found several open containers in the car.

Quidera was arrested on October 29, 2026, on charges of DUI, exceeding the posted speed limit by more than 20 mph, and possession of an open container in a vehicle. The arrest occurred on eastbound Interstate 10 after a trooper observed a vehicle traveling over 100 mph in a 65 mph zone near 79th Avenue. The trooper alleged Quidera's Dodge Charger failed to maintain its lane and drove on the left median shoulder. The trooper reported bloodshot, red, and watery eyes and six out of six cues on a Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus test. Quidera allegedly declined a preliminary breath test, and several open containers were found on the passenger floorboard.

Fenzel said the use of generative AI affected the case and that the court was unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations were authored in whole or in part by AI. Fenzel said the court was therefore unable to determine probable cause at this time. Fenzel added that his order did not mean the DUI case could not go forward in the future. Raul Garcia, who represents DPS, said the department uses Truleo to help draft reports. Garcia said AI tools may be used only as an aid, the trooper remains the author and is responsible for accuracy, and a supervisor must review reports before they become part of the official record.

Garcia said troopers must review drafts against body-worn camera footage and other evidence, verify times, names, locations, and actions, and correct errors. Garcia said troopers may not use the tool until they complete Department-approved training. Attorney information for Quidera wasn't available, and a spokesman for the Arizona DPS declined to comment. The case comes weeks after the Arizona Court of Appeals ordered Gabriel Paul Horcasitas to be resentenced for his manslaughter conviction. The September 30 appellate ruling found that the judge's consideration of an AI video so prejudiced Horcasitas as to render the sentencing procedure fundamentally unfair.

In October, ABC15 reported on Phoenix PD's trial program with Axon's Draft One AI report writing software. In September, an appeals court threw out a 10-year sentence in a road rage shooting after determining an AI victim impact statement influenced the sentence. The Arizona Supreme Court has declined to ban judges from using AI. The Court asked the Arizona Steering Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts to recommend rules or administrative orders for clear standards on responsible use of emerging AI technologies. The Court asked the Committee to send a status report by March 1, 2027.

An arraignment date was scheduled for Thursday, and Maricopa County Justice Court records show Quidera was eventually charged and scheduled to be arraigned on November 12th. The ruling raises new legal questions about how AI-generated or AI-assisted police reports may hold up in court. The articles do not say what happened at the arraignment or how the case was resolved. The articles do not give the outcome of any further probable cause review. The articles do not identify the trooper or provide Quidera's attorney information.

stories.Headline: Samsung breaks ground on HBM packaging plant in Asan and moves opening to June 2028
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics broke ground on a high-bandwidth memory packaging plant on November 12, 2026, to expand the artificial intelligence server supply chain. This new facility is located at the Onyang campus in Asan, South Korea, and focuses on advanced packaging for HBM memory. The company is accelerating the project to meet the rising demand for server memory used in various modern artificial intelligence systems. Construction of the plant is the first project under a regional industrial mega-project program led by the South Korean government. The facility is now scheduled to begin its operations in June 2028, which is one year earlier than previously planned.

The project requires 6 trillion won, or 4.48 billion dollars, for construction and 40 trillion won for advanced equipment installed in stages. Total medium and long term investment for the Onyang expansion is roughly 46 trillion won, including three clean-room floors of 31,000 square meters. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is investing 8 trillion won in package-substrate production for central processing units and graphics processors in the Chungcheong region. Samsung Display is investing 67 trillion won in an 8.6-generation production line for information technology displays within the same South Korean region. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will also spend 4.27 trillion won in South Korea and 2.51 trillion won in Vietnam for flip-chip ball grid array substrates.

The South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced the groundbreaking and said it would coordinate permits for the new projects. The ministry also stated it would help the company secure necessary transport infrastructure along with essential water and electricity for the site. Samsung said during its third-quarter earnings announcement that it had already completed negotiations over HBM supply volumes for the year 2027. The company noted that customers continued to seek additional supply, which prompted the decision to move the plant opening date forward. Samsung Electro-Mechanics disclosed in September that its substrate expansion for high-performance computing applications will start mass production in September 2028.

Customers seeking more high-bandwidth memory are affected by packaging capacity, which is a separate manufacturing step from producing the memory wafers. Advanced packaging connects stacked memory dies with processors and other components, making it a critical constraint on the finished HBM supply. The expansion at the Onyang campus was prompted because the existing Samsung campus in Cheonan has run short of available space. This makes Onyang a major production base for advanced AI memory to support the needs of various global technology customers. The project is part of a broader investment program across the Chungcheong region to bolster the regional industrial economy.

The South Korean government identified 112 materials, components and equipment suppliers with additional investment plans totaling about 23.6 trillion won around the projects. HBM combines stacked memory dies with high-speed connections for AI accelerators, which are essential for the operation of AI servers. The government is supporting these industrial projects by managing the infrastructure and permits required for the massive scale of the investments. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is focusing its substrate investments on AI servers and other high-performance computing applications to meet the growing market demand. These efforts are part of a strategic move to secure the supply chain for artificial intelligence hardware in Asia.

The investment for the Onyang plant will be deployed over several years, with equipment spending following the initial construction in phases. Samsung has not disclosed the planned output capacity of the new plant or the specific customer commitments for the facility. The company has also kept the expected financial returns from the 46 trillion won investment private at this current stage. It remains open whether the increased capacity will fully satisfy the rising demand for AI server memory by June 2028. The articles do not state the specific names of the customers who are seeking additional high-bandwidth memory supply.

stories.Headline: Vercel Labs releases UI SDK with over 50 interface behaviors for coding agents
stories.Summary:
Vercel Labs released UI SDK, an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents, on November 12, 2026. The library is headless, meaning it ships behaviors rather than finished components, and agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. It contains more than 50 behaviors, 51 component modules in the repository and 6 npm packages at version 0.1.0-beta.1. The packages are published under Apache-2.0 and run on any modern browser without a GPU, requiring React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC or plain Web Components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop and the ARIA they need, all living in @ui-sdk/core with thin adapters rendering it in each framework.

Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive, which declares state, an API and slots, and each framework then renders the primitive with createParts so one behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Setup is a prompt pasted into an agent that installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md pointing to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas, and prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. The agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders, where agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions and agent.act() runs an action such as renaming a project with setValue. Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions, change callbacks receive source "agent" and can cancel the change, and tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP.

Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on one project-settings task in which the agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved, with both agents using Sonnet through Claude Code and the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs: tool calls fell from 16 to 5, a 69% drop, text read fell from 39.8k to 6.8k characters, a drop of 83%, time fell 61% from 41 s to 16 s, and cost fell 56% from $0.073 to $0.032. Vercel cautions that the figures should be treated as directional, because the sample is one task and the browser-tools run used a different component library, and it does not name the Sonnet version. The project site explains the idea with a Select: instead of handing the agent a finished Select, you hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead, and those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox or a component nobody has designed yet. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery whose Clear button appears only when there is text, and pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev per the skill listing.

stories.Headline: Majority of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors in BCG survey
stories.Summary:
A Boston Consulting Group global survey found that 61 percent of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors. This study was conducted during July and August 2026 and included 9,914 consumers across 10 different countries. The findings were published on November 15, 2026, by Sumit Jha in a report about the consumerisation of health care. This shift shows that more people in India are using digital technology to seek medical information instead of professionals. The report indicates that patients are increasingly seeking greater control over their treatment decisions, convenience, and their healthcare expenditure.

India scored 66 out of 100 on the Healthcare Consumerization Index, ranking second behind China, which scored 72. The United Arab Emirates ranked third at 63, while Brazil followed in fourth place with a score of 62. In India, 60 percent trust digital health information as much as professional advice, which is 19 percentage points above average. Additionally, 78 percent of Indian respondents want more control over treatment choices, and 73 percent want control over costs. Around 68 percent expect retail level convenience, and 58 percent view medicines as common consumer goods.

Chris Meier of BCG stated that consumer patients are reshaping rules to expect more intuitive, responsive, and personalized health care experiences. He is a managing director and senior partner who co authored the report on the consumerisation of the health industry. Sabrina Kristic, also a managing director and senior partner, noted that health care decisions are more complex than cosmetics. She warned that these decisions have potentially serious consequences, even if products blur the line between health and lifestyle categories. Both authors believe that providers must now balance patient choice and convenience with clinical quality and patient outcomes.

Millennials were most likely to prefer instant AI answers at 52 percent, followed by Generation Z at 47 percent. Baby boomers showed the lowest preference for these digital tools, with only 25 percent choosing AI over a doctor. Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that AI mass surveillance can cause chronic anticipatory stress and physical sickness. Vulnerable groups, including undocumented immigrants, may avoid clinics or pharmacies due to a fear of persecution from surveillance tools. These experts argue that AI surveillance is a structural determinant of health that can create avoidable health inequities.

The BCG report explains that digital platforms can improve information access but may also expose users to fragmented services and misinformation. People with limited digital literacy or confidence may be excluded from these new digital first models of health care. Meanwhile, the New England Journal of Medicine highlights how private companies now control the data ecosystems used for surveillance. Traditional surveillance required human oversight, but AI can continuously comb through social media, financial transactions, and geolocation records. This allows private actors to analyze vast amounts of personal data and share it with government agencies.

Next, healthcare providers must find ways to balance transparency and convenience with equity and the overall quality of patient outcomes. Clinicians can help by documenting patient fears about data usage to provide evidence for policymakers and various legal litigators. Some states, including Washington, Nevada, and Connecticut, have passed laws to extend privacy protections to certain consumer health data. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with Palantir and ICE. The articles leave open whether AI will serve population health or become a driver of structural harm.

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI could make cancer and Alzheimer's relics of the past within a decade
stories.Summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a 42-minute investor roadshow video released on Nov. 10 that artificial intelligence could transform medicine enough to make cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease and mental illness relics of the past in less than a decade. He described the possibility of an age of miracles in which scientific advances help humanity solve problems unresolved for generations. His comments came as Anthropic increases its involvement in biological research and pharmaceutical development. In an Oct. 27 company update, Anthropic said it had established research partnerships with six organizations developing medicines and had begun its own drug discovery programs.

The company said some research focuses on rare childhood diseases, including forms of muscular dystrophy, though it acknowledged most of this work remains in the preclinical stage and has generally not reached human testing. Amodei's optimism reflects a broader belief among technology executives that AI could substantially shorten drug development, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has also discussed accelerating pharmaceutical research. During a fireside chat at the Indian Institute of Science, Hassabis said developing a new drug typically takes about 10 years and suggested AI could potentially reduce that to months or even weeks. He cited AlphaFold, DeepMind's protein structure prediction system, which has generated predictions for more than 200 million protein structures.

Hassabis acknowledged that predicting protein structures is only one part of developing medicines, since researchers must also establish whether compounds work as intended, have appropriate properties and avoid harmful side effects. The pharmaceutical industry has been considerably more cautious, and Jeff Leiden, executive chairman of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, challenged claims that AI could independently produce effective medicines at the pace technology leaders suggest. Speaking to The Wall Street Journal, Leiden said Vertex had evaluated approximately 50 AI companies using a database of 10,000 drug compounds, and none had independently generated any working drug. He dismissed as complete nonsense claims that AI could cure 90% of human diseases within seven years.

Drug development involves several stages beyond identifying promising compounds, and potential treatments must undergo laboratory research, preclinical studies, human clinical trials and regulatory review to establish safety and effectiveness. AI could help researchers identify promising targets, analyze biological data and improve the efficiency of early-stage discovery, but these capabilities do not establish that the technology can eliminate the scientific uncertainties involved in developing treatments. For now, Amodei's prediction reflects the possibilities he sees in AI rather than an established medical timeline. Whether those expectations translate into treatments for some of the world's most challenging diseases within a decade remains an open question.

stories.Summary:
Cisco reported quarterly results that beat estimates on both revenue and profit, and it raised its forecast for AI infrastructure sales to hyperscalers to $9 billion for the fiscal year, more than double the prior year, according to an article by Brian Sozzi published on Yahoo Finance on November 13, 2026. Cerebras, an AI infrastructure company, also beat on sales and earnings, and it guided to a core gross margin of 47% to 49% and sales of $310 million to $330 million for the current quarter, against analyst estimates of a 42.1% margin and $271 million in sales. CoreWeave beat on the top and bottom lines earlier in the week and pushed back on the view that it would need high-yield debt to fund growth, and its shares rose 22% over the week. The article tied the moves to an AI trade that may be back after an early fall slumber, in a week dominated by coverage of scandals involving Jensen Huang, whom the article described as having lost the CEO role at Nvidia.

Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins said the company was executing against its strategy and seeing growing demand as customers invest in infrastructure for what he called the AI or SI era, and KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel said the stock looks attractively valued after earnings. Barclays analyst Tom O'Malley said key customers remain intact and Cerebras is adding new hyperscalers, but the industry is seeing delays across many providers that are slowing the OAI ramp and could push the timing of revenue. O'Malley added that the stock had fallen 33% over the past month against a 14% drop in the SOX index, and he said clearing the bear case and adding customers should more than offset industry-wide concerns about those delays in the near term. Cerebras shares rose 13% in premarket trading on Friday, and the article said the new focus should be on execution of OAI and the new customer set.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said the company already has a robust pipeline of customers competing for capacity, and at current pricing levels the 2027 renewals would generate approaching $4 billion of incremental annualized revenue with no additional capex required. Intrator said that figure grows to nearly $10 billion of annualized incremental revenue when 2028 renewals are included, and he said that if data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute would become scarcer and GPU pricing might stay higher for longer. The article listed related headlines, including one saying Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed a CoreWeave stock plunge and said he was optimistic, and another saying CoreWeave stock sank as the resignation of Jensen Huang rippled through the AI trade. The article gave no further detail on the Huang resignation beyond those references and the mention of scandals.

stories.Headline: South Africa and China plan an AI talent development and innovation center
stories.Summary:
South Africa and China plan to establish an Artificial Intelligence Talent Development and Innovation Center to expand their scientific and technological cooperation. Deputy Minister Nomalungelo Gina and Vice Minister Zhang Guangjun discussed this initiative during a working visit to Wuhan, China. These talks occurred from November 10 to 13, 2026, during the China-Africa Innovation Cooperation and Development Forum. The partnership aims to strengthen Africa's digital sovereignty and develop homegrown technological expertise to influence the global AI revolution. This bilateral effort seeks to bridge digital skills gaps and increase innovation capacity through collaborative research and practical applications.

The proposed center requires a visit from a Chinese technical expert team to South Africa to conduct an initial technical assessment. It focuses on deepening institutional cooperation between universities, research organizations, and industries in South Africa and China, specifically in Wuhan and Pretoria. The partnership prioritizes the digital economy, artificial intelligence, and new energy, as agreed upon in September 2024 in the new era. South Africa also identifies biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, and fifth-generation mobile technology, known as 5G, as priority areas for further engagement. These initiatives follow the elevation of relations to an all-round strategic cooperative partnership between the two nations in September 2024.

Deputy Minister Nomalungelo Gina stated that the center will help South Africa address digital skills gaps and strengthen overall innovation capabilities. She expressed excitement that this cooperation benefits people and ensures that science remains relevant to both of the national economies. Vice Minister Zhang Guangjun noted that relations have grown steadily under the leadership of Presidents Cyril Ramaphosa and Xi Jinping. Zhang explained that President Xi emphasized pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation in the digital economy, AI, and new energy sectors. Both officials stressed the importance of turning scientific research into practical solutions that improve people's lives and economic development.

The project affects African scientists, engineers, and young researchers who need opportunities to design and develop emerging technologies for the continent. Local universities and entrepreneurs are expected to benefit from pathways that make research commercially and socially useful for the public. The initiative could eventually serve as a platform for broader regional cooperation, benefiting researchers and institutions across the entire African continent. However, the center must ensure that research priorities reflect South African development needs rather than external geopolitical or commercial interests. AI applications should specifically target healthcare delivery, agricultural productivity, industrial modernization, education, and the efficiency of various public services.

The partnership builds on a substantial history, including the 1999 Science and Technology Agreement which produced over 240 joint research projects. South Africa possesses advanced research institutions by African standards but still faces a digital skills gap that could constrain global competitiveness. China has emerged as a major global force in telecommunications, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, and artificial intelligence over the last decade. African countries are increasingly seeking partnerships that provide investment and research expertise instead of simply importing finished foreign technological products. This shift reflects a broader transformation in international economic relationships as Africa seeks to avoid becoming just a data source.

Next, the Chinese technical team will visit South Africa to perform the preliminary assessment needed to start the center's construction. The partnership must prioritize responsible AI development, which includes cybersecurity, transparency, data protection, and the establishment of ethical governance frameworks. Success will be measured by the number of skilled African professionals developed and the strength of local research institutions. The articles leave open how the center will secure sustained investment and find the qualified instructors needed for its programs. It remains unclear how the two nations will establish clear mechanisms for cooperation between academic institutions and private businesses.

stories.Headline: AWS releases a free local cloud emulator built entirely by AI agents
stories.Summary:
AWS released AWS Emulator, a free local emulator of its cloud APIs, on November 11, 2026. The tool lets developers run a stand-in for more than 200 AWS services on a laptop, a dev server or in CI, with no AWS account and no service fee. The AWS CLI and SDKs talk to it instead of AWS, and code does not need to change. The unusual part is that autonomous AI agents wrote and reviewed all of its code, and the team has not written or reviewed any code itself.

The emulator is built from 438 AWS API models, with one Rust crate per service. It runs on Linux x86_64 and aarch64 through RPM or Debian packages, or in Docker on macOS and Windows with a 2 GiB memory limit, while source builds need 100 GB of free disk. In release v1.0.322 it passed 24,243 of 42,857 scored fidelity tests, or 56.6%, and 49,810 of 68,007 individual steps, or 73.2%. AWS KMS scored best at 93.9%, Amazon SQS reached 89.8%, and AWS CloudFormation was worst at 15.8%. Cross-service workflows passed 2,752 of 6,569 tests, or 41.9%, and unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 NotImplemented.

The project began with a prompt to Kiro, which returned a passable Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. AWS then split the work across three teams of agents: test writers derive scenarios from the public Smithy API models and check each against real AWS, issue finders replay those tests and file failures, and fixers take one issue each and submit a patch. Every patch passes a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity, and several security agents run adversarial reviews. Matthew Goldberg reports hundreds of concurrent agents fixing thousands of issues a day, and the release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools with CodeCommit as the agents' repository.

The articles compare the tool with LocalStack, Moto and Floci. AWS Emulator is free under CC0 1.0, covers 200+ services, needs no vendor token and serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 by default. LocalStack has free non-commercial and paid plans, Moto is free under Apache-2.0, and Floci is free under MIT. SK hynix shares fell 3.03% to 1,216,000 won at the November 13 regular-session close in Seoul, according to GuruFocus. The Kospi finished 0.98% lower at 5,290.53. The swing reflected a market caught between two stories, the article says.

Early buyers bet that AI memory demand does not depend on who runs Nvidia. Voices quoted by Korea JoongAng Daily argued that leadership uncertainty at Nvidia is separate from memory demand. Nvidia kept its fiscal third-quarter report on November 17, with the board saying customer commitments and the product roadmap should continue without interruption. SK hynix is described as the purest Korean play on Nvidia's accelerator volumes, so its swings track Nvidia's guidance more tightly than Samsung's. GuruFocus gives the stock a GF Score of 98/100, combining profitability, a strong balance sheet and momentum.

Its GF Value is 1,408,258.33 won, putting the shares 13.7% below that estimate with a "Modestly Undervalued" label. The next test is Nvidia's revenue guide on Tuesday and any change to its HBM ordering pattern, according to the article. stories.Headline: Entrepreneurs build custom AI agents for recurring tasks as United Airlines bans bots from bookings
stories.Summary:
Entrepreneurs are building custom AI agents to handle recurring jobs like reporting, marketing, video editing, and scriptwriting during November 2026. Ben Angel wrote that these tools help business owners focus on running their companies instead of managing every small task. Meanwhile, United Airlines announced a ban on AI agents making customer bookings during the same week in November 2026. This move aims to stop bots from handling sensitive data or making unwanted transactions that bog down the process. These events show a divide between business internal productivity and the external consumer market for automated agent services.

The United Airlines ban addresses privacy concerns and the risk of exposing sensitive data to third parties during the booking process. Bots cannot acknowledge that travel bags lack explosives, which might violate rules from the Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration. A 2026 G2 survey of 1,019 B2B decision-makers found that 66 percent of organizations had agents in production. DoorDash launched a texting feature for agents in September, but CEO Tony Xu reported only several hundred total orders. Uber reported that only 500 out of 320 million trips during the Halloween week were placed by AI agents.

Ben Angel says entrepreneurs should identify a worthwhile first job for an agent without trying to automate an entire business. He warns that moving too quickly can create a new bottleneck instead of removing one, turning agents into more work. Angel suggests using the free AI Success Kit and his book, The Wolf is at The Door, to survive AI. He believes that the work an entrepreneur chooses to hand off first could make a difference against faster competitors. He explains that agents differ from chatbots and that the first assignment is more important than it might seem.

United Airlines believes that allowing bots to check safety boxes on a person's behalf could violate federal aviation and transportation rules. Brian Chesky, the CEO of Airbnb, told investors that traffic and bookings from Muse and Instinct are very non-material. These companies and their customers are affected by the friction and inconvenience that injecting an AI agent can create. Many consumers do not want agents handling their business, and businesses do not like dealing with these automated intermediaries. The reports suggest that most people are simply not using these tools for their daily consumer transactions.

The articles state that AI agents were supposed to be game-changers by handling bookings, support, and services twenty four hours daily. This would theoretically free humans for other work, but the actual adoption in consumer commerce has been very low. Some entrepreneurs are already using these tools to manage the steps between a business idea and a final result. This process includes research, content creation, editing, distribution, and reviewing what worked for a specific marketing campaign. The background shows a shift where agents move from experiments into real workflows for some B2B decision-makers.

The next step for entrepreneurs is to learn how to turn tool access into useful support for their specific businesses. They must find recurring jobs that drain time, such as reporting and scriptwriting, to avoid falling behind their competitors. The articles leave open whether consumer adoption will increase or if agents will remain irrelevant to everyday cash flow. It remains unclear if the non-material traffic seen by Airbnb will grow or if the Uber figures will stay low. The future of AI agents depends on whether they remove bottlenecks or simply create new jobs for humans.
