stories.Headline: Central Washington University survey finds 57% of English teachers report worse attitudes since AI arrived
stories.Summary:
Fifty-seven percent of high school English teachers in a new Central Washington University survey said their attitude toward teaching has gotten worse since AI showed up. Faculty in CWU's College in the High School program ran the survey in May 2026. They asked 222 math and English teachers about their attitudes toward AI, their school's policies, the training they'd had, and how they and their students use the tools. Josh Aubol, Steve Stein and Peter Klosterman wrote up the results in a commentary published by the Washington State Standard. The same English teachers were also far more confident than their math colleagues about teaching students to use it responsibly: 45.5% against 24.4%.

Clear AI policies and useful training both went with more confident teachers. Neither had any measurable link to how teachers felt about their jobs or how worried they were about cheating. Integrity concerns produced the widest gap: 83.7% of English teachers reported them, against 54.9% of math teachers, a difference of nearly 29 points by simple subtraction. Yet English teachers were also more than twice as likely to require students to experiment with AI in class, 34.1% against 14.6%. In roughly one-sixth of survey responses, teachers said they had moved all writing to in-class, pen-and-paper work because of integrity fears.

The authors offer a plain explanation: large language models turn out convincing prose, sometimes with factual errors, and are often reported to stumble on simple calculations. So the tool works well in the English classroom and poorly in the math one. On that reading, the split comes from the tools themselves and says little about which department is better prepared. For English teachers, the authors say training should mean designing assignments AI can't easily write and building responsible AI use into the writing process. For math teachers, it means using AI to save time on prep work, such as rewriting story problems or redesigning learning tasks.

Nancy Weinstein, founder of an edtech company, noted in THE Journal that the country's two largest school districts adopted one-year AI bans. She also cited American Psychological Association guidance that warns against blanket rules: the APA says an edtech tool's effect depends on what it asks the learner to do, how adults bring it into the classroom, the child's age and needs, and what the tool replaces. A Wharton and Penn working paper, "Generative AI Can Harm Learning," tested AI with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey, as Knowledge at Wharton reported. Students using an open ChatGPT-style interface scored 48% better than a no-AI control group during practice, then 17% worse on the exam once the AI was taken away.

A version with teacher input that gave hints rather than answers raised practice scores 127% and matched the control group on the exam. Stanford's SCALE Initiative published an update to its review of K-12 AI evidence on November 10. Seth Walker, Lily Fesler, JP Martinez Claeys, Chris Agnew and Susanna Loeb counted only randomized trials and quasi-experimental studies that met a strict standard for causal evidence. The review now holds 52 strong causal studies, up from 20 in March 2026.

Of 868 papers added to the repository from October 2025 to June 2026, 32 met the causal bar, and 5 new student-facing studies were run in U.S. K-12 settings, against none in March. The research repository held 1,686 papers at the end of June 2026, up from 818. Earlier research found AI cut lesson-planning time without hurting quality, and AI-drafted suggestions helped teachers give more and better feedback in the same amount of time. But one new study found that giving teachers an AI support tool lowered student motivation and confidence.

The SCALE team cautions that most papers in its repository are unreviewed arXiv preprints, and that its findings shouldn't be treated as broadly generalizable across U.S. K-12 schools. A principal investigator at University of Hawaii Maui College showed students how he used AI tools, then required them to explain when and why they used AI on each assignment, with AI for research allowed and AI for answering exam questions not. The National Applied AI Consortium, run with Miami Dade College, Houston City College and Maricopa Community Colleges, has reached 3,500 educators at 480 colleges in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, and is offering 19 free online faculty training events through mid-November. SCALE plans its next full review for spring 2027, and the CWU data covers attitudes and confidence but not outcomes.

stories.Headline: Marcos orders national AI governance framework and creates council to oversee it
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered the adoption of a national Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework to guide the development and use of AI in the country, putting guardrails around a technology that is rapidly changing how people live and work. Under Executive Order 131, which the President signed on November 12, he also created the National Artificial Intelligence Council to coordinate and monitor how the framework is carried out. The council will bring government agencies, the private sector, academe, and civil society together so that the country's AI ambitions do not turn into a case of technology moving faster than the rules. The framework adopts a whole-of-government approach, and its priorities include responsible innovation, stronger public institutions, public trust, better data governance, expanded AI infrastructure, and strategic investments.

The National Artificial Intelligence Council will be chaired by the Executive Secretary, with the secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development serving as vice chairperson. Its members will include the heads of the departments of Information and Communications Technology, Science and Technology, Trade and Industry, Finance, Education, Labor and Employment, and Budget and Management, along with the Commission on Higher Education chairperson and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority director general. Marcos will also appoint a private sector representative to the council, and that person will serve a three-year term. The AI Governance Framework has four interconnected components, namely ethics and principles, standards and assurance, a risk-based policy toolkit, and enabling resources.

The framework requires AI development and use to uphold transparency, explainability, security, safety, accountability, integrity, human-centricity, fairness, equity, and sustainable development. The council must review the framework at least once every two years, or sooner if major technological, regulatory, or market developments warrant an update. The articles do not say what penalties or enforcement steps will follow if agencies or firms fail to comply with the framework. They also do not say when the council will first meet or when the private sector representative will be named.

stories.Headline: Pax Christi members urge Ed Miliband to back a treaty on AI weapons as Humphriss warns of ethical risks
stories.Summary:
Aaron Humphriss, founder of the Montini Center for Peace and the Common Good and a Pax Christi member, told an online Pax Christi presentation on AI, security and peace on Thursday that humanity may have already crossed a red line on lethal autonomous weaponry. The gathering of some forty Pax Christi members and supporters heard that there is evidence such weapons have already been used in international conflict, despite there being no treaty to govern their use. Pax Christi England and Wales, Pax Christi Scotland and other Christian leaders co-signed a letter to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband urging him to support international negotiations towards a legally binding treaty on autonomous weaponry at the upcoming review of the convention guiding armaments. The letter was sent ahead of the CCW Review Conference at the United Nations in Geneva this week, running from 16 to 20 November, which the representatives described as a decisive moment. The letter warned of the grave moral implications of lethal autonomous weapons systems, meaning weapons guided by artificial intelligence that can decide to kill, and said machines must never be trusted with moral judgements like the decision to take a life.

Humphriss said lethal autonomous weapons pose ethical and existential challenges, and that as well as being prone to error, such as miscategorising and striking a civilian vehicle instead of a tank, their use blurs the line of moral judgement and responsibility. He explained that should a weapon misfire and kill civilians as well as enemy combatants, it is unclear whether moral responsibility lies with the programmer, the government that authorised its use, or the soldier who activated it. The Holy See has called for a moratorium on development of such weapons until a treaty is in place, and Pope Leo dedicated a section of his encyclical on artificial intelligence, Magnifica Humanitas, to the use of AI in warfare. Pope Leo has dedicated Peace Sunday 2027, which will fall on 17 January, to the theme of disarming technology and serving peace. Speaking after the event, Humphriss urged Catholics to contact their local bishop and communicate their concerns, and The Tablet understands that the Bishops' Conference of England and Wales is considering putting together some form of guidance around AI.

He urged people to have these conversations with people in their parish and bishops, to send a letter or write an email, and to see what they can do in their parish or start something themselves or with their parish council. Humphriss and other Pax Christi members, including Emmanuel Fissehsa, who spoke to the online gathering about the legality of lethal autonomous weapons, had previously presented on AI and warfare at The Tablet Festival in July. Humphriss said the buzz in the room following that presentation indicated that Catholics with an interest in social justice were clearly interested and passionate about the moral use and regulation of AI. Pax Christi England and Wales has been involved in conversations about the ethics of AI in warfare for almost a decade, including collaborative work with the organisation Drone Wars in 2012 and 2013 around the use of unmanned vehicles in warfare.

stories.Headline: Northwestern professors set individual classroom rules for student AI use
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 9, MIT Distinguished Professor of Computing Sam Madden visited the University of Wisconsin-Madison for a fireside chat with Mike Swift, associate dean for academic affairs in UW-Madison's College of Computing & Artificial Intelligence, at Morgridge Hall in Madison, Wis. The Daily Cardinal reported the discussion on Nov. 12, 2026. The Daily Northwestern reported on Nov. 13, 2026, that Northwestern professors were considering ways to incorporate AI into classrooms while combating difficulties it poses to traditional assignments. Weinberg History Prof. Susan Pearson said Weinberg allows instructors to tailor individual AI policies to their classrooms. French Prof. Margaret Dempster directs the French Language Program at Northwestern.

Weinberg's AI policy bars students from using AI-generated work as their own, but individual classroom policies are up to the instructor if clear guidelines are set. Liz Trubey, Weinberg's associate dean for undergraduate academic affairs, said the lack of a unified policy is partly because administrators consider faculty "best positioned" to write their own policies. Pearson said faculty and graduate students cannot use AI to grade undergraduate student work. Dempster said new French learners are completely prohibited from using AI tools, intermediate learners are heavily restricted and advanced learners may use AI with instructor permission. All French students must fact-check generated information and cite the tools used and the manner of use.

McCormick Prof. Neelesh Patankar, who teaches mechanical engineering, said McCormick faculty are "exploring" its AI policy and considering the goal of education and how AI should be taught. Patankar permits and encourages AI on homework and asks students to share their prompt or conversation with him. McCormick Prof. Samir Khuller, who chairs the computer science department, permits AI on homework but tells students they must explain their answers if prompted. McCormick Prof. Sara Sood, associate dean for academic programs, does not permit AI in her introductory programming course and turns it on at the end of the quarter after fundamentals are learned. McCormick and SESP Prof. Michael Horn said his introductory Python class, which previously had a blanket ban, is now more lenient and requires students to cite how they used AI tools.

Medill Prof. Michael Spikes said students must obtain explicit permission from their instructor to use AI and must explain how it was used. In his class "Journalism 201-2: Fundamentals of Video Journalism," Spikes adopted a blanket policy under which students work collaboratively with AI as an "accelerator" for work they already know how to do. Pearson said students sometimes admit to using AI for editing rather than idea generation, which she said homogenizes voice. Dempster said AI work "lacks emotion, it lacks humor, it lacks the creativity" and the vocabulary mistakes students make.

Madden said students increasingly use AI on assignments instead of spending time in office hours or working with peers. Madden co-directs two MIT research groups, the Data Systems and AI Lab and the Data Systems Group. Madden said coding agents make him feel "like a superhero" because work that would have taken weeks can be done quickly. Madden said some students are not developing confidence in their own thinking and feel uncomfortable answering without consulting AI first.

Madden said there probably needs to be more emphasis on hands-on group projects where students come into labs and classrooms and work on things together. In one MIT course variation, students will use AI tools to build complex systems while learning software engineering principles like specification and interface design. Madden said he expects 50 of the 250 or 300 students who would take the normal variation of the class to take the AI variation next semester. Madden said the approach is intended to let students do projects previously too difficult to complete within a semester, adding "Maybe it'll fail.

Maybe it won't." Pearson said the danger with AI is "cognitive surrender," or handing over critical thinking tasks, and said she would rather see spelling and grammatical errors because they signify human writing. Khuller compared learning to mountaineering, saying a helicopter to the top reaches the destination but does not make you a mountaineer. Sood said students with academic integrity violations gave up when they struggled and that AI capitalizes on students with low confidence.

Articles.Title: To AI or not to AI? NU professors talk AI usage in the classroom - The Daily Northwestern

stories.Headline: Lafayette council rejects permit for Plush Syndicate AI bar and mayor suspends new downtown bar applications
stories.Summary:
The Lafayette City Council rejected a conditional use permit for Plush Syndicate, a planned downtown venue at 201 Jefferson Street that became known online as an “AI bar,” KLFY reported on Nov. 13, 2026. The council’s decision came after the venue drew attention for its proposed automated drink system. Following the council’s decision, the administration of Mayor-President Monique Blanco Boulet suspended taking new conditional use permit applications for downtown bars. Officials said the suspension would last while they evaluate the approval process. The decision sparked a broader debate regarding public safety, crowd sizes and licensing procedures for nightlife establishments in downtown Lafayette.

Quintin Borel, the proprietor of Plush Syndicate, envisioned the venue as more than a standard bar, proposing a space that included food service, social areas and office space. Borel explained that the technology behind the concept was widely misunderstood, stating that the system acts as an inventory control unit to dispense drink components for human bartenders to mix. He said the setup did not employ robots to serve patrons. “There was no robot going around pouring your drink,” Borel said, adding that the inventory control unit dispenses into what the bartender then mixes and provides. Following the permit refusal, Borel noted he is contemplating proceeding with other elements of his business plan without the bar operation.

Borel expressed annoyance that the council’s ruling focused heavily on alcohol service rather than the property’s proposed alternative uses. Downtown Development Authority CEO Kevin Blanchard said the organization’s opposition was not focused on the technology or on Borel personally. Instead, Blanchard cited concerns about the venue’s proposed 325-person capacity and the difficulties large crowds congregating outside bars past midnight pose for law enforcement and nearby businesses. Blanchard also raised concerns about permit wording that might have allowed venue capacity to expand without an additional public hearing. He emphasized the DDA’s duty to protect existing downtown investments and achieve a better balance between nighttime entertainment and daytime commerce.

“So I’m here for the 770 businesses that are already downtown, that already have their permits to operate and then have put a significant amount of investment in,” Blanchard said. Blanchard noted that the DDA is not advocating for a permanent prohibition on new bars. Instead, he expressed a desire for bar operators, downtown business owners, law enforcement, city officials and members of the public to participate in discussions regarding methods to enhance safety while permitting ongoing investment. A schedule for those community discussions has not been established. Blanchard described the outcome as a chance to reexamine district policies, saying it was not how any of them would have preferred to get here but calling it a hopeful kind of reset.

City leaders and business representatives expressed concerns over the scale of new venues and their potential impact on the surrounding district. The articles state that all facts in the KLFY report were gathered by journalists employed by KLFY. Artificial intelligence tools were used to reformat information into a news article for the website, and the report was edited and fact-checked by KLFY staff before being published. The KLFY report carried a posting time of Nov. 13, 2026, at 05:47 PM CST and an update at the same time. The KATC headline reported that the Lafayette City Council rejected the proposed new downtown AI bar.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Northeastern Junior College advisers urge formal AI policy and training for students and faculty
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Nov. 12, Northeastern Junior College Advisory Council members and faculty members met for a roundtable discussion about how the college should approach AI and what employers look for related to it. The meeting was reported by the Sterling Journal-Advocate on Nov. 13, 2026. Before the discussion, new council member Lonnie Knudsen, Sterling Fire Department EMS Commander, was introduced. The college’s new vice president of academic affairs, Ayelet Zur-Nayberg, was also introduced. She comes to NJC from the Colorado Community College System.

NJC President Mike White opened the discussion with statistics on how students and businesses use AI. EAB, a national higher education consulting company, found that in 2024 the top three uses for Generative AI among two-year college students were generating ideas, therapy/companionship and specific searches. In 2025 therapy/companionship moved to the top use, followed by organizing their life and finding purpose. EAB also found men age 20-29 spend just under seven hours a day alone, not including sleep, and women of the same age spend closer to five hours a day alone. Approximately 66% of small businesses now report using AI, up from 23% in 2023, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, 2026.

White said the college wants to educate people about AI use for companionship and finding purpose. NJC recently started a campaign called “ChatGPT Is Not a Therapist,” with posters around campus. White said student services has been working to pull people into group settings and get them out of their dorm rooms. Camille Rose, vice president of student services, said the guidance coordinator has seen more students counseling this fall than in several previous years. Rose suggested the college look at how to teach students the ethical side of AI.

Council member Jayce Maker said he knows many people who use AI in their day jobs. Knudsen said he uses it to summarize his emails at the end of the month for an accurate report to his chief. Knudsen said firefighters have figured out how to use it to do coding, and their upcoming Christmas video is all done using AI. Rose said she knows someone who uploads construction plans and what used to take days now takes minutes, with AI providing lumber materials needed, drawings and measurements. Approximately 35% of employers rank AI fluency as their number one hiring priority.

Lisa LeFevre, vice president of administrative services, said NJC has opened up Google Docs to all faculty and some are embracing it. White said the college’s philosophy professor created an AI Socrates that gives students the Socratic method and asks a question back. Approximately 61% of college students use generative AI at least weekly, up from 42% one year ago, according to Tyson Partners, 2026. Zur-Nayberg said she completed a 40-hour course about incorporating AI in the classroom covering responsible use, ethical use and disclosure of use. She said the college needs to move from literacy to proficiency in AI, meaning prompting correctly, recognizing limitations and checking facts.

Zur-Nayberg will facilitate two faculty sessions about AI at NJC’s inservice at the beginning of the winter semester, one on Google Notebook. She said an instructor can upload a syllabus and ask AI to create a quiz, and she has used it to create a tutor notebook for her students. Knudsen said the fire department must find AI platforms that work around protected health information and confidential information. Research shows about 30% of AI references are fake and about 30% are real but taken out of context. Knudsen said someone submitted a resume clearly done with ChatGPT and not proofed, so he did not hire that person.

Maker said it is important to teach young people how to effectively use AI as they enter the workforce. Knudsen said the technology should be embraced, but there needs to be understanding of its impact on individuals. Council member Karla Rosas encouraged the college to develop a formal policy and formal training, with universal training offered to all students and faculty. Rosas said it is important to remind people that AI does not have judgement yet and to balance thoughts about AI with making sure you are not under-resourced. White closed by thanking participants and said AI “is a big issue” and the college has to move sooner rather than later to prepare students.

stories.Headline: Jonathan A. Powers examines the impact of artificial intelligence on human dignity and faith
stories.Summary:
Jonathan A. Powers wrote an article on November 14, 2026, regarding the impact of artificial intelligence on human life and faith. He argues that while AI is a new technological development, it does not fundamentally change the basic human condition. The author references a 1948 essay by C. S. Lewis titled On Living in an Atomic Age to provide historical context. He notes that the United States and China are currently competing for leadership in AI development for military and economic advantages.

Powers suggests that Christians should avoid simplistic answers and instead focus on moral responsibility and careful judgment. He believes that human dignity comes from being created in the image of God rather than from productivity or intelligence. The author notes that AI can produce misinformation, reinforce biases, and threaten privacy, which affects employment and national security. He warns that efficiency provided by technology is not the same as true human communion.

The text explains that previous inventions like the printing press and the Industrial Revolution also disrupted society and created new ethical questions. It describes how humanity has historically developed laws and practices to navigate overwhelming technological changes. The article asks if AI will make people less willing to seek answers through effort and how it shapes human desires. It leaves open the question of how to balance safety and innovation during international competition.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Things That Matter Most

stories.Headline: Agnikul invests ₹510 crore in Andhra Pradesh orbital data centre facility
stories.Summary:
Agnikul Cosmos plans to invest ₹510 crore in a dedicated facility in Andhra Pradesh to manufacture orbital data centre units. The Indian space-tech startup signed an agreement with the Andhra Pradesh state government at the CII Partnership Summit 2026. The facility will be set up in Tirupati district. The company aims to provide a platform for semiconductor majors to build graphics processing unit stacks. These stacks can be directly integrated with the upper stage of its launch vehicle.

The initiative aims to integrate AI computing hardware with the company's rocket upper stages. Srinath Ravichandran, cofounder and chief executive officer of Agnikul, said this will be the first such facility in Asia and one of the first globally. Bengaluru-based NeevCloud has signed on as Agnikul's first customer. Agnikul will launch an orbital AI data centre module developed by NeevCloud's AI SuperCloud platform into space. Space-based data centres offer advantages including access to solar power, natural cooling, and the ability to handle high-density AI workloads.

Ravichandran said the company expects its next launch during the first half of next year. This launch will showcase its reusable launch vehicle and unique upper-stage technologies, he said. Agnikul's Agnibaan SOrTeD mission lifted off in May 2024 from India's first privately operated launchpad at Sriharikota. This mission demonstrated technologies including the company's 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine. The company aims to be Asia's first and a global pioneer in orbital data centre manufacturing.

stories.Headline: US voters pass local measures to restrict AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Americans voted in midterm elections to slow the expansion of artificial intelligence through forty local ballot measures in ten states. These measures seek to tighten restrictions on data center construction and received overwhelming public support from the voting population. In thirty of these electoral contests, the measures to limit development won more than 70 percent of the total vote. This public anxiety grew as a 2026 Pew Research Center survey found 52 percent of Americans were more concerned than excited. Only 9 percent of those surveyed felt more excited than concerned about the growing use of AI in daily life.

The restrictions target data centers because they consume enormous amounts of water and electricity while concentrating power in a few companies. Public fear involves job displacement, surveillance, loss of privacy, and the rising tide of deep fakes and misinformation. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday amid a potential espionage scandal that fueled public anxiety. This event highlighted the competition between the United States and China, which are both considered to be AI superpowers. America currently leads in computing power due to advanced chips, but China is catching up fast in AI models.

Yasheng Huang, a professor at MIT Sloan School of Management, explains that the world faces two converging economic shocks. He describes the China Shock as the massive increase in Chinese exports to the United States in the early 2000s. This surge contributed to a sharp decline in American manufacturing and the loss of over two million regional jobs. Huang argues that the AI Productivity Shock could further widen the gap between global supply and demand. He suggests that AI might enable companies to increase output without raising the income of ordinary citizens.

Economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson originally coined the term China Shock to describe these effects. Shoumitro Chatterjee and Arvind Subramanian argue that low and middle income countries are the real casualties of this new shock. These nations in Southeast Asia and Latin America see local factories shuttering due to a flood of cheap goods. This process provokes a wave of new anti dumping cases and tariffs as workers lose their primary source of income. The affected populations depend on manufacturing for their jobs and their opportunities for upward social mobility.

China produces more than 80 percent of global solar panels and double the current global demand for batteries. Official statistics show urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 had a record unemployment rate of 18.9 percent in August 2025. The national minimum basic pension was raised to only 143 yuan a month in 2025, which is about one dollar. Labor compensation relative to total economic inputs in industry, agriculture, and utilities dropped from 21 percent in 1987 to 15 percent. China holds 35 percent of global manufacturing capacity but accounts for only 11 percent of global consumption.

The imbalance remains unsustainable because China's household consumption is 39 percent of GDP compared to 68 percent in America. Low domestic consumption forces Chinese businesses to sell products abroad at cutthroat prices to maintain their own production levels. This strategy risks undermining future demand for Chinese products if businesses fail and unemployment rises in the rest of the world. The articles leave open whether AI will follow the pattern of earlier automation by eventually creating new types of work. It remains a matter of debate if AI will generate wealth without creating corresponding jobs for the global workforce.

Articles.Title: The China Shock in the AI Era

stories.headline_source: The China Shock in the AI Era

stories.Headline: Researchers integrate AI into neuroscience to study brain connections and memory
stories.Summary:
Researchers are integrating artificial intelligence into neuroscience, and the results will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience. The human brain contains approximately 86 billion nerve cells that form trillions of connections. To understand this complex system, neuroscientists are turning to AI tools that can process vast amounts of data and simulate brain processes. Insights into the brain also inspire improvements to computational models, and the applications show potential to advance research and affect people's lives. The work includes several specific projects and tools.

Studying artificial neural networks and fruit flies revealed a shared learning principle for forming flexible, robust memories, according to Guanglong Sun of Tsinghua University. A new free, open-source AI tool lets neuroscientists with no programming experience analyze complex genomic data by asking questions in plain English, according to Vivek Swarup of the University of California, Irvine. The neuroscience community is also developing data standards collaboratively to break down data silos and streamline workflows, according to Oliver Ruebel of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Satrajit Ghosh, a computational neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the event moderator, said the bidirectional connections between neuroscience and AI go back a long time. He uses neuroimaging and machine learning to create predictive models for human health.

He said the findings show how AI can help researchers understand the relationships between brain structure and function. He also said the work helps appreciate the complex connections between genes, environments, learning, and behavior across species. The articles describe the research as showing transformative potential, and they present the work as a summary of findings ahead of the meeting. They do not say what happens after the presentations or announce further steps. The material is provided for information purposes only and is subject to copyright.

stories.Headline: F5 field CISO Joshua Goldfarb argues AI harms security by weakening creativity and critical thinking
stories.Summary:
Joshua Goldfarb, Field CISO at F5, wrote a SecurityWeek column published on 14 November 2026 asking whether AI is making the security industry worse. He described being asked to speak at an event but declining because of a prior speaking commitment on the same day. About a week later, someone who had agreed to speak in his place approached him to ask for content for the talk. Goldfarb said the person sent him what amounted to a prompt rather than asking for guidance, tips or lessons learned from experience. He concluded that AI is harming the security industry and illustrated this through several examples.

Goldfarb listed creativity, humor, emotion, messaging, communication and critical thinking as areas where AI causes harm. He said AI can rapidly curate and search through a tremendous amount of data but is no substitute for human creativity. He argued that humor is a soft skill that has helped security professionals operate more effectively for decades. He said AI can mock, mimic or play to certain human emotions but does not feel those emotions, which makes it feel insincere by nature. He said that at a large security conference, quite a few people noted that most companies on the expo floor were saying all the same things.

Goldfarb said marketing departments use buzzwords to attract attention and drive engagement, and that far too many marketing teams use AI to generate content. He said the resulting messaging is unremarkable, non-unique and woefully unprovoking. He said language has become less precise and less clear in recent years, and that AI is definitely one of the forces contributing to this decline. He said security is highly dependent on timely and accurate communication, and that AI is weakening communication skills and damaging the profession. He said critical thinking is fading because many people in the profession look to AI to perform analysis, offer suggestions and organize their thoughts.

Goldfarb said he has steadfastly refused to use ghostwriters throughout his career and writes everything that has his name on it. He said he has continued this principle into the AI era and will not use AI to suggest topics, do research, organize his thoughts, create an outline or develop any content. He said this may be old-fashioned but strengthens the quality of the content he puts out. He said security professionals should resist the temptation of AI for certain things and that everyone will benefit in the long run. He said he previously served as VP, CTO of Emerging Technologies at FireEye and as Chief Security Officer for nPulse Technologies until its acquisition by FireEye.

Goldfarb said he earlier served as Chief of Analysis for the United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team, where he built and ran network, endpoint and malware analysis and forensics capabilities. He said he worked as an independent consultant helping enterprises build network traffic analysis, security operations and incident response capabilities. He said he consulted for clients in both the public and private sectors at strategic and tactical levels. He said he is currently Field CISO at F5 and is on Twitter as @ananalytical. The article carried related headlines including one on AI changing attack speed but not security fundamentals and one on rethinking application security for the AI era.

The article listed other items including Amplifier Security emerging from stealth with an AI copilot and human-in-the-loop automation. It listed people on the move, including Jaya Baloo appointed CISO at Cohere and Jensen Huang resigning as President and Chief Executive Officer at NVIDIA. It said Sean Sweeney has become CIO of the City of Charleston, South Carolina. It said passkeys are better than passwords but not enough, and that attackers will look for opportunities around the authenticator. It said to keep patch management pipelines primed in case another round of Citrix NetScaler patches get released soon.

Articles.Title: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity?

stories.Headline: Eastern Illinois University student government appoints two members to university AI task force
stories.Summary:
Eastern Illinois University’s Student Government Association appointed two of its members to a university task force focused on artificial intelligence at its meeting in Booth Library on Wednesday, according to The Daily Eastern News. Student Body President Mason Tegeler and Executive Vice President Sam Erwin were named to the AI, Pedagogy and Classroom Engagement Task Force, which is meant to address student concerns about the use of AI in the classroom. The task force is overseen by Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs Holly Farley and includes student leaders, faculty leaders and administration. Its stated goal is to create a statement on what the university wants to do concerning AI in the classroom.

Tegeler said he joined the task force because he felt a value statement was not enough, and he plans to tell the meetings directly when he believes more should be done. He said that if the university regulates its use of AI, it can be a leader in the country in that field, and that higher education is already being shaped by AI. He also said the university should focus on the value of having a professor, asking how the value of one-on-one interactions with expert professors teaching material they created can be restated in an increasingly technologically driven world. Erwin said he joined to pressure those on the task force and to make sure students’ voices are heard, saying the stakeholders have forgotten that their greatest asset at Eastern is students and that his intention is to remind administration who the stakeholders really are.

The Student Government Association will hold a town hall about AI on Dec. 3 that will be separate from the discussions at the faculty senate and the task force. Speaker of the Senate Megan Fox presented the election timeline for the speaker election, since her graduation in December will leave her seat vacant. An elected senator must be nominated by a member of the association to become speaker, and nominations will happen during the Nov. 18 meeting. Nominees will give platform statements at that meeting, and the speaker will be sworn in at the final meeting of the semester on Dec. 2.

stories.Headline: Jeff Margulies uses Claude AI add-ons to streamline Good Earth landscaping operations
stories.Summary:
Jeff Margulies, owner of Good Earth landscaping and maintenance in Aspen, began using Claude AI about a year before the article, around late 2025, to streamline his business. The bots work inside AI add-ons he built to enhance his company software, Aspire. His brother, who once ran a custom software development business with around 30 offshore developers, helped him find where AI could apply. Margulies bought into Good Earth after a career in finance, and in 2018 the company had just a handful of employees. Good Earth has grown by a factor of six under Margulies, who is 41 and a father of two, and now employs 60 to 70 people.

The company does weekly maintenance and mowing, garden care, native plant management, restoration, irrigation and full landscape installations. Employees must use camera phones or tablets to snap pictures and clock in and out of each project, and project managers update the clock-in information daily to gauge efficiency against labor estimates. Margulies says he is exploring around a dozen different AI initiatives, including some for daily use, such as creating renderings for clients and handling back-end processes and analysis. Margulies said that at a smaller scale you can get away with a lot by keeping your eye on everything, but with 60 or 70 people you need everyone aligned and aware of issues early enough to correct them. He said the company needs clear processes so everyone knows what to do and can plan to deliver on promises to clients.

He said real time job cost information lets the company see labor and material costs immediately and compare them to budget, so it can intervene quickly instead of redoing a whole project. He said Good Earth has historically under-leveraged data on worker output, which limited its ability to manage crews and make good labor-management decisions. Margulies said the deeper the company goes with the AI he is building, the more encouraged they are that they can remove the paperwork, reporting and data crunching that tend to be weaker skill sets in the industry. He said there is still lots to figure out to use the technology to its full potential, but he is reaping benefits. He said the bots are going to help Good Earth keep growing.

stories.Headline: AI industry faces trust crisis over safety breaches and financial instability
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry is currently facing a four-pronged crisis of trust involving safety, politics, finance, and leadership. This collapse follows a period where top executives were given a mandate to police their own companies. The situation escalated after President Trump announced a voluntary safety accord with AI leaders just six weeks ago. Now, a combination of security breaches and political shifts threatens the rapid ascent of the technology. These converging problems have turned the industry from a Silicon Valley darling into a target of public skepticism.

The political landscape has shifted as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January and introduce numerous AI bills. During recent midterm elections, voters rejected data center measures in 40 out of 41 cases across the United States. This populist rebellion led to the defeat of incumbents like Texas Governor Greg Abbott and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio. Meanwhile, the safety crisis intensified after a July breach at OpenAI's Hugging Face and reports of unvetted agents accessing American bank accounts. OpenAI and Anthropic are currently investigating tens of thousands of security incidents that could potentially endanger humanity.

Financial instability has hit the sector as investors question if massive spending will ever yield high returns. Nvidia stock fell 13 percent this week and has lost nearly 25 percent of its value since late October. This decline followed reports linking founder Jensen Huang to a suspected Chinese spy and his subsequent resignation over personal affairs. Additionally, the projected valuation for Anthropic's initial public offering is roughly 600 billion dollars lower than previous investor expectations. These leadership scandals highlight the risks of concentrating immense power in the hands of a few executives.

Lawmakers now seek greater accountability and plan to bring powerful AI executives to Washington to testify about their operations. Some populist Republicans are also eager to join Democrats in establishing strict guardrails for the industry. Public perception has soured further through critical films like Musk and The Social Reckoning, which target figures like Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg. The industry is now experiencing a reckoning that mirrors the previous downfall of social media companies. Future developments will depend on how these titans handle the incoming flood of legislation and security demands.

Articles.Title: AI's four colliding crises

stories.headline_source: AI's four colliding crises

stories.Headline: AI tools help new ransomware groups claim nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer
stories.Summary:
Ransomware and data extortion attacks have risen sharply in recent months, according to researchers who track the field, as reported by WIRED on November 14, 2026. Some researchers put the number of alleged attacks posted on leak sites, where groups name supposed victims, at nearly 3,000 over the summer. By some estimates that is a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring. Researchers say the volume always moves up and down somewhat, but attacks have stayed consistently and worryingly high in recent years.

Cynthia Kaiser, a former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research at the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon, said most of the recent increase came from international attacks, while the United States was steadier but still high. She said the international rise is the really new part and is partly fueled by AI. Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, said AI is being used more heavily in parts of the attack chain, such as writing better phishing emails and handling negotiations, but successful groups are still largely run by humans. He said the heavy experimentation with AI means this could change, and change quickly.

Halcyon's analysis says around 111 ransomware groups claimed attacks between July and September this year. The Gentlemen, Qilin and Akira have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations, with smaller groups and new actors in their shadow. ReliaQuest's analysis found one new group, Global Secret Group, claimed 48 victims, more than half listed on the same day, while another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest, said the growth happened because AI has accelerated these actors, essentially letting them go out and start their own groups. Tirado said his team identified the person behind one new group as an inexperienced teenager who made more than $800,000 in under two weeks, and he declined to name the teen publicly.

Researchers told Kernel Panic they have seen more lone-wolf operators instead of people tied to traditional ransomware-as-a-service providers. Kaiser said more actors are using AI to try to strike out on their own, with abilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code and even compromise other groups' remote-access tools for backup access to a victim. She suspects many of these upstarts may surge and then burn out, because they lack the knowledge and resources of established groups. Liska said the number of attacks Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total for 2025, but the number involving encryption may actually fall year over year.

stories.Headline: Realtor Nathan White says AI lets agents hide knowledge gaps and urges disclosure rules
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, Realtor and instructor Nathan White wrote in Real Estate News that AI is helping real estate agents sound more knowledgeable than they are. White said he has used AI to run comps and watched it deliver wrong information in the same confident voice it uses when it is right. He said that because he has sold more than 500 homes, he can tell when the tool is wrong, while many agents leaning on AI the hardest do not have that experience. He wrote that AI is obscuring knowledge gaps rather than erasing them.

White described a proposal that NAR's board took up in June. It would have required Realtors to disclose when they lack the knowledge, information, or skills about a property type or geographical area to protect and promote their clients' interests. The Executive Committee recommended defeating it, and the board voted 497 to 356 to send it back to the Professional Standards Committee, which had already worked on it for two years. White cited NAR's latest technology report saying 23% of Realtors use AI daily, and he said other surveys suggest usage may be much higher. He also said NAR's AI policy kit for brokers states that agents and staff are fully accountable for the AI content they use.

White wrote that AI does not hold a license and agents do. He said he serves on the Ohio Realtors grievance and mediation panels, where every name on a complaint belongs to a person. He recalled that during the board meeting a director from Florida said that once an agent discloses a knowledge gap, trust with the consumer is lost. White disagreed, saying clients lose faith after finding out an agent never had the knowledge or skills to promote their interests. He said the standard should be to use AI as a tool, check its outputs against a reliable source, and tell the client first if you cannot explain the answer yourself.

White noted that NAR's directors met again in New Orleans the previous week. One session focused on the risks of using AI and the importance of maintaining consumer trust and compliance, but the knowledge gap proposal was not discussed. White wrote that he hopes that changes. He said he does not know if the proposal's wording is right and would want it fixed before panels like his had to apply it, but he argued that requiring agents to be honest about what they do not know is not what puts consumer trust at risk.

stories.Headline: UC Berkeley researchers use AI to identify heart signals that predict sudden cardiac death
stories.Summary:
Researchers at UC Berkeley discovered a hidden warning signal in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death. This AI-powered discovery was announced on November 14, 2026, and published in the journal Nature. The system outperformed conventional screening methods by identifying thousands of people at risk of fatal heart malfunctions. It uses artificial intelligence to recognize subtle electrical patterns that doctors might otherwise miss in ordinary scans. This technology could potentially save thousands of lives by recognizing vulnerable patients before a fatal event occurs.

The AI was trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms collected in Sweden over a period of six years. Researchers then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from Taiwan and a San Diego hospital system. The system identified a group with an annual death rate of 7 percent, compared to 4.6 percent using traditional measurements. It works with ordinary EKG images already collected in medical centers, requiring no entirely new type of medical test. This approach helps identify people who would be classified as low risk under existing medical guidelines.

Ziad Obermeyer, the study's lead author and an associate professor at UC Berkeley, led the research team. He stated that AI is exciting because it allows doctors to make better decisions for their patients. Obermeyer noted that many deaths are preventable if doctors can figure out who needs a defibrillator in time. He explained that assembling the necessary datasets took approximately 10 years of work. He also mentioned that accessing such medical data is a major reason why clinical AI is rarely used.

Sudden cardiac arrest affects more than 300,000 people in the United States every year, including healthy young athletes. Unlike heart attacks caused by blocked blood flow, cardiac arrest results from a failure of the heart's electrical signals. About 90 percent of people who experience this outside a hospital die within minutes without immediate intervention. Current screening focuses on how much blood the heart pumps, but two-thirds of resulting defibrillator implants are never used. Many high-risk individuals die unexpectedly because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The research involved contributions from two organizations established by Obermeyer called Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. The team linked Swedish EKG scans to death certificates to teach the AI to recognize deadly patterns. They compared these patterns against healthy individuals and patients with known heart risks to refine the algorithm. The study highlights how AI can uncover biological patterns that have resisted conventional medical approaches. This process allows scientists to investigate medical mysteries by identifying combinations of spikes and waves in recordings.

Obermeyer is now collaborating with medical systems in the United States, Taiwan, and Sweden to introduce the algorithm. High-risk patients may be offered a patch that continuously records electrical activity to provide more biological clues. A website has been created for people to provide personal information to learn about their own risks. Researchers still need to understand what specific changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns the AI recognizes. The articles leave open how these new insights will specifically change the way physicians prescribe implanted defibrillators.

He said explaining an idea is the fastest way to find the gaps in it. The announcement gave no other numbers or dates beyond the November 14, 2026 date and the reference to the next day.

Levin is the author of the newsletter and wrote the announcement himself. He described his view that the fastest self-learners work in a loop of trying, observing, and adjusting. He also said that thinking probabilistically about what a model will produce turns that loop into real skill. He said explaining an idea to someone else is the fastest way to find the gaps in it.

stories.Headline: Professor Sean Cho Ayres uses social interaction to rehumanize college classes for an AI-augmented workforce
stories.Summary:
A millennial college professor implemented a framework to rehumanize the classroom for students facing an AI-augmented workforce. This educator focused on interpersonal social skills during an English 101 Writing Composition course. The initiative took place throughout a semester, with specific details provided for week one and week twelve. The professor aimed to counter the devaluation of college caused by generative artificial intelligence. This approach sought to prepare students for the social demands of their future careers.

The framework requires students to engage in constant social interactions rather than listening to a professor for 90 minutes. In a class of 20 students, mostly freshmen, the professor asks them to discuss homework challenges and weekend activities. Students must spend five minutes at the end of class planning their homework and discussing it with peers. The course includes a week where students give 5 to 10 minute presentations on their work. These presentations cover topics like factory farming practices and the environmental impact of fast fashion.

The professor, Sean Cho Ayres, believes that AI risks stripping humanity from lives and devaluing higher education. Ayres stated that the classroom should not be an intermediary between two computers but a shared battle against exams. He argued that the most important part of learning is articulating material to a group to show why it matters. According to Ayres, the value lies in whether ideas originate from the person, regardless of whether ChatGPT helped with commas. He believes this process makes the work real and defines the true college experience.

Gen Z students are affected by this shift, as they are often characterized by doomscrolling and a lack of social skills. These young adults are aware that an AI-infused workplace awaits them immediately after their graduation. Some students, like Alex and James, form friendships over common struggles with other professors, such as Professor Smith. The professor notes that students often use AI for term papers or to write entire conclusions. However, the goal is to move their private thinking into the public sphere through peer pressure.

The background provided is that generative AI looms widely across higher education and threatens traditional learning. The author identifies as a young millennial who also struggles with eye contact and social cues at dinner parties. He describes a contemporary classroom where students sit silently with AirPods or scroll through AI-selected ads on their phones. The article was originally published by The Conversation on December 12, 2025, and republished on November 14, 2026. Ayres disclosed that he has no financial affiliations with organizations that would benefit from the article.

The process concludes in week twelve with a small-group discussion about adapting AI-augmented practices into daily life. The professor uses a Snapchat notification sound to regain the attention of students who are too engaged to stop talking. This interaction serves as a sign that the educator has successfully taught the students how to be human. The articles do not state if this framework is being adopted by other professors or institutions. They leave open whether these social skills will effectively translate to success in the actual AI-augmented workforce.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Project Glasswing finds over 129,000 software vulnerabilities with Claude
stories.Summary:
In August, researchers found flaws in the PHP programming language, which underpins roughly 70% of the world's websites, that could have allowed hackers to steal data or install malware on a huge scale. The finding prompted a warning from the National Security Agency and a global effort to patch the bug. Other flaws were recently found in systems ranging from Linux to OpenSSL to FreeBSD. Project Glasswing, a cybersecurity initiative started by Anthropic PBC, gave select companies and security researchers access to a specialized version of the Claude AI model. Between April and July alone, it found more than 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities, many of critical severity, and Anthropic independently found thousands more.

Many of these flaws had been lurking undetected for years, and discovering and patching them makes the broader system safer. AI-assisted defenders are proving especially adept at finding weaknesses in widely used software that traditional testing has missed, and problems in PHP had been evident as early as 2024, but it took AI to grasp their full significance. AI is also transforming the economics of security research, because defenders can now use agents to scan for weaknesses at unprecedented scale and speed and to scour places like old libraries and codebases that once would have been too costly or impractical to investigate. An AI tool that Microsoft Corp. tested on the Linux kernel earlier this year took, on average, about 22 minutes and just $3.60 to verify each suspected flaw.

So far, defenders appear to have at least a temporary advantage, and although criminals are using AI to find vulnerabilities and coordinate attacks, there is little evidence that they have achieved widespread success. A report by Google's threat-intelligence team found that while monthly vulnerability disclosures roughly doubled over the first half of the year, only about 0.2% of all those found had actually been exploited by hackers. For cybersecurity pros, the immediate challenge will be to advance from finding flaws to fixing them, and top AI models are quickly getting better at writing patches, yet deploying them widely and at the requisite speed remains a problem. One study found that companies fully fixed only 26% of known-to-be-exploited vulnerabilities last year, and at many organizations, 30 to 60 days remains the norm for critical flaws.

For policymakers, the goal should be to accelerate that process where possible. The White House should expand its efforts to get frontier AI cyber capabilities to as many vetted defenders as possible while modernizing the existing vulnerability management process. Federal procurement rules should insist on secure automated updating and other software best practices, along the lines of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's "Secure by Design" pledge, and Congress must invest in defending critical infrastructure, including essential open-source projects. The article says it is not hard to imagine a day when the entire defensive process unfolds behind the scenes, seamlessly and automatically, with internet users blissfully unaware, though getting from here to there could be an eventful journey.

stories.Headline: Alpha School charges up to $75,000 a year as only 42% of students meet its AI learning goal
stories.Summary:
Alpha School, a network of AI-driven private schools, has faced scrutiny after internal data revealed many students are not meeting learning goals. The network charges wealthy parents up to $75,000 a year for a model that replaces traditional teachers with guides. These guides focus on motivation rather than lesson planning or grading. The reports surfaced on November 14, 2026.

The school uses an AI tutor app called TimeBack to help students learn twice as fast in reading and math within two hours of daily academics. However, only 42% of students met this goal, with about half of K-8 students missing the math target. The network has grown to roughly 50 campuses with between 1,200 and 1,500 students. Additionally, more than 2,600 public school students in South Carolina and Texas now use the platform.

Cofounder MacKenzie Price stated that the app accelerates learning to allow more time for workshops on relationship building and public speaking. U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon praised the model in September 2025, calling it the most exciting thing she had seen in education. Other supporters include Bill Ackman and Reid Hoffman. Meanwhile, Houston Independent School District Superintendent Mike Miles noted that students spent more time on the apps than intended.

The expansion occurs as schools struggle with declining test scores and concerns over AI dependency. Some former employees claimed the AI created faulty lessons, while parents reported that students suffered stress and anxiety. Public school pilots face further challenges because they cannot remove struggling students. Experts warn that over-reliance on AI may hinder critical thinking and the ability to read long sentences.

The Federal Aviation Administration introduced a new artificial intelligence tool while air traffic control problems were being reported, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the tool was not connected to those issues, according to NBC News on November 14, 2026. Duffy, the transportation secretary, said the new AI tool was not connected to the air traffic control issues, and the company behind the FAA's AI tool said the technology did not cause the ground stop. Microsoft said its outage did not appear to be connected to the ground stop, and Duffy said there was no evidence of a hack causing the flight issues. Duffy said the ground stop was due to lines being switched to fiber, and he said data inconsistencies triggered the FAA ground stop. He also called on Congress to fund improvements to the air system.

stories.Headline: Survey finds 84% of security chiefs say physical and cyber threats are inseparable as AI speeds up attacks
stories.Summary:
A June 2026 Wakefield Research survey of 300 U.S. security and wealth professionals, commissioned by 360 Privacy, found that 84% of CISOs and CSOs and 87% of senior security and privacy executives agreed it is now impossible to separate physical security from cybersecurity. 64% of CISOs and CSOs said their organizations have merged the two functions or are in the middle of doing so, and another 25% have a merger planned. The article says AI has removed most of the slow, tedious work of building a profile of an executive, such as pulling property records, cross-referencing social accounts, finding the spouse and working out the gym schedule. 89% of CISOs and CSOs believe automated AI systems that probe and exploit digital vulnerabilities will be an existential threat to personal and corporate security within the next two years.

360 Privacy's monitoring records, taken when individuals enrolled and before any remediation, show the median person had personal information on 121 distinct sources and a home address on 112, and nearly 60% of those exposure records also named a family member. 87% of CISOs and CSOs and 88% of security and privacy executives said it is difficult to keep the people they protect technologically literate enough to stay safe from AI-driven threats, compared with 68% of wealth professionals. In early 2024, a finance employee at the engineering firm Arup sent about $25.6 million after a video call with what turned out to be deepfakes of the company's CFO and colleagues. 60% of CISOs and CSOs are spending more time on physical threats to the people they protect than they were a year ago, and 85% of CISOs and CSOs plan to put more emphasis on family members' behavior that raises exposure.

Charles Randolph, Chief Strategy Officer at 360 Privacy, wrote the article. He said merging teams on an org chart is the easy part and that he has seen plenty of converged org charts with no converged decisions behind them. He recommended giving exposure one owner, so it does not fall into a gap depending on whether someone decides an issue is cyber or physical. He advised running the same kinds of AI-assisted reconnaissance tools an attacker would use against your own executives and their households, with their consent, and then briefing the principal with that output. He also said to watch the second ring of executive assistants, chiefs of staff, spouses and kids, and to rehearse a cross-domain week with cyber, physical, legal and communications in the same room.

The article says the argument over convergence is settled, and the harder part is making a merged team work against an adversary who now has AI doing the legwork. It says the raw material for an AI-assisted attacker is already sitting there and costs them almost nothing. Randolph said that in any risk environment the adversary has a vote, and that AI just lets them cast it faster. He concluded that convergence was the right call and that the merged team now has to move at the speed of the tools pointed at it.

Articles.Title: AI does the reconnaissance now. Convergence has to keep up.

stories.Headline: Survey finds 70% of CISOs have 11 or more AI agents connected to internal systems
stories.Summary:
A survey of 100 CISOs by Andreessen Horowitz found that internal AI agent security had the largest year-over-year jump, 28 percentage points, in becoming a top five priority, as reported on 2026-11-14. Agen.co by Frontegg also published a report, The State of Autonomous Agent Governance, based on a survey of 300 CISOs and CSOs. After highly publicized agent breakouts at OpenAI and other major AI labs that summer, more than four in five of those leaders tightened policy, added tooling, or opened a review. The report found that 83% of these leaders oversee environments where agents are connected to internal systems or data, and 70% have 11 or more agents connected.

The report says 84% see more than a thousand agent actions a week, and one in five sees more than ten thousand. Three quarters of the CISOs said they are confident they know how many agents are connected, yet half said their teams found an agent running in production this year with access it never should have had, and a quarter found more than one. More than half had an agent incident in the past twelve months, and six in ten learned about it only afterward, from a log, an employee, a customer, or an audit. Some 42% said they cannot block a specific harmful action before it runs, and 53% still run agents on shared or long-lived API keys, while 40% use an employee's personal credentials and only 18% check an agent's identity before each action.

Sagi Rodin, co-founder and CEO of Agen.co by Frontegg, wrote that he believes the CISOs are not careless, but that checking the door and knowing what happens inside the building are different things. He said perimeter security and identity-native runtime enforcement are not the same. Only 43% said they can keep policies current by hand comfortably, and the top answer for cutting effort was an agent or AI system that sets and updates agent policies on its own, ahead of better rules, fewer tools, or more people. Asked about trusting an AI system to make agent access decisions in real time within limits they set, 23% would trust it fully, 60% within tight limits, and 1% not at all.

Rodin wrote that autonomous governance must be fast enough to sit in the path of an action, citing the PaperCut attacker in September who used hundreds of agents to break into eleven organizations in 26 seconds. He said it must be specific to each company and stay bound by people who remain accountable. He said it does not happen overnight and comes one rung at a time, each level learning from the one below. Two thirds of the leaders want their organizations to keep adopting agents and plan to spend more on controls, and Rodin wrote that governance will sooner or later need to move autonomously too.

stories.Headline: Survey finds 65% of US adults hold companies responsible when an AI agent commits fraud
stories.Summary:
A recent survey of 2,026 U.S. adults found that 65% of respondents place responsibility on the company behind an AI agent when that agent completes a fraudulent transaction. The survey also found that 68% of respondents use an AI agent at least once a week for a personal task. Axios reported that Morgan Stanley started blocking third-party agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are placing restrictions on their use. Banks struggle to tell whether a customer authorized a given agent, and a shared login makes that harder because the credentials look exactly like the customer's.

Half of respondents, 50%, are uncomfortable with an agent using their credit card details to complete a purchase even if they requested it, and a further 32% won't share any information with an agent at all. Discomfort ranges from 65% among Boomers to 34% among Millennials. Willingness to share data decreases as it becomes more sensitive, with location at 38%, purchase history at 34% and calendar access at 34% leading the list, while only 15% would share financial information. Of the 885 respondents who gave an opinion, 14% pointed to themselves, 11% to the merchant and 10% to their bank or card provider, and 43% say they lack confidence in telling whether a request for information or account access is legitimate.

A scammer gaining access to the agent or their accounts, and the agent sharing personal or financial information without permission, each topped the list at 20%. RFC 9396 extends OAuth so that a client can request fine-grained permissions rather than a broad scope, similar to how a valet key allows a driver to access a car without opening the trunk. For example, a payment of a stated amount can be made to a named merchant from a specific account, with certain permitted actions such as initiating or canceling said payment. Asked what would increase their trust in agents, 50% pointed to human support when something goes wrong, 42% preferred the ability to reverse mistakes, 39% chose strong identity verification and 23% said nothing would increase their trust.

Permissions like this give banks something to compare against, so any agentic session that fits the granted and limited scope can proceed without friction. Anything that steps outside the scope, or arrives with identity, device and behavioral signals that don't match the customer's history, receives a closer look before money moves. Banks can also record which agent acted and under what authority, so that an investigator can later reconstruct a disputed transaction. Support and reversal are operational capabilities, so fraud teams will have to build them with customer service and payments operations rather than alone. A bank that can scope an agent's authority, record what it did and reverse a mistake quickly answers the question customers are already asking.

Articles.Title: When an AI Agent Commits Fraud, Proof of Authority Will Decide the Dispute

stories.Headline: Kishan Kumar says MBA programs teach AI building but not operational deployment
stories.Summary:
Kishan Kumar, a buyer at Pearse Bertram in Bloomfield, Connecticut, wrote in Poets&Quants on 2026-11-14 that MBA programs teach the cheap part of AI, building it, but miss the operational side. He described a newly minted MBA three months into a supply chain role at a midsize manufacturer whose supervisor handed him a forecasting pilot that performed well in a sandbox about a year and a half ago but hasn’t moved since. The planners don’t trust the model, the item master in the ERP is riddled with duplicates, no one has decided who can override the forecast when it’s wrong, and procurement is still placing orders on spreadsheets because no one told the buyers the forecast had changed. Kumar said his MBA prepared him brilliantly for the first week of the project but didn’t give him the skills to survive the next 18 months. Kumar has spent nine years in sourcing, procurement and supply chain across the manufacturing, industrial automation and FMCG sectors and recently completed his MBA.

A GMAT Panda study published by Poets&Quants in April documented 191 AI courses across 20 leading MBA programs, and of the 166 courses that could be reliably classified, 157 were electives and only nine were required in the core curriculum. Yale SOM added an AI course to its core requirements this fall, taught by an operations management professor, Georgetown McDonough’s new curriculum includes a required applied AI course and a hands-on AI bootcamp in the first term, and NYU Stern offers an AI specialization that includes a practical course on building AI agents. Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business enrolled every student, faculty member and staff member in a Gen AI 101 course, and all Kelley majors must now complete nine credit hours of AI-integrated coursework. Kellogg’s 10-week Applied AI Lab puts students in small cross-functional teams to identify, build and deliver AI solutions for company partners, and Yale’s new core has students build agents rather than just learn about them. Ethics and policy is the top category among the 191 courses, and in a survey reported by Poets&Quants in February, MBA students named AI ethics and governance as the course they most need.

Kumar wrote that schools grade the model while industry grades the deployment, judging a project by whether the technology is still in use six months later. MIT’s Project NANDA studied enterprise generative AI in 2025 and found that 95% of companies saw no measurable return and only 5% of custom enterprise tools reached production, which the researchers attributed to unreliable processes and poor fit with business operations rather than weak models. Gartner predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 due to escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Kumar wrote in Supply Chain Management Review earlier this month about why predictive AI implementations fail in supply chains and reached a similar conclusion, that the bottleneck is rarely the algorithm. Gartner predicts that by 2028, at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agentic AI, and says success depends on redesigning workflows from the ground up.

Kumar wrote that operations courses teach inventory management, capacity and queuing as if a human controls every input, while AI courses teach agent techniques with generic examples, and the two rarely intersect. He asked how safety stock policy changes when an agent places the purchase orders, who sets an agent’s spending limit, and what purchasing even means when software generates the orders. He wrote in Poets&Quants last month about preparing a “who is affected by this” document before launching any predictive model, arguing that governance is a stage in the process, not a seminar. In GMAC’s 2026 Corporate Recruiters Survey, half of employers said graduates are struggling or unprepared to work with AI in their organizations. Kumar proposed a pilot-to-production capstone assessed on whether a solution survives 90 days in a real workflow, with deliverables including a data-readiness audit, a business owner assigned to each KPI, a change management plan and a fallback plan if the system fails.

Kumar proposed agentic workflow design in the operations core, taking a real process such as sales and operations planning, supplier onboarding or purchase-order management and redesigning it for humans working alongside AI agents. He proposed AI economics for operators, covering data cleansing, ERP integration, model monitoring, retraining and the cost of confidently wrong recommendations, because projects rarely fail because the technology doesn’t work but because no one calculated the full cost before the pilot. He advised applicants to ask admissions whether AI is part of the operations core or appears only in electives, whether any course involves an actual deployment rather than a theoretical model, and whether students will work with a real company’s operational data and need a process owner’s sign-off. He wrote that the business schools that stand out over the next decade won’t necessarily be the ones offering the most AI electives but the ones whose graduates can walk into a stalled pilot on day one and deliver results by the end of the month. Kumar holds a Supply Chain Strategy & Management certification from the Indian Institute of Management and is a certified Six Sigma Green Belt, SAP Certified Implementation Consultant and Agile Leader Certified professional.

Kumar is an active member of the Association for Supply Chain Management and has written for Poets&Quants, SCMR.com, TechTarget and ExpressPharma. The article is copyrighted 2026 by Poets&Quants, which states it may not be republished, rewritten or otherwise distributed without written permission. The page lists related items on AI, accreditation and the future of faculty and staff roles, a commentary that the MBA is splitting in two, what business education can learn from Escoffier’s kitchen, and the business school world’s response to Chris Marquis. The article gives no date for the stalled pilot beyond about a year and a half before the piece and no name for the manufacturer or the new graduate. It does not say whether any school has adopted Kumar’s three proposed changes or how admissions offices answer his three questions.
