stories.Headline: A parent and edtech leader urges schools to rethink assessments as AI makes take-home work unreliable
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Kumar Srivastava, published by the Seattle Times on November 14, 2026. He writes as the father of two girls, one of whom is applying to college for admission next fall, and he compares her application steps to his own several decades earlier. He says little has changed since the late 1990s in what students submit, including transcripts, personal statements, portfolios, standardized test scores and AP scores. At the same time, he says everything has changed because AI can now produce each of these final products in seconds.

He describes how large language models can generate personal statements and high school essays, so the results of take-home projects or exams are not necessarily a sign of learning. He also says software engineering has been fundamentally altered, with work that used to take a year done over a weekend and debugging that took a night diagnosed in seconds. About six months before writing, he says, his hiring saw candidate take-home tests arrive flawless and highly produced, and when he asked one candidate to explain their finished product and decisions, the candidate fell silent and moved between reading code and describing the software as if a team member had written it. He calls this a shift across all information work, not cheating, and compares it to how calculators changed middle school math and online search changed how dissertations were written. He warns that performance and productivity without a solid learning foundation is dangerous, and says anyone can now reach 75% to 80% of the quality for any generic task at the same speed.

He says online coding platforms started introducing cheating detection, and schools in the Pacific Northwest have introduced network logging and scanning to detect whether students were logged on to ChatGPT during an assessment. Responses range from banning AI outright to postponing adoption to allowing it completely, and where AI is banned teachers are asked to talk to students when use is detected. He notes students have sued schools for being unfairly charged with cheating while the number and proportion of perfect scores has never been higher, citing Harvard putting a ceiling on the number of A's in a class. Drawing on his early career in online safety at Microsoft, he says detection is never complete and the AI detection contest is an unwinnable arms race, and that pretending AI does not exist or does not change learning is a bad strategy.

He argues the assessments that carry the most weight are those that can be observed and measured, where a student must show their thinking, defend it and correct it when new information is introduced. He says the objection is cost, since no district has enough staff for live recording and verification of every assessment with an instructor. What he calls for is evidence of learning and a rethinking of assessments as a continuous process that observes students and corrects misconceptions in real time, with future assessments forcing students to predict, test, revise and defend their thinking. He says the key lies in how software engineers and Ph.D. candidates have been evaluated, and that what is needed is a soft version of whiteboards that is AI-immune, dynamic, transparent and streamlined. The article identifies him as having spent two decades hiring engineers, leading Quantum Learning Machines, an education technology company working on assessment, and being the parent of a Washington high school senior.

stories.Headline: Dr Lohani says AI detects diseases and predicts outbreaks but clinicians must make final decisions
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is currently transforming the global healthcare system through disease detection, medical diagnosis, laboratory investigation, and drug discovery. These advancements were detailed by Dr. Lohani in an article published by The Rising Nepal on November 15, 2026. AI is also reshaping hospital management and patient monitoring to improve the overall quality of modern medicine. The technology aims to increase the affordability, efficiency, and accessibility of health services for various populations. These improvements are especially significant for developing economies like Nepal that face many systemic healthcare challenges.

The system requires reliable electricity, digital devices, digital literacy, and reliable internet connectivity to function without widening existing inequalities. It utilizes X-rays, MRI images, CT scans, electronic health records, and laboratory values to identify precise disease patterns. AI can detect lung cancer, tuberculosis, and breast cancer, while retinal imaging helps identify diabetic retinopathy to prevent blindness. It predicts cardiovascular diseases, infectious disease outbreaks, and pregnancy complications, but qualified healthcare professionals must make the final clinical decisions. Telemedicine systems can help local health workers in mountainous and isolated areas provide preliminary assessments and refer patients.

Dr. Lohani, the clinical director at the Nepal Poison Information Centre, is responsible for these observations and recommendations. He stated that AI can strengthen public health programs like resource allocation, health planning, and disease surveillance. He noted that AI can predict the spread of infectious diseases using population movements, weather patterns, and epidemiological data. The author argued that AI should serve disadvantaged populations rather than only benefiting affluent communities in urban areas. He emphasized that researchers must ensure scientific integrity, protect participant confidentiality, and maintain transparency with AI-generated data.

People living in rural and remote places are affected because they often travel long distances to consult medical specialists. Local health workers can use AI to identify warning signs for patients who lack access to quality healthcare. Public health authorities are affected as AI helps them plan for hospital bed demand and distribute essential medicines. Policymakers can use digital health technologies to analyze national health data and develop evidence-based policies for health interventions. Research institutions like the Nepal Health Research Council can use AI to translate research findings into actual health policies.

The articles explain that Nepal suffers from limited health investment, geographical barriers, and shortages of qualified healthcare professionals. Inadequate infrastructure continues to challenge the delivery of healthcare services across the developing nation. AI can monitor communicable diseases such as seasonal influenza, tuberculosis, malaria, and dengue to provide early warnings. Drug development is described as a complex, expensive, and time-consuming process that AI can accelerate by identifying drug targets. However, the integration of AI raises practical, legal, and ethical issues regarding data security and patient confidentiality.

The government must now promulgate accountability systems, data protection, ethical standards, and regulatory policies before implementing AI on a large scale. Stakeholders including the Nepal Health Research Council and the Ministry of Health and Food Safety should collaborate on development. Investment should be allocated for AI innovation in emergency preparedness, non-communicable diseases, infectious diseases, and maternal and child health. Pilot programs in selected rural and urban facilities must evaluate the safety, affordability, and effectiveness of these interventions. The articles leave open the specific details of who is legally responsible for harm caused by AI-assisted treatment.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop AI framework to assess seaworthiness of damaged ships in real time
stories.Summary:
A research team developed a rapid evaluation framework to assess the seaworthiness of damaged commercial vessels and offshore platforms by November 14, 2026. This system uses artificial intelligence to reconstruct three-dimensional geometry from field optical imaging to determine if compromised ships can safely navigate. The process integrates linear potential flow boundary element analysis and structured emergency decision-making to provide actionable navigational advisories during emergencies. It replaces conventional methods like manual visual surveys, high-precision scaled testing in wave flumes, and numerical simulations relying on pristine design files. The framework eliminates traditional modeling bottlenecks to allow for real-time hydrodynamic safety assessments in salvage and emergency response operations.

The workflow requires multi-view imaging of four hull quadrants, including the bow, stern, port, and starboard, using unmanned aerial vehicles and remotely operated vehicles. These images are processed by the OpenCV library and the HunYuan3D foundation model, which was developed by Tencent Hunyuan to synthesize spatial representations. The pipeline uses the LATTICE shape foundation model, 3DShape2Vecset, and MeshLab software to create a watertight stereolithography file for numerical suitability. Hydrodynamic simulations are then performed using Capytaine, an open-source package derived from the Nemoh solver, analyzing frequencies from 0.05 to 2.0 radians per second. The system was validated using a cargo ship measuring 239.44 meters in length, 48.54 meters in breadth, 18.0 meters in draft, and 143,000 metric tons.

The researchers stated that conventional post-accident assessment methods struggle to deliver quantitative rigor and rapid turnaround during time-critical emergency response operations. They explained that high-precision scaled testing is impractical for field scenarios because it requires weeks of model fabrication and specialized facility access. The team noted that single-point numerical simulations are constrained by their reliance on preexisting computer-aided design files that ignore irregular physical buckling. They claimed that controlling geometric deviations within a three percent margin provides an adequate foundation for numerical simulation of stability reserves. The authors asserted that their automated computational chain bridges the gap between initial on-site data gathering and definitive risk classifications.

The system affects operators of commercial vessels and offshore platforms that suffer structural deformations from accidental collisions, grounding incidents, or cumulative seawater corrosion. These users need to know if a vessel can withstand ambient sea states or if the damage degrades hydrostatic stability reserves. The framework evaluates motion responses across four wave headings, including head seas at 180 degrees and beam seas at 90 degrees. It also analyzes bow oblique seas at 45 degrees and stern oblique seas at 135 degrees to yield vessel-handling recommendations. The resulting response curves show dominant surge and heave under head seas and pronounced sway and heave under beam seas.

The articles explain that raw generated surface meshes often contain topological anomalies that can derail hydrodynamic boundary element solvers. To fix this, the pipeline uses region-growing methods to close structural apertures and eliminates non-manifold edges or duplicate polygonal faces. The system treats ambient seawater as inviscid, incompressible, and irrotational, ensuring the flow velocity potential satisfies the Laplace governing equation. Researchers benchmarked the reconstruction process against regular geometric primitives, such as cubes and cylinders, as well as intact and deformed vessel models. They found that ship hulls introduced slightly higher errors than regular solids due to complex, doubly curved surface geometries.

The framework concludes by using an automated decision tree to synthesize hydrodynamic performance metrics with significant wave heights and structural deformation severities. This process produces definitive risk classifications and specific recommendations for handling the damaged vessel in volatile marine environments. The researchers successfully replicated a collision scenario involving a localized depression dent across the forward bow region on the port side. The articles do not state how the system performs with different types of structural failure beyond localized hull indentation. They also leave open whether the framework can be integrated into existing shipboard emergency management software for autonomous use.

stories.Headline: Researchers find high methodological bias in AI models predicting lung disease in preterm infants
stories.Summary:
Researchers Alejandro Avila-Alvarez, Rossana Valentina Martínez-González, and Sara María Fernández-González published a systematic review in Frontiers in Pediatrics on November 14, 2026. They evaluated artificial intelligence and machine learning models designed to predict bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants. The team synthesized eighteen studies published between 2016 and 2026 to assess computational architectures. These models targeted newborns born under thirty-two weeks of gestation or weighing under fifteen hundred grams. The investigation found that existing literature is undermined by substantial methodological weaknesses and unproven clinical superiority.

The review analyzed studies from China, the United States, South Korea, Canada, Denmark, France, Italy, Poland, Turkey, and Japan. It used the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool and followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. The researchers searched PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library up to February 28, 2026, registering the protocol as CRD420261466494. They found that 72.2 percent of the studies had a high risk of bias due to missing data and calibration metrics. Only Khurshid and colleagues and Torchin and colleagues reported formal calibration slopes, intercepts, or calibration curves.

The authors stated that high discrimination statistics often concealed critical caveats regarding statistical overestimation and model complexity. They noted that models achieve highest accuracy only after chronic disease develops and the therapeutic window for prevention closes. The researchers argued that early models with moderate discrimination may hold greater clinical utility than late-stage models. They found that algorithmic complexity provided no clear advantage over standard statistics in moderate clinical datasets. The team concluded that the literature lacks external validation and suffers from notable outcome heterogeneity.

Affected newborns face elevated rates of late mortality, extended hospitalizations, and long-term sequelae including pulmonary hypertension and neurodevelopmental impairments. Clinicians prioritize early risk identification to establish a therapeutic window for individualized preventive regimens and respiratory support adjustments. Other researchers, including Romijn and colleagues in 2023, previously reported a median c-statistic of 0.84 during development. The review noted that five distinct diagnostic definitions were applied across the eighteen studies. This inconsistency, along with different handlings of death, precluded a standardized clinical synthesis.

Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is the most prevalent chronic respiratory complication for infants born at extreme prematurity, caused by pulmonary immaturity and postnatal trauma. This condition involves an arrest in alveolar and vascular development triggered by mechanical ventilation, hyperoxia exposure, and inflammatory cascades. Historical advances include antenatal corticosteroids, exogenous surfactant replacement therapy, and less invasive ventilatory strategies, yet incidence has not declined. Traditional statistical models struggle to capture non-linear interactions of pulmonary pathogenesis and often suffer from restricted external transportability. These limitations accelerated interest in artificial intelligence frameworks capable of parsing high-dimensional clinical inputs.

The review analyzed various algorithms, including Random Forest in eleven studies and XGBoost in eight separate investigations. Other methods included support vector machines, Naive Bayes, multilayer perceptrons, and deep convolutional neural networks like DenseNet121 and ResNet18. Models incorporated gestational age, birth weight, respiratory support, proteomic markers, serum interleukins, prenatal Doppler parameters, and whole-exome sequencing. Some used chest radiographs, retinal photography, and spectral data from neonatal gastric aspirates obtained shortly after birth. The articles leave open how to standardize diagnostic definitions and improve calibration to ensure meaningful clinical progress.

stories.Headline: Banks grow reluctant to finance AI deals as borrowing costs rise
stories.Summary:
Some banks that had recently lined up to fund AI deals are now reluctant to finance more, Reuters reported this week, even when the deals carry guarantees from major names like Alphabet and Anthropic. The shift followed a selloff last week that wiped $2.5 trillion from the Nasdaq-100 in one day and pushed it into correction. The article compares the moment to the 2001 telecom crash, when companies borrowed heavily to build fiber networks before demand arrived. It says the AI buildout is once again being financed largely with borrowed money before the profits are there to justify it.

The numbers in the article trace the dependence on debt. Last year Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet together spent nearly $300 billion on capital expenditure, and that figure is expected to more than double to $635 billion this year. Annual debt issuance tied to AI and data centers rose from $166 billion in 2023 to $625 billion last year. At JPMorgan, loans backed by income-producing properties, a category that includes data centers, totaled $29 billion at the end of the third quarter, and data centers and similar properties now make up 12% of its commercial real estate loans, up from 8% three years ago. Goldman Sachs Research projects global hyperscaler debt issuance will reach $420 billion in 2027, more than 60% above its estimate for 2026.

Chris Poggi, a finance partner at Ropes & Gray, said debt investors' books have become full and that they are assessing whether they have extended themselves as much as they will this year. Bank of America credit analyst Yuri Seliger said big cloud companies are paying more to borrow, with their borrowing costs up about 0.5 percentage points this year, compared with 0.2 points for other financially strong companies not tied to AI. The article says some planned bond offerings tied to data centers and chips are already being shelved, and that Nebius Group scrapped plans for a bond sale. It also says CoreWeave is down 33% this year and its bonds have dropped sharply.

The article says none of this means the AI boom is over, and that the telecom companies of the late 1990s were not wrong about the internet but wrong about how long lenders would keep paying for it. It says the constraint on the buildout could shift from chips and power to capital if lenders keep pulling back while borrowing needs keep climbing. It adds that delayed projects mean orders that never get placed, which could weaken demand for chips, power and construction. The author says his November issue, due out on Monday, will examine what else lenders are signaling about the AI boom's staying power and will include a new energy recommendation.

stories.Headline: US nurses who perceive supervisory and organizational support show higher generative AI use, study finds
stories.Summary:
A nationwide cross-sectional study of 1,136 practicing nurses across the United States found that workplace supervisory and organizational support were positively associated with generative artificial intelligence use. The survey was conducted using the Centiment research panel between June 5 and July 3, 2026. The findings were published in Nursing Open, volume 13, issue 11, as article e71000, by G. A. Carter in 2026. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology reporting guidelines and received institutional review board approval. From an initial export of 1,239 completed submissions, quality-control filters excluded respondents who lacked active nursing licensure or did not provide or supervise direct clinical care.

Analysis revealed that 65.3 percent of respondents, representing 742 clinicians, had used generative tools for occupational duties over the preceding 12 months. On an unbounded habitual frequency scale, 73.9 percent acknowledged at least occasional clinical application, 46.5 percent used generative models weekly or more, and 23.3 percent reported daily or near-daily usage. Each single-point increase on a five-point Likert scale of supervisory support was associated with a 42 percent increase in adjusted odds of using generative tools. Each additional point of perceived organizational support corresponded to a 43 percent increase in adjusted odds. Approximately 47.0 percent of respondents reported an active employer policy on artificial intelligence in patient care, 32.5 percent reported no policy, and 20.5 percent were uncertain.

The authors state that the cross-sectional design means the associations do not establish causality, as nurses who use generative AI may perceive support differently from non-users. They emphasize that the training-status variable reflects training receipt and interest among untrained respondents rather than a causal estimate of training effectiveness. They note that the survey assessed self-reported frequency rather than verified output quality, patient outcomes, adherence to data privacy regulations, or clinical safety. They conclude that future longitudinal and prospective studies are needed to establish the direction of these associations. They add that such studies should test whether policy communication or training changes behavior and directly measure verification behaviors and safety outcomes.

Nurses who did not know whether an institutional policy existed demonstrated significantly lower odds of both general work-related use and frequent clinical deployment, while the confirmed existence of a policy was not significantly associated with adoption compared to having no policy. Exactly 50.4 percent of surveyed nurses had completed formal educational modules on artificial intelligence, 31.6 percent of the remainder expressed an explicit desire for training, and 18.0 percent remained untrained and uninterested. Untrained clinicians lacking interest demonstrated dramatically lower odds of usage compared to trained peers. Descriptive profiling indicated that 81.5 percent of participants identified as female, 50.3 percent held a baccalaureate nursing degree, and 19.1 percent possessed graduate credentials. Bedside nurses constituted 33.9 percent of the cohort, charge nurses 23.4 percent, advanced practice registered nurses 19.3 percent, and nurse managers or administrators 15.9 percent, with approximately 63.4 percent practicing in acute care hospital settings.

Prior health services evaluations, such as analyses of the 2023 American Hospital Association Annual Survey, noted that approximately 65 percent of United States hospitals used predictive models to predict inpatient health trajectories, identify high-risk outpatients, monitor health, and automate scheduling and billing. Among adopting hospitals, approximately 79 percent relied on models supplied by their electronic health record developer. Controlled evaluations of machine-generated medical literature demonstrated that up to 47 percent of generated references were entirely fabricated, while another 46 percent were authentic citations applied inaccurately, leaving only 7 percent both authentic and accurate. Additional investigations testing commercially available models across realistic clinical vignettes revealed that algorithms frequently perpetuated debunked, race-based medical misconceptions and displayed erratic variability when identical clinical prompts were queried repeatedly. General-purpose tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are freely available to individual clinicians and can be applied to clinical questions, patient education, and documentation tasks largely outside institutional oversight.

Standard demographic variables including age, gender, years of nursing experience, formal educational attainment, and geographic census regions displayed no statistically significant independent associations with adoption once workplace governance and clinical roles were accounted for. Cross-tabulations confirmed that the two behavioral outcomes operated under distinct cognitive recall frames rather than strictly nested hierarchical subsets, leading researchers to treat the frequency metric as a dedicated measure of clinical intensity rather than an exact annualized prevalence benchmark. The authors emphasize several methodological limitations inherent to cross-sectional survey designs that necessitate cautious interpretation of the empirical conclusions. The researchers recruited a diverse national nonprobability sample of practicing, licensed nurses, with clinical experience spanning from novice practitioners to seasoned veterans possessing more than twenty years of bedside experience. The article was written by Ophelia Keating and published on November 14, 2026, by Scienmag.

stories.Headline: Ohio State and Microsoft launch five-year AI and cloud partnership
stories.Summary:
Ohio State and Microsoft announced a five-year AI and cloud partnership on November 10, 2026, covering research, clinical care and education. The announcement was published by CASRAI on November 14, 2026. Microsoft's announcement said the proposed move of 70 to 80 percent of storage and compute to Azure is an ambition rather than a completed migration. The announcement identifies digital pathology and imaging among the targeted workloads. Wexner Medical Center is building a shared data foundation with Microsoft Fabric and OneLake, and its high-level design is complete.

The release describes a potential Azure research environment offering governed access to appropriate, de-identified data. Microsoft says the smart hospital platform is in use at Richard M. Ross Heart Hospital and James Outpatient Care. The partners plan to expand AI learning, Microsoft Learn resources and certification opportunities for researchers, faculty, staff, students and caregivers. Ohio State's October 7 AI Fluency newsletter described research-focused AI workshops and innovation microfunds for faculty, staff and student employees, with funding extending beyond undergraduate education. The university's AI Fluency learning outcomes include evaluating AI outputs for accuracy and relevance and considering the implications of implementation within a field.

The article says a completed design does not establish that a dataset is available for a particular study. It says the research-office implication is to distinguish infrastructure planning from project authorization, including which environment will host the work, who can approve access and which data the project can actually use. It says these are questions of research data governance alongside the technical work of de-identification. It says the smart hospital deployment has a different status from the broader migration ambition and the proposed research environment. It says the October 7 initiatives predate this announcement.

The article says tool familiarity and certification are parts of readiness, while judgment about appropriate research use remains a separate capability. It says the practical implication is to assess migration progress, data access and staff capability separately. It says a cloud target describes intended infrastructure, a research-access decision concerns a specific project, and training concerns what people can do with the tools. Ohio State's security and privacy guidance states that institutional data above S1, its public classification, should not be entered into unvetted AI tools. That guidance also tells users to cross-check AI-generated information for accuracy.

The article says the useful benchmark for universities assessing similar arrangements is evidence at each stage: migration actually completed, research access actually authorized and staff able to evaluate outputs. It says that is an editorial implication of the announcement and Ohio State's guidance, rather than a new university requirement. It says this connects the infrastructure programme to responsible AI practice without treating anticipated research or clinical benefits as demonstrated outcomes. It cites Microsoft's Ohio State-Microsoft five-year strategic partnership announcement of November 10, 2026, checked 2026-11-14. It cites Ohio State Office of Academic Affairs documents on AI Fluency and an Office of Technology and Digital Innovation security and privacy statement, all checked 2026-11-14.

The article does not say when the Azure migration would be completed or which workloads would move first. It does not say when the potential Azure research environment would be available or who would approve access to it. It does not give the value of the partnership or the terms of any agreement. It does not say how many people the expanded AI learning would reach. It does not say what happens next beyond the planned expansion of AI learning, Microsoft Learn resources and certification opportunities.

stories.Headline: Treasury Secretary questions whether Nvidia knowingly sold AI GPUs to shell companies and holds the company responsible

The same report states that the Treasury Secretary said the company itself is responsible for the matter. It also does not say whether an investigation has been opened or what penalties, if any, are being considered. The report offers no timeline for any next step.

The Treasury Secretary placed responsibility on Nvidia as a company rather than on any named person, according to the report. The report does not include any response from Nvidia or any statement from the company about the question raised. It also does not say whether the Treasury Department has contacted Nvidia about the matter.

The article provides no context on what prompted the Treasury Secretary's remarks and does not say what happens next. It does not describe any prior action by the Treasury Department against Nvidia or any other chipmaker over shell company sales. The report gives no indication of whether the question will lead to an investigation, a penalty, or no further action at all. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ranmore's Sean Peche calls himself a bear on AI stocks as Microsoft forecasts $175 billion in capex
stories.Summary:
Sean Peche, founder and portfolio manager of Ranmore Fund Management, raised concerns about artificial intelligence-related stocks, pointing to substantial infrastructure investment by major technology companies and the possibility that market expectations have moved ahead of financial returns. He said he remains cautious about the sector despite the attention AI companies have received from investors. He said he is a bear for AI-related stocks. He said the large technology companies are spending an absolute fortune on AI capex and that investors need to be very careful. His comments followed recent declines in technology shares and renewed scrutiny of the financial commitments associated with artificial intelligence development.

Microsoft has forecast approximately $175 billion in capital expenditure for the 2026 calendar year, illustrating the scale of investment taking place across the industry. Such spending includes the development of data centres and the acquisition of computing equipment needed to support AI applications. Peche questioned whether future financial returns would be sufficient to support the current level of investment. His concerns reflect uncertainty about the timing and scale of revenue generation from AI services relative to the capital required to develop them. The Nasdaq Composite recorded its largest one-day decline since April 2025 during the previous week.

Peche highlighted the tendency of investors to assume that recent market trends will continue. He argued that past share price performance can influence expectations about future returns, even when underlying financial conditions change. He said history shows that is not always the case. He said Ranmore looks at the numbers, not the story, and that most people listen to the story, but the problem with falling for stories is knowing when you are wrong. He said you have got to exit these waves before they crash, and that in AI there is a big wave going on.

Bernstein said in a recent research note that it did not find the bearish argument on AI particularly compelling. The firm maintained a positive longer-term assessment while acknowledging that near-term market developments were difficult to predict. Companies associated with AI infrastructure were among those affected by the selling. The decline followed Democratic victories in the US midterm elections, which raised concerns among some investors about possible delays to data centre construction. Uncertainty surrounding project schedules added to existing questions about infrastructure expenditure and the financial performance of companies supplying the AI industry.

Meta and Alphabet recorded negative free cash flow during the third quarter, according to the report. The report also stated that Meta, Alphabet and Amazon had suspended share buybacks while increasing their use of debt and equity financing. These developments indicate that infrastructure investment is influencing capital allocation decisions among large technology businesses. Investors are assessing how spending commitments affect cash generation, financing requirements and the capacity to return capital to shareholders. The eventual financial returns from these investments remain an important consideration in evaluating AI-related equities.

The market movements illustrated how expectations about future development activity can influence technology stock valuations. Peche has focused on the risks associated with substantial capital expenditure and elevated expectations, while Bernstein continues to see longer-term investment potential. As companies report further financial results, capital expenditure, cash generation and returns on investment will provide additional information for evaluating the sector. The differing perspectives reflect uncertainty about how quickly companies will generate financial returns from their AI investments. The outlook for artificial intelligence-related stocks remains a subject of debate as major technology companies commit substantial capital to infrastructure development.

Articles.Title: AI Investment Spending Draws Scrutiny as Ranmore’s Sean Peche Questions Technology Stock Outlook

stories.Headline: FBI warns that hackers weaponize ARTEX agentic AI framework to automate global intrusions
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Federal Bureau of Investigation released a TLP:CLEAR FLASH report regarding the ARTEX autonomous penetration testing framework. This advisory warns that malicious cyber actors have weaponized the open-source, agentic platform to automate intrusions at machine speed. The FBI reports that these actors have used the tool since at least August 2026 to target organizations globally. The report identifies a variety of affected sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal. These attacks move from initial reconnaissance through data exfiltration using large language model driven agents.

The framework requires external LLM providers, including frontier models like OpenAI GPT and Anthropic Claude, or Chinese models such as DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi. The FBI notes that DeepSeek Flash family models are most prevalent due to low cost and a lack of observable guardrails. The developer, known as Autumn-27, released the Go-based code on GitHub in July 2026 and removed the repository on October 8, 2026. Despite this, the tool remains available through mirrors, community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. Researchers found over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.

The FBI is responsible for the FLASH-20261113-001 report, which it issued through the Internet Crime Complaint Center. The agency stated that agentic offensive frameworks are now a mainstream threat rather than a research curiosity. It warned that the tool allows actors with minimal technical expertise to run complex, multi-target operations simultaneously. The FBI recommended that organizations inventory and shrink their external attack surfaces to mitigate risks. It also asked organizations to vet indicators of compromise before blocking them, as it does not endorse any commercial entity.

Microsoft reported that some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders very little time to respond. The tool affected more than 2,250 downstream tenants of ConnectWise Cloud Backup, an activity Microsoft attributes to the China-state aligned actor Storm-0940. Financially motivated Chinese speakers targeted South Korean banks in early October, exfiltrating personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals. CrowdStrike reported ARTEX use against more than 200 organizations, including Japanese companies. Other affected areas include iOS application distribution infrastructure, which agents modified via exposed cloud credentials.

The FBI based its findings on reports from eleven sources, including Akamai, Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant, Censys, CrowdStrike, Zscaler ThreatLabz, CERT-EU, and Check Point Research. The framework uses a planner agent to convert goals into intents, which are then executed by worker agents in a loop. It abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents to automate enumeration and exploitation. The tool gained between 1,500 and 2,000 GitHub stars within ten weeks of its initial release. Other similar frameworks, such as PentAGI, have also been used by threat actors.

Organizations must now review every Microsoft 365 tenant where affected ConnectWise applications were authorized and keep those connections disabled. The FBI continues to track infrastructure, such as the host 38.244.50[.]120 and the domain xcai[.]pro, tied to South Korean financial attacks. It also monitors command and control infrastructure from a Storm-3358 campaign that was active as of November 6, 2026. The articles leave open how defenders can effectively coordinate responses when attack speeds compress the detection window. It remains unclear how many other localized variants of the tool are currently active in the wild.

Articles.Title: FBI FLASH on ARTEX: Agentic AI Hacking Frameworks Move From Pen Testing Tool to Mainstream Threat

stories.Headline: A bibliometric study finds AI education research in four journals rises tenfold from 2020 to 2025
stories.Summary:
A bibliometric analysis published in Discover Artificial Intelligence found that AI-related research in four education journals grew tenfold between 2020 and 2025. The study examined 1,397 AI-relevant publications after applying a strict topical screen to a larger corpus. The surge in output coincides with the public release of generative AI tools. The observational design of the study does not establish a causal link between the technology and the increase in publications. The research focused on Interactive Learning Environments, Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, Journal of Learning Analytics, and International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education.

The researchers applied a lexical screening process to 2,719 articles and reviews retrieved from Scopus. This screen retained 1,397 records and excluded 1,322 that did not meet predefined criteria for AI relevance. Retention varied by journal, with 98.0% of records from Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence retained compared to only 25.7% from Interactive Learning Environments. Within the screened corpus, AI-relevant output rose from 54 publications in 2020 to 558 in 2025, a 10.3-fold increase and a compound annual growth rate of 59.5%. The sharpest acceleration occurred from 2023 onward, aligning temporally with the widespread adoption of generative AI tools like ChatGPT.

The study notes that the four-journal sample is not a probability sample of the entire field, meaning the findings characterize these specific journals rather than the broader academic landscape. The author outlined future research directions, including conducting database-wide topical queries across Scopus and validating dictionaries through supervised text classification. The author also proposed generating time-sliced collaboration graphs to observe co-authorship stability and mapping the geographic and institutional distributions of educational artificial intelligence scholarship. The study emphasizes that topical relevance screening is important in bibliometric studies, demonstrating how unscreened data can produce artifacts that do not reflect the actual focus of the literature. The study underscores that rapid growth in generative AI research highlights a shifting intellectual landscape that requires careful mapping to identify trends and gaps.

Thematic analysis identified eight predefined lexical themes, with generative AI and large language models recording the largest count, growing from one publication in 2020, 2021 to 307 in 2024, 2025. Learning analytics and intelligent tutoring grew in absolute terms but declined in relative share, suggesting a thematic reorientation rather than a complete replacement of earlier research areas. The 1,397 publications received a total of 44,872 citations, with a median of 9.0 citations and a mean of 32.1 per publication, and the corpus h-index was 101. Of 4,121 distinct authors, only 112 had at least four publications in the corpus, and the largest connected component of this restricted network contained 74 authors divided into eight sub-groups. Betweenness centrality identified authors like Ng, Lin, and Gašević as occupying the most structurally central positions.

The screened corpus comprised 1,285 original research articles (92.0 percent) and 112 review papers (8.0 percent). Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence published the highest share of reviews at 12.5 percent, followed closely by Interactive Learning Environments at 11.4 percent, whereas the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education and Journal of Learning Analytics published no articles classified as reviews between 2020 and 2025. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence and Journal of Learning Analytics operate entirely as gold open-access periodicals, while Interactive Learning Environments left 92.8 percent of its artificial intelligence articles behind a paywall. Across the combined collection, 57.8 percent of papers were gold open access, 40.0 percent closed, 1.4 percent green, and 0.7 percent bronze. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence provided the largest single volume with 489 articles (35.0 percent), recording the highest mean citation count of 52.8 and the highest journal-level h-index of 85.

Limitations of the study include its reliance on a four-journal sample and a lexical screening process that may exclude AI-related studies using non-standard vocabulary or retain studies that mention AI without substantively investigating it. Citation counts are a snapshot at the retrieval date and are affected by publication timing, making it difficult to compare the impact of recent generative AI work with earlier research. The collaboration network is aggregated over the full period, so it cannot establish whether research groups persisted, formed, or dissolved over time. Assessment and feedback automation accounted for only 3.1 percent of the corpus, showing that the evidential weight of the literature is unevenly distributed. The study leaves open whether the growth in AI research will continue at the same pace or how the four-journal findings would compare with a database-wide sample.

Articles.Title: AI Education Research Grew Tenfold in Four Journals

stories.headline_source: AI Education Research Grew Tenfold in Four Journals

stories.Headline: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney criticizes Steam's AI disclosure label as unfair to developers
stories.Summary:
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney criticized Valve's Steam storefront over its rule that developers must add a label when a game uses artificial intelligence, in comments reported by GamesBeat and covered by MP1st on November 14, 2026. Sweeney has been critical of Steam on social media in recent months, and this time he defended AI while attacking the disclosure requirement. His remarks came amid a growing debate about AI in the gaming industry. He said large-scale game development will be totally changed by AI and that teams which do not adopt it will be left behind and become uneconomical compared with their peers. Sweeney argued that one team may soon make a game four times more efficiently, and perhaps 10 times more efficiently, than another team making the same game, leaving no way to compete the old way.

He said no game developer has 75% to 95% profit margins that they can risk by not being as productive as possible. He rejected the idea that the label simply informs players, saying he does not buy it in the slightest, and argued that reviews already cover a game's quality, scope and entertainment value. He said AI can be used to make good games and bad games, and that tying AI to bad games is unfair to developers who use it well. Sweeney described the label as a guilt by association pattern that all developers need to push back on. He said a large resistance movement against AI seems focused on bullying developers into not adopting it by attacking individuals and review-bombing projects, and that he has been trying to make his views known to as many developers as possible.

He said the industry has to power through this and build games with maximum acceleration because it is a survival issue for all companies in the industry. He also said the label is absolutely being used by anti-AI advocates to undermine developers' reputations and the viability of their projects. The article says nearly 20% of games released on Steam in 2025 disclosed using generative AI, an 800% increase from the previous year. It also notes that Metal Gear Solid and Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima has been both fascinated and cautious about artificial intelligence. The article asks whether players have a right to know how the games they buy are made and whether AI was used, and it does not say what Valve or Steam has done in response or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Epic Games CEO Sees Steam’s Policies as “Unfair to Developers Who Use AI to Make Good Games”

stories.headline_source: Epic Games CEO Sees Steam’s Policies as “Unfair to Developers Who Use AI to Make Good Games”

stories.Headline: Noah Sander launches Zionist Investor to pair AI property search with Israeli real estate experts
stories.Summary:
Noah Sander, a Canadian-born real estate agent who made aliyah and served in the IDF, launched Zionist Investor, a platform for international buyers of Israeli property, and it has been live for several months. He announced it in a ynetnews.com article dated 2026-11-14T06:00:00Z, writing that he had spent years helping overseas buyers and had shared his experience in columns on ynet. The platform combines AI-powered property searches with personalized guidance from Israeli real estate professionals. Sander wrote that buying property in Israel for foreigners remains far more complicated than it needs to be. He said he built the platform after asking why someone should have to speak with five different agents and visit ten different websites.

Zionist Investor lets prospective buyers browse Israeli residential developments, compare prices and locations, and explore properties on an interactive map. Its central feature is AIgent Z, an AI-powered real estate advisor that helps buyers compare Israeli cities, assess budgets and identify suitable properties. Sander gave the example of a buyer who insists on Tel Aviv but, after discussing budget, lifestyle and preferences, may find a nearby city connected by light rail offers a more suitable property at a significantly more attractive price point. He wrote that AIgent Z's knowledge, personality and conversational style were shaped by his years of client conversations and his approach to advising buyers. The platform pairs the AI with a real team of professionals on the ground in Israel who guide buyers through the entire purchase process.

Sander said he does not believe artificial intelligence should replace human expertise in real estate, calling buying property a high-trust industry. He said no amount of technology eliminates the importance of experience, judgment and accountability, and that experienced professionals still matter enormously when evaluating an opportunity, understanding a transaction, negotiating terms and navigating the purchase. He said the goal is not to remove the human element but to give buyers tools and knowledge to engage professionals from a position of understanding rather than a blank slate. He wrote that the challenge is not that people lack information but that they lack a clear, reliable way to make sense of it all in one place. He said clear information is crucial when making a major financial decision like buying property in Israel.

Sander wrote that a bad investment does not magically become a good one simply because it is located in Israel, and that prices, financing costs, location and long-term appreciation are essential considerations. He said that for many Jews around the world purchasing property in Israel carries an additional dimension, such as a connection to family history, a place for holidays, a future home for their children or a foothold in the Jewish homeland. He described buyers who arrive with spreadsheets and investment models applied in other countries, others with childhood memories of visiting Israel, some thinking about retirement, others making aliyah, and many who already live in Israel. He said there is no single reason to buy property in Israel and there should not be a one-size-fits-all approach. He wrote that he grew up in Canada, made aliyah, served in the IDF and built his life and career in Israel.

Sander wrote that he had approached the problem the way most real estate professionals do, one client conversation at a time, spending hours understanding a buyer's priorities, explaining neighborhood differences, identifying suitable properties and guiding them through the Israeli market. He said he still does that today and genuinely enjoys it. He wrote that technology has transformed how people travel, manage finances and make major purchasing decisions, yet discovering and evaluating real estate in Israel, particularly from abroad, remains surprisingly fragmented. He said he wanted to build something bringing together real opportunities, market knowledge, personalized guidance and professional expertise in one place, leveraging AI, rather than another website filled with listings and real estate jargon. He wrote that he and his team spent the past year building the platform.

Sander wrote that the platform's ambition is bigger than helping someone find their next property, and that they are building Zionist Investor to become the natural starting point for Jews around the world considering purchasing property in Israel. He said it is available for anyone to explore. He wrote that buyers can begin without scheduling an appointment just to ask their first questions, and that the platform is designed to help people figure out what they are looking for rather than requiring them to know before they start. He said the goal is to help people ask better questions and approach their property search with greater clarity. The article does not say what the platform costs, how many properties or developments it lists, or when it will expand beyond its current features.

Articles.Title: Buying property in Israel made easier: where AI meets human expertise

stories.headline_source: Buying property in Israel made easier: where AI meets human expertise

stories.Headline: P.E.I. RCMP say AI-generated child abuse material rises to a third of online investigations
stories.Summary:
Prince Edward Island RCMP say there has been a notable increase in child sex abuse material made using artificial intelligence across parts of the province. P.E.I. RCMP senior communications adviser Scott Ferris said in an email it is a safe estimate that one third of Island RCMP online child abuse investigations now involve AI-generated material. That estimate considers only areas under RCMP jurisdiction, which excludes Charlottetown, Summerside and Kensington. Internet watchdog reports indicate a trending global rise in AI-generated child sex abuse content, previously known as child pornography.

In St. John’s, N.L., this summer, a 17-year-old boy was charged with nearly 60 counts related to the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse material. Police allege he used AI tools to alter images of 19 minors and make them explicit. The 17-year-old boy, who was hit with 58 criminal charges, faces 19 counts of making child sexual exploitation material after allegedly using AI to digitally alter photos of teenage girls. In an email, Summerside police reported at least one instance where a suspect used AI-generated child sex abuse material in a sextortion attempt this year.

Const. Stephanie Myers with the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary told CBC News On the Go host Krissy Holmes the case is probably one of our first if not the first specifically involving AI being used to create child sexual exploitation material. Mauranne Ste-Marie, senior research analyst with the national RCMP’s sensitive and specialized investigative services unit, said in many cases AI-generated content is either produced to create material of a child that is in the family or the neighbourhood of that offender. She said it increases the demand for the material and normalizes the abuse. Ste-Marie said it is a stepping stone and one step closer to sexually abusing a child, and that after viewing material for a certain number of weeks or months it may not meet their needs anymore.

Jacques Marcoux, director of research for the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, said AI-generated or manipulated material is increasingly used in sextortion attempts. His organization operates Cybertip.ca, Canada’s national tip line for reporting online child abuse. Marcoux said that in lieu of being able to trick the child into giving them an intimate image, offenders will simply create one using AI, then threaten to release images online claiming they are real. P.E.I. RCMP media relations officer Gavin Moore said there were 26 reported instances of sextortion last year in Island areas under RCMP jurisdiction, and noted reporting rates are typically very low for this type of crime.

Certain generative AI models, which are ultimately trained on images of real people, can create abusive images or videos either in the likeness of a specific person or by generating a non-existent, synthetic child from scratch. Some offenders also use AI-powered nudify tools to create explicit deepfakes, realistic fake images or videos of a victim. Mainstream generative AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude have strict safeguards in place that are designed to block the generation of any child abuse material, and confirmed violations are supposedly then reported to law enforcement. To circumvent these controls, offenders often rely on freely available open-source software to generate abusive media offline, where it is far harder to detect, and since these models are typically used without an internet connection, any exploitative content they produce can be incredibly difficult for police to track.

Under the criminal code, AI-generated child abuse is treated the same as authentic abuse material, and altering or generating explicit media with AI through written prompts can constitute making child sexual abuse material. In April 2023, 17-year-old Harry Burke from Fortune Bridge, P.E.I., took his own life hours after telling his parents he had been victimized by a sextortion scam. Ste-Marie said every time you post a picture or a video of yourself or your children there is a risk it could be used by someone with bad intentions, and one recommendation is to take precautions like covering a child’s face in photos. She said your child is never responsible for the creation of that type of content, even if they posted images online and they feel like it was their fault, and they have the right to post and to share without thinking that someone will use it against them.

Articles.Title: Rise in AI-generated child sex abuse fuels real-life risk, police and experts warn

stories.Headline: Healthcare AI Literature Emphasizes Fairness While Marginally Representing Patient Autonomy
stories.Summary:
Healthcare artificial intelligence literature emphasises fairness while marginally representing patient autonomy, according to a review by researcher Abduladhim Ashtaiwi published in Discover Artificial Intelligence. The study analysed seventy-three peer-reviewed healthcare publications for explicit representation of nine predefined ethical principles. It used automated natural language processing with statistical evaluations rather than a broad comparison of general principles. The review found substantial statistical disparities across thematic categories. Algorithmic equity and regulatory compliance received substantial focus while patient rights and ecological impact appeared far less often.

The corpus began with one hundred and ninety-eight candidate publications from IEEE Xplore, Elsevier, Google Scholar, ACM and Web of Science, found through an automated query developed with ChatGPT. Python routines removed duplicates, yielding one hundred and thirty-seven unique works, and expert manual screening produced a final corpus of seventy-three papers, about fifty-three percent of the deduplicated set. The papers held roughly 1,579,850 raw tokens, about 6,319 standard pages, and cleaning with pandas, nltk, spacy, gensim and matplotlib produced 746,570 processed tokens across an estimated 2,986 pages. The nine-theme codebook drew on guidance from the World Health Organization, UNICEF and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, covering privacy, transparency, fairness, accountability, safety, patient autonomy, innovation and progress, collaboration and partnership, and sustainability and environmental impact. The Thematic Completeness Index reached 0.2542 despite a Theme Coverage score of one, reflecting an average Theme Depth of 0.2542.

Ashtaiwi designed the Thematic Completeness Index so that completeness equals zero when no predefined themes are present and zero when themes are nominally present but lack associated keywords. Completeness reaches its maximum of one only when every predefined theme and every associated keyword appears in the corpus. The index multiplies Theme Coverage by average Theme Depth, a structure the author described as conceptually analogous to the information retrieval F1-score. The author argued that ethical corpora characterised as broad-but-shallow or deep-but-narrow fail true representational completeness. The author computed a paper-level adjusted occurrence rate because raw frequency counts can be distorted by document volume and uneven keyword counts per theme.

Fairness recorded the highest Theme Depth at 0.4615 with approximately 3,200 raw keyword mentions, and accountability ranked second at 0.3846 with about 2,500 occurrences. Privacy showed a Theme Depth of 0.2727 with roughly 2,000 raw mentions, transparency 0.3333 with about 1,300 instances, and collaboration and partnership also 0.3333. Safety reached 0.1538 across roughly 1,024 occurrences and innovation and progress 0.1818, while patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact both recorded the minimum Theme Depth of 0.0833, with environmental sustainability registering a mere 87 raw keyword occurrences. On the paper-level measure, accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate at 1.3008, followed by fairness at 1.2302 and privacy at 1.0576, with transparency at 0.4425, safety at 0.3977, innovation and progress at 0.2361 and collaboration and partnership at 0.1170. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact both registered median adjusted occurrence rates of exactly zero, confirming that at least half of the seventy-three publications contained zero matched keywords for either theme.

A Friedman test yielded a chi-square of 349.253 with eight degrees of freedom, a p-value below 0.001 and Kendall's W of 0.598, and a parallel robustness test reported a chi-square of 327.781 with eight degrees of freedom, p below 0.001 and Kendall's W of 0.561. Follow-up Wilcoxon signed-rank tests adjusted via the Holm step-down correction established that accountability and fairness possessed significantly higher paper-level Theme Depth than patient autonomy. The conceptual framework originated from the historical evolution and rapid operational deployment of artificial intelligence and machine learning in clinical environments. Early healthcare artificial intelligence emerged in the late 1950s with rule-based architectures such as the MYCIN expert system, designed to use logical if-then statements for pathogen identification and antibiotic recommendations. Statistical machine learning models were developed through the 1980s and 1990s to refine clinical diagnostic decision-making, followed by artificial neural networks and deep learning architectures from the late 1990s through the early 2010s.

Modern clinical practice increasingly incorporates convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks and transformer architectures alongside emerging platforms like the Internet of Medical Things and augmented reality. Technical capabilities have expanded much faster than formal ethical safeguards, raising concerns regarding patient safety, algorithmic bias, unverified clinical autonomy and institutional accountability. Clinical medicine traditionally expects computational tools to uphold the four classical bioethical pillars of patient autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Autonomy protects the patient's independent right to make informed decisions, beneficence mandates acting in the patient's best interest, non-maleficence enforces the duty to do no harm, and justice requires fair, equitable distribution of healthcare resources.

Translating these standards into algorithmic systems introduces profound friction, particularly when predictive models favour population-level statistical outcomes over nuanced individual circumstances or when opaque diagnostic outputs hinder informed consent. The investigator constructed nine Theme-Based Corpora by extracting matched codebook keywords alongside five contextual words appearing immediately before and after each target keyword within the cleaned text. This windowing configuration allowed targeted computational scrutiny of localised semantic environments surrounding specific ethical subjects without the interference of broader narrative noise. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Healthcare AI Literature Emphasizes Fairness While Marginally Representing Patient Autonomy

stories.Headline: Visa warns AI shopping agents can be fooled by counterfeit merchants as Adobe forecasts AI retail traffic to rise 130%
stories.Summary:
Adobe forecasts that AI-driven traffic to US retail sites will rise 130% year over year this season, November 1 to December 31, and 159% on Thanksgiving. It expects a record $275.1 billion in US online spending. Amazon renamed Rufus as Alexa for Shopping on May 13, 2026. Its Buy for Me button lets Amazon buy an item from another merchant's website for you. Prime members can ask it to auto-buy an item when it hits a target price.

Google's agentic checkout in Search and AI Mode can buy from eligible US merchants with Google Pay. Google says it always asks permission first and buys only after you confirm the purchase and shipping details. Meta's Muse agent, launched in September, picks products and proceeds to checkout with your approval. Amazon notifies you after the order is placed and gives you a free 24-hour cancellation window. Scamwise users report a new fake store roughly every three minutes, according to its October holiday report.

In the US, the Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute credit card charges for things you didn't accept or weren't delivered as agreed, as the FTC explains. Regulation Z section 1026.13 gives you 60 days from the first statement showing the error to send your dispute. Debit cards fall under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and its Regulation E. Its definition of unauthorized excludes transfers made by someone you gave access to, unless you told your bank that access was withdrawn. Per the FTC, the most you might owe for unauthorized credit card charges is $50, and for a debit card it can reach $500 if you report late.

Visa has warned that AI shopping agents can be deceived by sophisticated counterfeit merchants engineered specifically to exploit them. In October, Inc. reported Visa repeating that warning for the holiday season. Savi Security's Scamwise holiday report, published October 20, says a new fake store is reported roughly every three minutes, about 500 a day. Fake holiday-themed stores reported to it grew fivefold in the previous 60 days. Nearly 40% were less than 90 days old when first reported, and 85% were gone within two weeks.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security put the core idea in one line in its online shopping guidance: treat AI-generated recommendations as guidance, not assurances of legitimacy. Fortune reported in April that Amex pledged to protect cardmembers from erroneous transactions made by agents registered with Amex. In September, six banks, including Bank of America, Capital One, ING and NatWest, published shared principles for trusted agentic commerce. Fox Business reported that their paper flags agents requesting customers' card details and entering them directly into websites as one of the risks. A study from Columbia Law School's Center for Law and the Economy, reported by Reuters in July, tested Amazon's Alexa for Shopping and Walmart's Sparky.

The study found the assistants can often detect when Made in USA product labels are false, yet those labels stayed in front of shoppers. The Alliance for American Manufacturing has since asked the FTC to open an inquiry into AI shopping assistants. Scamwise found an impossible discount in one in four scam stores. The Scamwise report says fake delivery texts, order confirmations, and refund scams spike after big shopping days. In the US, report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and in Canada, report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Articles.Title: Before You Let AI Do Your Holiday Shopping: 7 Rules From a Security Expert

stories.headline_source: Before You Let AI Do Your Holiday Shopping: 7 Rules From a Security Expert

stories.Headline: Humans in Control holds Cedar Rapids forum to push AI rules into 2028 race
stories.Summary:
Community members in Cedar Rapids gathered on Saturday, November 14, 2026, to discuss the future of artificial intelligence and how to push 2028 presidential candidates to act on the technology. The event was part of a series called AI Reality Checks held across 30 states, which aims to build a grassroots movement calling for guardrails on the most powerful AI systems. The AI Reality Check events are local kickoffs for Humans in Control, a grassroots, cross-partisan organization working to put commonsense ground rules for AI on the national political agenda. The group wants those ground rules to become part of the 2028 presidential campaign conversation.

Gavin Nelson, the state director of Humans in Control, said the movement's success depends on local involvement. He said the big thing is getting involved in the community and working together on a holistic solution on the ground. He added that focusing on that in the community is one of the biggest targets the nation needs to focus on right now. Humans in Control Action also launched an AI primary presidential tracker that puts 2028 presidential candidates' views on AI on the record.

The forum was held as part of a series of AI Reality Checks across 30 states, and the Cedar Rapids gathering was one of those local kickoffs. The organization behind the events, Humans in Control, describes itself as grassroots and cross-partisan, and it is working to put commonsense ground rules for AI on the national political agenda. The movement's stated goal is to make those ground rules part of the 2028 presidential campaign conversation. The tracker launched by Humans in Control Action is meant to put candidates' views on AI on the record.

Articles.Title: Cedar Rapids forum urges guardrails for powerful AI ahead of 2028 presidential race - KGAN

stories.Headline: Voters reject data center measures in 40 of 41 local ballots across 10 states
stories.Summary:
Voters rejected AI data centers in dozens of communities in the 2026 midterm elections, with data centers on the ballot both directly and indirectly. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign.

Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state, and as governor-elect she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800.

Barbara A. Trish is a professor of political science, with a Ph.D. from The Ohio State University, who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. Her forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. She writes that the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. She writes that the seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. She writes that it matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and that so far the reported evidence is limited.

The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities, and opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote, and the bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models, and these massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Trish writes that as the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, many Democratic and Republican hopefuls should be expected to emphasize their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. She writes that we need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. She writes that despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. She cites Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform, that “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.
