stories.Headline: Boost CTO Rinku Sharma advocates blending human oversight with AI in payment design
stories.Summary:
Rinku Sharma, the chief technology officer at Boost, laid out his approach to artificial intelligence in payments in an article published by Crowdfund Insider on November 13, 2026. Boost provides business-to-business payment solutions, handling commercial card payments and acting as a bridge between buyers and suppliers. It also offers card-to-account services for companies that do not accept cards. Boost handles only the flow of funds, not the funds themselves, and it structures payment data from many forms into usable information for authorization and settlement.

Sharma said agentic development has completely changed the game, because people no longer need extensive training to design solutions. He warned that people thinking they are developers when they are not is risky for companies. He said the days of entry-level designers writing lines of code are over, but designers are not headed for extinction. He argued that a continuous mix of programming, artificial intelligence and humans in the loop is the best path to design success.

Sharma said you must still invest a lot of time into design, because feeding wrong assumptions into a model can produce a nice product that still misses the mark. He sees this driving demand for more senior software developers with intimate knowledge of system architecture. He said Boost sanitizes its data first, then tracks the end-to-end data flow across the organization, and its cloud-based system provides a single source of truth. He said there is a high likelihood that artificial intelligence generates slop and takes you in a different direction, which is why human touch and control at different stages of the life cycle matter.

Boost's process is multi-layered, with human and artificial intelligence contributions frequently checking each other. Teams create products that are refined by artificial intelligence agents, and the tech team reviews the work before explaining it to the production side. When both sides are comfortable, it goes to the agent for completion, then an independent model reviews it as a check against system bias. Developers then have the final say.

stories.Headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan to discuss AI safety and nuclear weapons at a joint meeting in China
stories.Summary:
Ian Bremmer explained that governments are struggling to regulate artificial intelligence because the technology is moving very fast. He noted that AI is becoming smarter and more dangerous, which creates risks like rogue agents and bioweapons. These concerns grew after a few months of breakthroughs in mathematics and medicine alongside several troubling incidents. Bill Gates also warned that the consequences of this powerful technology could be potentially catastrophic for the world. Nearly three quarters of Americans now support a slowdown in the development of these artificial intelligence systems.

The articles do not provide specific requirements or changes for AI regulation, but they mention a meeting in China next week. President Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping plan to hold an unprecedented joint meeting to discuss nuclear weapons. Trump will also travel to the Philippines and China with Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla. The Nvidia scandal is expected to be on the agenda for Trump and Xi Jinping during their talks. These leaders will likely discuss AI safety, including the danger of rogue bots and humans using technology for harm.

Ian Bremmer stated that competition with China makes it especially difficult for governments to regulate fast moving artificial intelligence technology. He questioned if the enormous promise of AI is being overshadowed by the risks of moving too fast. Dylan Loh from Nanyang Technological University predicted that the Nvidia scandal would not dominate the agenda or affect relationships. Administration officials said Elon Musk is a valuable adviser to Trump due to his economic and national security interests. Democratic senators ordered Musk to preserve records regarding SpaceX restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces are affected by these restrictions because Starshield is vital for frontline communications and drone operations against Russia. The general public is affected by the race for AI control as the technology becomes more powerful and dangerous. People are concerned about the potential for AI to be used to develop biological weapons or escape testing. Many Americans feel the risks of rapid development outweigh the benefits, leading to widespread support for a slowdown. The global community remains concerned about how big tech providers and governments will manage these powerful new tools.

The background provided is that AI models are making breakthroughs in medicine and mathematics while becoming potentially more dangerous. GZERO Media, a Eurasia Group company, provides the commentary and insights regarding these events through various multimedia properties. The articles also mention a separate nationwide ground stop on Friday caused by old air traffic control equipment. This outage led the Trump administration to request fifty billion dollars for air traffic control funding after thousands of flights halted. Other news includes a tanker collision in New Orleans and India's goal to triple clean energy capacity by 2035.

The next steps involve the historic meeting between Trump, Putin, and Xi in China to discuss nuclear weapons and AI. Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10 regarding chip sales. The articles leave open whether the Nvidia scandal will actually impact the personal relationship between Trump and Xi. It remains unclear if the United States will successfully implement regulations to prevent rogue AI or AI assisted bioweapons. The text does not state if the requested funding for air traffic control will be approved by the government.

stories.Headline: Chinese study links strong clinical reasoning in nurses to higher AI literacy
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a cross-sectional study in China that concluded on November 13, 2026. The investigation found that registered nurses with stronger clinical reasoning skills also possess higher artificial intelligence literacy. This link suggests that basic reasoning abilities help healthcare workers better understand and use digital tools. The study was published in the journal BMC Nursing.

The project involved 306 registered nurses from healthcare institutions in Guangdong Province. Participants used the SO JUMP platform to provide data via the Nurse Clinical Reasoning Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. The nurses earned a median literacy score of 90.00, with a range between 79.00 and 97.00. Statistical tests showed a positive correlation between reasoning and literacy, with coefficients from r = 0.289 to r = 0.551.

The research team, including authors such as Yang, Lu, and Peng, managed the data analysis. They used multiple linear regression and the Mann-Whitney U test to evaluate the results. The authors stated that clinical reasoning is a vital cognitive trait for managing intelligent systems. They argued that training programs should teach reasoning skills alongside technical instruction.

The study used Cognitive Load Theory to explain how clinicians handle the high demands of automated systems. It posits that advanced reasoning helps nurses organize complex digital information during patient care. The findings highlight a need for updated nursing curricula to integrate these cognitive skills. This approach aims to improve how professionals employ machine intelligence in routine workflows.

stories.Headline: Columnist Gary Stallard argues that AI cannot replace real intelligence and calls using it to create work unethical
stories.Summary:
Gary Stallard wrote a column published by The Lufkin Daily News on November 13, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence cannot replace real intelligence. He described using an AI tool to restore an old black-and-white photo of his mother and grandmother, which came out crystal clear. He then ran a color photo of his brothers and himself with their dad through the same tool, and the restored faces did not match them at all. He also tried clearing up a recent sports photo he had shot, and the AI gave the kid a third ear and jersey lettering that looked like hieroglyphics. He recalled reading an AI-generated recap of a sporting event that got both the final score and the winning team wrong.

Stallard wrote that AI is here to stay and does have value, citing a panel of business and state leaders who fielded questions on the future of artificial intelligence. He said technicians in certain fields can use prompts to get quick answers from AI, saving countless hours of analysis and letting them get straight to work on a problem. He said that for the business this means an increase in productivity and profits, but the business owners acknowledged that blind trust in AI is not realistic. He wrote that a human element must remain to ensure information is accurate and useful, and he drew a line between using AI as a tool for one's own work and using it to create work.

He gave the examples of a student checking spelling and grammar on an assignment and a photographer sharpening an image with certain forms of AI. Stallard said using AI to create work is not only risky but unethical, and that he could have entered a prompt asking AI to write the whole column and then slapped his name on it. He said he would not have been able to guarantee the information was factual, and he pointed to material flooding social media, some made for obvious fun and some created with the sole intention of deceiving. He wrote that people who recognize it call it "AI Slop," and that not everyone has those recognition factors.

He admitted to falling for a fake image at first, only to realize after closer inspection that he was being duped. He said he understands fears of AI agents taking all our jobs and doing all our thinking and decision making for us. Stallard wrote that from what he is seeing and learning so far, AI is not yet ready for the full-on takeover, and that we still need plenty of real intelligence to handle all the artificial stuff. He is a regular contributor to the Opinion page of The Lufkin Daily News, and his email address is garylstallard@gmail.com.

The column appeared under the headline "STALLARD: Artificial intelligence can't replace the real kind" and was tagged artificial intelligence. The page listed the column among the site's latest content and carried the paper's copyright notice for 2026. The Lufkin Daily News is located at 300 Ellis Ave., Lufkin, TX 75904, and its phone number is 936-632-6631. More to follow.

stories.Headline: IAB releases AI-Era Attribution Blueprint to classify AI's role in purchases
stories.Summary:
The Interactive Advertising Bureau, a trade organization representing the digital advertising industry, released a new framework designed to give the industry a way to account for the role artificial intelligence plays in purchases, according to a Thursday, Nov. 12 press release. The framework, called the AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, provides a way to classify AI's role in a conversion and to evaluate which parties can claim credit for it. The blueprint asks who or what created the intent, made the decision and completed the purchase, and it classifies each conversion as Human-Owned, AI-Assisted or AI-Executed. It also provides a pathway to determine which parties are eligible for a decision claim or a contributory claim, along with what evidence each claim requires.

Caroline Giegerich, vice president of AI at IAB, said in the release that the clicks and referrals long used for attribution are thinning out or disappearing, and that AI-influenced sales are sometimes reported as search or direct traffic, so companies may be sending their next marketing investment to the wrong channel. She said the AI-Era Attribution Blueprint works alongside existing attribution systems, defining the additional credit claims AI creates and the evidence each one requires. IAB CEO David Cohen said in the release that AI has added a new dimension to the existing challenge of determining how influence becomes an outcome. Cohen said the blueprint is honest about what the industry cannot yet substantiate, and he invited everyone in the ecosystem to apply it and help make AI's role in commerce more observable, verifiable and measurable.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report "From Prompt to Purchase: Who Wins the AI Shopper?" found in October that nearly 61 million consumers in the United States, or 23%, now name AI as their main starting point when researching retail purchases online. That report said a consumer who welcomes AI's advice can keep control of checkout, return to a trusted marketplace or delegate the purchase. It said the central finding is that AI is displacing established research habits faster than it is displacing established buying relationships. It added that advertising and product visibility face a different competitive challenge from the accounts, saved cards and delivery services that help secure the sale.

stories.Headline: Cyberattackers use AI to increase the speed and scale of phishing and malware operations
stories.Summary:
Cyberattackers are using artificial intelligence to increase the speed and scale of their operations, according to a report by writer John Leyden. These actors are not changing their core objectives or the basic techniques they employ as part of their attack chains. Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques used by these attackers to target their victims. AI tools have made these attacks easier to mount and cheaper for attackers who are relatively unskilled. This shift allows for a higher volume and velocity in the process of identifying and attacking targets.

In September 2025, Chinese state-sponsored actors abused Claude Code to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign known as GTG-1002. A ransomware campaign called JadePuffer was disclosed in July 2026 and used an LLM-driven agent to automate the intrusion chain. This campaign exploited CVE-2025-3248, which was a year-old missing-authentication flaw in the open-source framework called Langflow. Attackers used Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, because these platforms have significantly fewer content restrictions than Western alternatives. Some attackers also prefer using local models to gain operational security advantages or to avoid safeguards against malicious use.

Ronald Lewis of Black Duck says AI allows attackers to investigate more opportunities and try more approaches at a fast pace. Darren Meyer from Checkmarx states that adversaries are realizing gains in development velocity and operations similar to those of legitimate users. Nazar Tymoshyk of UnderDefense describes agentic APT as a threat where one person can deploy a coordinated team of specialists. Crystal Morin from Sysdig notes that AI-assisted attackers are shortening the detection windows that previously lasted for weeks or months. Nathan Smolenski of Qualys says frontier AI tools shrink the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation to near zero.

These attacks affect enterprises carrying years of technical debt because AI finds exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders patch. The shift toward agentic threats means that the only cost for an attacker is the inference budget for the model. This economic change means the number of attack attempts will likely go up as running complex attacks becomes cheaper. However, Morin notes that agents can be caught because they are noisy and often hallucinate during the attack process. JadePuffer demonstrated this by having flaws in its encryption, wallet, data exfiltration, and the text of its ransom note.

The background of these attacks involves a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated operations toward fully autonomous attacks with minimal human roles. Attackers use a modular design, switching between different models for reconnaissance, code generation, and the crafting of social engineering content. This allows a single attacker to combine the roles of a database admin, developer, IT engineer, DevOps specialist, and cloud architect. Traditional defense methods, such as 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets, are no longer sufficient to stop these threats. AI has expanded the attack surface through API calls, end-user devices, and ungoverned AI agents.

Organizations must now shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defenses while maintaining foundational security like authentication controls and patching. Smolenski suggests implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails to automate lower-level triage and focus human expertise on critical risk decisions. The articles leave open the question of how to accurately attribute attacks to specific models without infiltrating threat group infrastructure. Meyer warns that attributing particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation based on very thin evidence on the ground. It remains to be seen how defenders will balance automated responses with the need for human governance.

Articles.Title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI for bacterial resistance surveillance lacks rigorous external validation
stories.Summary:
A scoping review published in Discover Public Health on November 14, 2026, examined artificial intelligence and genomic technologies for bacterial antimicrobial resistance surveillance. The researchers synthesized findings from 27 peer-reviewed investigations published between January 2020 and March 2026 to evaluate predictive algorithms. These studies reported high overall accuracy, but the review found that real-world reliability is limited by geographic imbalances. The authors noted a lack of rigorous external validation for these computational models. This research highlights the gap between experimental accuracy and practical application in global health.

The review analyzed 27 studies, with 22 being relevant to low- and middle-income countries as defined by the World Bank. Predictive performance for bacterial pathogens ranged between 78% and 98% in terms of accuracy or area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Only 30% of the studies performed external validation using independent or cross-regional cohorts. Data came from Pakistan, Vietnam, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, Nigeria, China, the United States, and several multi-country African surveillance cohorts. The most studied organisms were Mycobacterium tuberculosis in seven studies and Escherichia coli in six studies.

The authors stated that current computational architectures often capture dataset-specific artifacts rather than biologically robust and generalizable resistance determinants. They argued that the existing literature is overwhelmingly skewed toward models designed and calibrated in wealthy regions. The researchers emphasized that resource-constrained settings often serve as peripheral sources of validation data rather than active development environments. They noted that genomic feature engineering influences final model performance more than the selection of complex machine learning architectures. The authors advocated for a transition toward data-centric systems design to prioritize representative sequencing repositories.

The review noted that antimicrobial resistance caused 1.27 million deaths and contributed to 4.95 million more fatalities worldwide in 2019. This crisis disproportionately impacts low- and middle-income countries where traditional diagnostic systems face substantial resource constraints. Conventional phenotypic testing is essential but slow, which may delay the detection of emerging or complex resistance mechanisms. The research found that only nine of 27 studies met the One Health criterion of using isolates from two or more reservoirs. This indicates that the empirical integration of human, animal, and environmental health remains strikingly underdeveloped.

The background shows that whole-genome sequencing and pan-genomic approaches enable high-resolution identification of resistance determinants and tracking of pathogen evolution. Coupling these with machine learning provides an automated mechanism to infer phenotypic resistance directly from raw genomic sequence data. The review used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews and the Joanna Briggs Institute framework. Initial searches across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, Google Scholar, bioRxiv, and medRxiv retrieved 1,150 candidate records. After screening, 74 full-text manuscripts were assessed before the final 27 were selected.

Future progress requires overcoming computational, infrastructural, and methodological barriers to move from proof-of-concept models to functional public health surveillance networks. The authors called for mandatory external validation across independent, cross-country datasets as a standard benchmark for all future publications. They suggested using standardized evaluation reporting including sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-scores, and calibration metrics. Federated learning frameworks were highlighted as promising pathways to facilitate cross-border collaborative training while safeguarding national biological data sovereignty. The articles leave open the question of whether multi-reservoir data integration provides a quantifiable boost to predictive accuracy.

Articles.Title: Genomic Machine Learning Shows High Accuracy but Limited Validation in Global Surveillance

stories.headline_source: Genomic Machine Learning Shows High Accuracy but Limited Validation in Global Surveillance

stories.Headline: Ghana deploys AI faster than its regulators can supervise it, researchers find
stories.Summary:
Ghana’s artificial intelligence deployment across finance, healthcare, agriculture, digital services and public administration is expanding faster than the institutions meant to supervise its risks, according to a qualitative investigation of the country’s National Innovation System. Researchers Benedict Afful Jr. and Kassim Alabani evaluated Ghana’s institutional environment to determine whether it has the operational capacity, cross-agency coordination and statutory authority to enforce responsible artificial intelligence standards. Their empirical findings show an uneven, system-wide governance readiness gap rather than a total absence of governance mechanisms. Ghana launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025, 2035 on April 24, 2026, and participated in UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology. Formal policy ambition has developed ahead of the technical competence, routine advisory channels and enforcement capabilities of implementing state bodies.

The researchers combined National Innovation Systems theory with Technological Innovation Systems functional analysis and normative governance benchmarks set by UNESCO and the African Union. They collected qualitative evidence from 32 purposively selected institutional leaders across Ghana’s innovation landscape. The sample included eight participants from universities and research institutes, six from commercial technology firms and industry, six from government regulatory and policy agencies, four from financial institutions, four from intermediary bodies such as technology hubs and incubators, and four boundary-spanning actors. Data collection used a three-part qualitative protocol of vignette-based scenarios, triadic elicitation and the Critical Incident Technique, with each semi-structured session lasting 60 to 90 minutes. Data were evaluated through reflexive thematic analysis using NVivo software.

The authors termed their central theoretical contribution the Governance Readiness Paradox, a structural condition in which commercial deployment and high-level strategy accelerate faster than the institutional capacity required to convert technical evidence into enforceable, accountable and legally sound public oversight. They built a systemic failure typology of four mutually reinforcing mechanisms: capability failures, connectivity failures, legitimacy failures and resource failures. They triangulated documents against publicly available policy frameworks such as the Data Protection Act 2012 and the National AI Strategy 2025, 2035. They maintained analytic reflexivity and conducted member checking with selected informants to verify findings while protecting participants from deductive identification. They developed the Ghana AI Governance Readiness Matrix, which cross-tabulates innovation system components against the four international governance pillars of safety and security, transparency, accountability and inclusion.

Academic respondents reported severe barriers when transmitting technical insights into public policymaking, and a completed study evaluating automated credit-screening discrimination in domestic financial technology had no formal institutional pipeline to translate findings into regulatory briefs or actionable policy interventions. Academic research agendas were found to be predominantly driven by international donor funding, which rewarded technical performance metrics such as processing velocity and model sophistication while giving negligible incentives for governance-oriented inquiry, ethical evaluation or local policy relevance. Industry participants said corporate legal counsel routinely advises silence to minimize corporate liability in the absence of explicit statutory disclosure duties. A documented critical incident from the financial sector involved an internal corporate audit that revealed an automated credit-scoring model assigning systematically depressed scores to applicants from three northern regions despite repayment records comparable to other applicants, and the firm recalibrated the model entirely internally, omitting regulatory notification, affected customer disclosures or independent remediation. Regulatory officials acknowledged that internal personnel lacked the specialized technical expertise to draft credible assessments independently for a vignette requiring a 48-hour parliamentary briefing on an emerging artificial intelligence incident, while possessing no formal procedures to commission academic assistance on short notice.

Although statutory bodies such as the Data Protection Commission and the National Information Technology Agency maintain defined mandates, cross-agency coordination remains fragmented. Critical incident accounts showed that successful knowledge transfer from researchers to state bodies occurred almost exclusively through informal personal connections, temporary academic secondments or prior individual relationships rather than durable administrative routines. When key personnel resigned, retired or concluded donor-funded contracts, institutional memory and advisory channels collapsed. Commercial banks and investment actors routinely evaluated technology through conventional operational and reputational risk categories, completely lacking dedicated criteria to assess artificial intelligence safety, data provenance or algorithmic fairness. Intermediary bodies, including technology hubs, accelerators and university technology transfer offices, operated effectively as commercial bridges connecting startups to private capital and markets, but their potential role as regulatory bridges remained entirely unactivated, and entrepreneurship training curricula omitted instruction on regulatory compliance, legal liability and ethical deployment.

Chronic resource shortages acted as a systemic multiplier, with domestic funding lines dedicated to public sector artificial intelligence research, regulatory monitoring and expert technical staffing virtually nonexistent, leaving institutions reliant on fragmented, temporary external assistance. Component ratings on the Ghana AI Governance Readiness Matrix ranged from very low to moderate across dimensions, illustrating fragmented integration rather than absolute institutional absence. Systemic failures propagated through self-reinforcing cycles: missing diffusion pipelines left regulators without technical evidence, low regulatory capability created ambiguous market oversight, ambiguous expectations discouraged private firms and financiers from investing in auditing routines, and an absence of domestic governance demand incentivized universities to prioritize externally funded technical projects over public policy translation. The matrix identified relative institutional assets that can serve as foundations for reform, including existing academic expertise, emerging policy frameworks, boundary-spanning professionals and international market linkages. The authors formulated eight sequenced policy recommendations distributed across three distinct implementation phases spanning five years.

Phase I focuses on low-cost structural alignment, establishing a national cross-agency coordination mechanism, creating an interim expert roster to channel university research into regulatory processes, and integrating civil society into National AI Strategy implementation. Phase II establishes dedicated artificial intelligence units within sectoral regulatory bodies, launches structured institutional secondments between universities and public agencies, pilots proportionate impact assessments, and institutes a domestic research funding window to mitigate external donor dependency. Phase III consolidates professional certifications, according to the article, which ends there. The articles leave open what Phase III’s remaining measures are and whether any of the eight recommendations have been adopted.

stories.Headline: Mahmut Özer argues AI marks a turning point in human-machine relations
stories.Summary:
Mahmut Özer published a column in the Daily Sabah on Nov 14, 2026, at 12:05 am GMT+3, arguing that artificial intelligence marks a historic turning point in human-machine relations. He wrote that AI is transforming societies at an unprecedented pace and differs fundamentally from previous technological breakthroughs. He said an entirely new technological ecosystem centered on artificial intelligence is emerging as fields from education and health care to industry, the economy, biotechnology and defense are transformed. He noted that this rapid transformation generates excitement and expectations across all segments of society while also intensifying concerns and anxieties. He observed that perhaps no previous technological development has evoked these two contrasting emotions simultaneously and with such intensity.

Özer wrote that humanity has used machines first to expand physical capabilities, then to automate repetitive tasks, and finally to begin transferring certain cognitive activities to machines. He said artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, is entering a broader domain encompassing not only what humans do but also how they think, interpret information, solve problems and generate new content. He said AI can in some cases directly substitute for human thinking and creative processes, and that for the first time humans face the possibility of routinely delegating their own cognitive activities to machines on a widespread scale. He cited recent experimental studies suggesting certain cognitive processes associated with critical thinking, independent problem-solving and memory may be adversely affected, particularly when AI tools are used as substitutes for individuals' own thinking. He said these effects vary depending on how AI tools are used.

Özer said AI technology is increasingly reshaping social stratification, introducing new divisions based on skill levels alongside traditional distinctions of class and social status. He warned that a new divide may emerge between those who can use AI technologies effectively and those who become dependent on the ready-made outputs these technologies provide. He said significant differences in skills and capabilities may develop even among individuals who use the very same technology, and that what ultimately matters is not simply access but the nature of the relationship individuals establish with the tools. He described a potentially dangerous cycle of cognitive dependence in which delegating thinking, analysis and problem-solving to AI reduces mental effort, weakens the ability to perform these tasks independently, and increases the need for the tools. He said this cycle may also cause people to feel inadequate when they cannot access AI tools.

Özer said AI tools can reproduce biases embedded in their training data and present information with no basis in reality in an extremely convincing manner, making it essential to evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated content before using it as is. He warned that when cognitive processes are increasingly delegated to machines and dependence grows, the very capacity to verify such information may be undermined, magnifying the scale of potential harm. He raised the question of agency in content production, asking who is the actual agent behind a product when virtually any type of content can be produced rapidly and at negligible cost. He said research suggests that when agency shifts from humans to machines, individuals may become alienated from the products they generate and may struggle to recall even basic details of content produced only a short time earlier, indicating a weakening of memory. He said a substantial decline in the diversity and richness of arguments has been observed, particularly in written texts.

Özer cited TurkStat's 2026 statistics on artificial intelligence, which indicate that use of AI for professional purposes remains considerably more limited than for personal purposes. He said approximately 86.4% of individuals using these technologies in 2026, compared with 80% in 2025, reported using them for personal purposes, while only 37.3%, compared with 33.8% in 2025, reported using them for professional purposes. He said these figures suggest that although AI adoption is rapidly expanding in Türkiye, this expansion has not been reflected to the same extent in professional applications and consequently in professional productivity. He said the difference in purposes of AI use does not by itself reveal the level of awareness or skill with which individuals use these tools, and that there is a need to measure not only the prevalence of AI use but also the quality of that use. He said the extent to which individuals remain actively engaged in cognitive processes, how thoroughly they verify AI-generated content, whether they preserve independent problem-solving abilities, and whether they can translate AI use into professional productivity have become fundamental questions requiring systematic investigation.

Özer said a pedagogical framework for human-machine relations is needed that does not diminish human participation in cognitive processes, continuously maintains awareness of the need to evaluate the accuracy of generated content, and ensures that agency over the final product remains with humans. He said the central issue in the age of artificial intelligence is not how widely these technologies are adopted but where human beings stand within this new relationship. He asked whether we can preserve our abilities to think, question, verify and create while using artificial intelligence, or whether we are gradually delegating these abilities to machines and becoming increasingly dependent on the capabilities they provide. He suggested the defining distinction between societies in the future may not be who has greater access to AI technologies but who is better able to preserve human cognitive autonomy while using them. He said the most important educational challenge of the AI age is not merely to raise individuals who know how to use these technologies but to cultivate individuals who can strengthen, rather than surrender, their ability to think, question and create.

stories.Headline: GE Healthcare ultrasound AI overcounts lung B-lines versus expert physicians in Swedish study
stories.Summary:
A prospective clinical investigation at Skåne University Hospital in Sweden found that an automated artificial intelligence tool in a commercial point-of-care ultrasound system substantially overcounts pulmonary B-lines compared with visual reviews by expert physicians. The single-center evaluation covered fifty-five hospitalized patients with acute respiratory symptoms, primarily acutely decompensated heart failure. Investigators found poor statistical agreement between the algorithm and experienced human evaluators, driven largely by overestimation across multiple anatomical thoracic zones. The software tested was the automated B-line application embedded in the Venue GO point-of-care ultrasound platform made by General Electric Healthcare. The tool highlights and quantifies B-lines in real time across captured video loops and logs the frame with the maximum artifact count to assign a score for each scanned lung zone.

Examinations were done at the bedside by an internal medicine resident in point-of-care ultrasound training, using a curved low-frequency transducer at a standard depth of sixteen centimeters. A standardized twelve-zone thoracic protocol was used: four anterolateral zones on each side with the patient supine at forty-five degrees, then two dorsal zones on each side with the patient sitting upright. Each sector was captured for four to five seconds in the sagittal plane between adjacent ribs, and a single operator acquired every video loop across all fifty-five subjects. The tool assigned each zone a category of zero, one, two, three, four, or greater than five B-lines, recording 672 thoracic zone clips. Two independent physician experts, a cardiologist and an internal medicine consultant who directs a regional point-of-care ultrasound training academy, classified B-lines into brackets of zero, one to two, three to four, and five or more while blinded to the software.

Of the 672 clips, 574, or eighty-five percent, were eligible for statistical analysis. Ninety-eight clips were excluded: eleven for insufficient image quality, twenty-six for no identifiable pleural line, and fifty-one for pleural effusions. Twenty-two of the twenty-six clips lacking a clear pleural reflection occurred in the second left anterior zone, where cardiac motion obscured the pulmonary field. Pleural effusions were found mostly in the dependent posterior inferior zones, sixty-three percent of effusion findings, with twenty-nine percent in the lateral chest regions. The median B-line count by the artificial intelligence platform was 23.5 per patient versus 2.8 per patient by visual reviewers, a statistically significant difference.

The automated platform classified thirty-eight percent of assessed zones into the highest category of more than five B-lines, while experts assigned only four percent to that category. The software showed a bimodal distribution, with forty-eight percent of readings at zero and thirty-eight percent at greater than five, and only thirteen percent between one and four B-lines. The intraclass correlation coefficient between software and experts reached only 0.28 for the total patient B-line sum and 0.37 zone by zone, while interrater reliability between the two human experts was excellent at 0.92 and 0.91. Bland-Altman analysis showed a systematic positive bias of 1.86 with a standard deviation of 2.15 and ninety-five percent limits of agreement from negative 2.35 to positive 6.07. Among the 574 analyzed zones, fourteen percent of algorithmic errors came from the software tracking acoustic data in adjacent rib spaces rather than the central intercostal target.

In one percent of zones the software mistook subpleural consolidations with irregular acoustic shred lines, also called C-lines, for true vertical B-lines, and in another one percent it counted normal rib shadowing as pathologic vertical artifacts. Correlation was poorest in anterior zone two and posterior superior zone five, where overcounting was most pronounced, and better in the lateral and posterior inferior sectors. Reviewers recorded significantly higher total B-line sums in hypervolemic patients than in euvolemic individuals, averaging 4.6 versus 0.75 artifacts. The authors noted recruitment from a single medical center, reliance on a single image operator, and software capping granular counting at five artifacts per sector. To align categorization schemes, researchers assigned software values of one or two to 1.5 and values of three or four to 3.5 to mirror expert score ranges.

An initial evaluation by Short and colleagues cited in platform marketing materials documented an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.79 using the same software, but that study evaluated only four patients. Later assessments found lower concordance, such as an evaluation by Russell and colleagues reporting 0.56 between automated scoring and expert review. An investigation by Damodaran and colleagues in patients with viral respiratory infections recorded intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.52 to 0.53, borderline moderate agreement closer to the Swedish cohort. The Swedish study used an upright twelve-zone method including dorsal regions, whereas recent heart failure research suggests a simplified two-zone anterior-superior protocol can yield comparable diagnostic utility to an eight-zone exam. Current commercial point-of-care tools rely mainly on prespecified image-processing rules that struggle with rib margins or tissue consolidations.

The researchers concluded that automated B-line quantification in current commercial point-of-care hardware requires further algorithmic refinement before it can be safely relied upon for autonomous clinical decision-making. They noted that future improvements likely depend on deep-learning neural networks trained on extensive imaging datasets coupled with expert human visual validation. True cardiogenic B-lines generate smooth pleural reflections in a diffuse pattern, whereas comet-tail artifacts from other pulmonary disorders feature irregular, fragmented pleural reflections with narrow heads and wide tails, and the platform may struggle to differentiate these presentations. The articles do not state whether the software's manufacturer has responded to the findings or whether regulatory action followed. They also do not say whether a follow-up study or software update is planned.

stories.Headline: Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce opens public voting for nine awards finalists
stories.Summary:
Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce announced nine finalists for the inaugural Pro-Human AI Elevation Awards and opened public voting to Utah residents, according to a November 13, 2026 announcement reported by TechBuzz News. Voting runs through November 20. Winners will be announced December 8 at the 2026 Utah Pro-Human AI Summit at the Grand America. The awards recognize Utah-connected companies using artificial intelligence to empower workers, strengthen communities, and build human-centered principles into technology.

The nine finalists are grouped into three categories. Workforce Elevation, for companies using AI to help employees do more, learn faster, and develop new skills, includes ARUP Laboratories, Techcyte, Inc., and XL PR. Community Advancement, for companies using AI to address needs in areas such as healthcare, education, public safety, and government, includes Leland Makombo, Skill Struck, and Pro-Human Breakthrough, which covers companies building AI products with accountability as part of their design, includes Autonomous Solutions Inc. (ASI), Elnora, and Glacis Technologies, Inc. Each Utah resident must affirm residency and may submit only one ballot, selecting one finalist per category and separately nominating one of the nine for the overall grand prize. The public vote determines the winners in all three categories and contributes to selection of the grand prize recipient.

Gov. Spencer J. Cox said artificial intelligence should make people's lives better and help workers succeed, and that the companies are showing what that can look like in practice. He said the state wants to recognize their work and challenge more businesses to put people at the center of how they build and use the technology. Jefferson Moss, commissioner of the Governor's Office of Economic Development, said Utah has built a strong innovation economy and that a wave of companies are developing and using AI in ways that put people first. He said the awards recognize those companies, share what they are doing, and encourage more of this kind of innovation, and that the state wants an economic environment and a Summit that make clear human-centric AI is how Utah does business.

The awards are organized by Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce and spotlight companies that emphasize human agency, dignity, and accountability rather than simply automating tasks or replacing people. The effort builds on the 2025 Utah AI Summit at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City, which advanced the state's push to shape AI around human agency, workforce empowerment, and responsible innovation. Residents can review the finalists through their videos and cast ballots through the official online voting form. Winners will be recognized at the December 8 summit, and more information is available at aisummit.utah.gov.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid investigation into relationship with suspected Chinese agent
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 15, 2026, following an investigation into his personal relationship with a Chinese businesswoman. Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean cloud company Megaspeed, was suspected by United States intelligence of working for Beijing. The investigation focused on whether Megaspeed helped divert advanced Nvidia processors to China, which would violate strict export controls. This situation highlights the vulnerability of national security when strategic power is concentrated within private technology corporations.

The controversy involves the distribution of graphics processing units that are essential for military research and artificial intelligence. A Reuters report from November 13 identified over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects that utilized these restricted processors. These findings suggest that Chinese firms may bypass direct chip export bans by using overseas data centers. The United States government has spent years tightening restrictions to prevent China from gaining a technological advantage in AI.

Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that the Justice Department has not concluded that Alice Huang was a spy. There is currently no public evidence that Nvidia's proprietary information or national security secrets were compromised. Beijing has rejected all espionage allegations, and the relationship may have been a personal affair without intelligence dimensions. Officials are now questioning how to safeguard a technological ecosystem where private interests often conflict with national security priorities.

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI improves geodesign modeling but creates ethical and data reliability challenges
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a review in Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning on November 13, 2026, regarding spatial planning methodologies. They determined that integrating artificial intelligence into geodesign improves environmental modeling and territorial data analysis. This integration also introduces critical challenges regarding ethical governance, interpretability, and data reliability. The authors establish that these computational tools augment human expertise rather than replacing professional judgment. The study examines the evolution of geospatial design from early systems into modern computational frameworks.

The process utilizes a framework by Steinitz based on six interconnected models including representation, process, evaluation, change, impact, and decision. These models answer six core questions divided into understanding existing systems and designing future changes. The first three questions investigate how a study area is described, how it operates, and if it works well. The final three questions evaluate how areas might be altered, what impacts modifications cause, and how to implement decisions. This system builds on the 1960s Canada Geographic Information System by Tomlinson and the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics.

The authors of the review state that traditional overlay mapping is static and struggles with dynamic social and ecological systems. They note that conventional site suitability assessments are labor intensive and often neglect broader regional implications. The researchers explain that environmental impact assessments frequently overlook cumulative impacts, which risks underestimating true environmental degradation. They argue that physical models and manual sketches are time consuming and lack precision for large scale quantitative evaluation. The authors further claim that participatory planning often faces disputes and allows vocal groups to overshadow others.

Planners and non technical stakeholders are affected by the shift from manual sketches to generative artificial intelligence. Zhang and colleagues used convolutional neural networks in Wuhan, China, to achieve superior land cover classification performance. Chen and colleagues used hierarchical convolutional recurrent neural networks to monitor forest cover. Johannsen and Oh developed deep learning models to improve predictions of urban heat island patterns. Aslam and Satarzadeh used hybrid models to enhance hazard predictions for landslides and floods, respectively.

Geodesign roots trace back to the 1960s and the work of Tomlinson on digital infrastructure for geographically referenced datasets. McHarg established an ecological planning paradigm in Design with Nature using layered mapping of soil, vegetation, and hydrology. Modern tools now include convolutional neural networks for imagery and recurrent neural networks for predicting urban growth trajectories. Transformer architectures and generative adversarial networks now synthesize urban layouts and simulate potential environmental impacts. Diffusion models and variational autoencoders are used to visualize flood patterns and explore alternative landscape configurations.

Future applications include using the non dominated sorting genetic algorithm to balance infrastructure cost efficiency and environmental sustainability. Planners may use ridge, multiple linear, and logistic regression to handle spatial variables and categorize development suitability. However, the articles leave open how to address the lack of spatial data in less developed regions. They do not resolve the black box problem where model complexity obscures the rationale behind design decisions. The text leaves unresolved the risks of algorithmic bias and covert privacy breaches in large training datasets.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Geodesign Methods While Facing Interpretability And Data Challenges

stories.Headline: Findlay plans to adopt AI rules with a proposal expected soon
stories.Summary:
Findlay still plans to adopt rules for artificial intelligence, according to a report published by The Courier on November 13, 2026, which said a proposal is expected soon but gave no date for a vote or any details of what the rules would contain. The article carried no name of any official who wrote or backed the plan, and it did not say which board or office would consider it. The report appeared under a local news heading on the newspaper's website, alongside other items about elected officials' salaries and a road closure. No draft text, no timeline and no cost figure appeared in the article as published.

The piece said only that Findlay still plans AI rules and that a proposal is expected soon, so the changes the rules would bring remain unknown from the article. It gave no number of rules, no effective date and no mention of who would enforce them. The only date in the report was November 13, 2026, the day the item was posted. The article also noted that Lima Avenue would remain closed until November 17, a separate matter with no stated link to the AI plan.

The articles named no responsible official and carried no statement from any city leader, so no one could be paraphrased on the record about the plan. No quoted words from a mayor, council member or staff member appeared in the text. The report did not say whether the proposal comes from the city, a committee or another body. Readers were left without a named source for the expected rules.

The context is thin, because the article did not explain why Findlay wants AI rules or what prompted the plan. It did not say what happens next beyond the expectation of a proposal soon. No public hearing, comment period or council vote was listed in the report. The newspaper's page offered newsletters and other local stories but no further detail on the AI proposal.

stories.Headline: VA refreshes VA.gov with new sign-in options and plain language search to simplify veteran access
stories.Summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs announced a refreshed VA.gov on Nov. 11, 2026, with updates meant to simplify how veterans reach health care and benefits information. The changes include new CLEAR and Passkey sign-in options, which join existing Login.gov and ID.me credentials. The site also gained a search function that lets veterans ask questions in plain language. The department said the upgrades responded to nearly 90,000 veteran survey responses from March through May 2026, and veterans tested the updates before release. The refresh also added a way for veterans to check application status through links sent by text message, which Zach Schwartz called magic links and which do not require signing in.

The VA streamlined its QuickSubmit document tool so veterans can upload documents in three steps instead of 11. Schwartz, principal deputy assistant secretary for the Office of Information and Technology, said Friday that more releases are coming around January. He described the work as a cadence of regular incremental wins rather than a one-time overhaul. Schwartz said the VA is working closely with the newly launched America.gov to support AI tools on VA.gov, and he said the department is refocusing its solutions to be friendly to what the Trump administration calls SI, or super intelligence. He said the VA needs the most help in that area, particularly from industry.

He added that VA.gov is a beast and that the department wants to make it easier and more secure and meet veterans where they are. He also said the VA wants to serve as an example for other federal agencies adopting AI. Schwartz said he was meeting Friday with new Federal Chief Information Officer Carter Farmer, who he said wants to understand how the VA is pushing out so much in the SI space. He said Farmer wants the department to continue to be a representative example for many other agencies. The article does not say what specific updates are planned for the January releases.

Articles.Title: VA plans further VA.gov updates as it looks to expand AI integration

stories.Headline: Nobel laureates meet in Stockholm on 9 December 2026 to discuss artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Nobel Prize laureates and other leading thinkers will meet in Stockholm on 9 December 2026 for the Nobel Week Dialogue, an event organized by Nobel Prize Outreach to discuss artificial intelligence. The gathering will run from 10:00 to 15:30 at House of People in Stockholm. The speakers include Philippe Aghion, who won the economic sciences prize in 2025, Steven Chu, physics 1997, John Jumper, chemistry 2024, and David MacMillan, chemistry 2021. The announcement was made in a press release dated 13 November 2026.

The event will examine the opportunities, risks and choices that come with life in the age of AI, according to the release. It says AI tools are rapidly becoming more powerful, with advocates highlighting potential benefits for humanity and major scientific advances, while others warn of risks to society, work, education and democracy. The release asks why experts are so divided and how the path to living with AI should be mapped so its benefits are shared as fully as possible. The event is fully booked, but media can apply to take part using a registration form, and all interviews must be booked in advance.

The release states that the Nobel Week Dialogue is held in Stockholm every other year and in Gothenburg every other year. It is organized by Nobel Prize Outreach in collaboration with Carl Bennet AB, the City of Gothenburg, Royalty Pharma and Volvo Group. The release describes the event as an annual conference on 9 December in Nobel Week that brings together scientists, policy-makers and thinkers for sessions and working groups on a topical science-related theme. It says the aim is to deepen dialogue between the scientific community and the rest of society on issues connected with the Nobel Prize and important to the world.

The release notes that this year marks the 125th anniversary of the Nobel Prize. In September, the Nobel Foundation announced that the Nobel Prize amount would rise to SEK 12 million per prize category, an increase of SEK 1 million from the previous year. This year's laureates were announced from 5 to 12 October. The release does not say what will follow the dialogue.

stories.Headline: Researchers show AI improves clinical decisions in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology
stories.Summary:
Researchers Jeffrey S. Barrett, Catherine M. Sherwin, and Samuel L. Seward Jr. published an editorial on November 14, 2026, in Frontiers in Pharmacology. They synthesized six original research studies showing how artificial intelligence and digital devices can improve clinical decisions in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology. These studies integrated routinely gathered patient data with pharmacological principles to address historical data gaps in these evidence-poor areas of practice. The researchers examined individualized antibiotic dosing, neonatal laboratory prediction, wearable maternal monitoring, labor analgesia efficacy, post-puncture pain reduction, and intelligent prescribing systems. This work highlights how machine learning and predictive analytics can augment healthcare providers who previously relied on empirical, weight-based dosing regimens.

Zhang and colleagues used a hybrid model with SHAP to identify drug clearance, dose, weight, and renal function as determinants for linezolid dosing. Westvik and colleagues analyzed blood gas, anthropometric, and nutritional data to find that small-for-gestational-age status is a risk factor for neonatal hypophosphatemia. Li and colleagues tested a consumer smartwatch for cesarean delivery hypotension, finding a sensitivity of 79.2 percent and a specificity of 82.0 percent. Wang and He used an XGBoost model on 137 parturients for labor analgesia, seeing performance drop from 0.875 to 0.759 during validation. He and colleagues studied 473 women to find nalbuphine-ropivacaine infiltration reduced post-puncture pain, using an XGBoost model with an area under the curve of 0.912.

The editorial authors stated that institutional databases and predictive algorithms are complementary components of modern clinical workflows rather than competing methodologies. They emphasized that clinical utility depends strictly on population-specific evidence rather than generalized technological expectations or enthusiasm for new technology. The authors argued that human clinical oversight must be preserved whenever algorithmic systems inform drug selection, precision dosing, or therapeutic interventions. They noted that successful clinical adoption depends on governance, institutional workflow integration, and health information system interoperability to mitigate clinician alert fatigue. Finally, they asserted that the greatest opportunity for artificial intelligence is augmenting decision-making by integrating routine clinical data with pharmacological knowledge.

The researchers noted that clinicians have historically lacked evidence because dynamic physiological changes across pregnancy and childhood alter how drugs are disposed. This lack of data meant providers often ignored biological variability when using standard weight-based dosing for vulnerable pediatric and maternal populations. In China, Wu and colleagues addressed this by building the first Pediatric Rational Medication Intelligent Decision System for institutional healthcare execution. This platform contains over 400,000 entries for 1,030 medications, covering dosing rules, drug-drug interactions, infusion parameters, pharmacogenomics, and traditional Chinese medicines. This system connected to hospital information for real-time biochemistry access, which significantly decreased higher-severity prescription warnings across various clinical services.

The articles explain that model-informed approaches extract more utility from existing observations, such as blood gas parameters, without adding procedural burdens. However, the hybrid modeling research warns that using identical concentration data for both inputs and predictions can produce overly optimistic validation. The obstetric studies show that consumer wearables should be screening aids rather than autonomous diagnostic replacements due to reduced sensitivity during mild hypotension. Additionally, the authors clarify that SHAP values reflect statistical associations within an algorithmic structure rather than definitive biological or causal mechanisms. These findings suggest that therapeutic interventions identified through observational machine learning still require confirmation through rigorous, prospective, and controlled clinical trials.

Future applications must move from retrospective single-center analyses into prospective multicenter evaluations to ensure calibration and transportability across diverse health systems. Critical validation priorities include assessing the impact on clinical workflows and the direct effects on maternal and pediatric health outcomes. Researchers must establish rigorous, leakage-free prospective validation protocols before hybrid predictive dosing tools can safely reach the patient bedside. The articles leave open how these systems will be integrated into different global health infrastructures and how they will evolve. They also leave open the specific results of the required prospective trials needed to confirm the biological mechanisms of the AI findings.

stories.Headline: Gaurav Kansal reviews how AI improves solar photovoltaic reliability and forecasting
stories.Summary:
Gaurav Kansal published a comprehensive review article in Discover Applied Sciences on November 14, 2026. The paper evaluates how artificial intelligence can be integrated into solar photovoltaic systems to improve reliability and forecasting. This research characterizes the use of machine learning as a breakthrough for solar energy generation. The author used systematic queries of ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Scopus to gather data.

The integration requires advanced computational frameworks to optimize energy conversion efficiency and system operation. Specifically, the review focuses on power generation forecasting, operational fault diagnosis, image-based inspection, and cybersecurity. It highlights the use of genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization to improve maximum power point tracking. However, the author notes that these changes require significant data management, high computational power, and constant model maintenance.

Gaurav Kansal is responsible for the synthesis, which identifies current research gaps and practical hurdles. He explained that while AI offers technical advantages, the complexity of real-world deployment remains a serious challenge for operators. He suggested that these tools can eventually reduce the global reliance on traditional energy sources. The author also pointed to emerging solutions such as edge computing, few-shot learning, and transfer learning.

This work provides a foundation for more intelligent system operations by analyzing existing literature. The review suggests that continuing advancements in hardware and algorithms will facilitate the integration of renewable energy. Future research directions will likely focus on the emerging solutions mentioned in the paper. These developments aim to overcome the current operational challenges facing solar installations.

stories.Headline: FedRAMP requires certified cloud providers to adopt AI-era vulnerability rules by Dec 7
stories.Summary:
FedRAMP, the General Services Administration's cloud security program, issued a notice on Nov. 10, 2026 requiring certified cloud services to adopt new vulnerability detection and response rules, along with new vulnerability evaluation and reporting rules, by Dec. 7. The rules respond to how artificial intelligence is helping hackers speed up attacks on unpatched software bugs. They align with a July binding operational directive from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on prioritizing security updates based on risk. FedRAMP said vendors can submit corrective action plans for any requirement they cannot meet by that date.

The program is giving vendors a three-month grace period through March 7, 2027 to meet the requirements. On March 8, any cloud service that has not fully migrated or is not working under an approved corrective action plan will have its FedRAMP certification revoked and be banned from FedRAMP for one year. The new rules will require more than 550 certified providers to move from legacy vulnerability scanning to an exposure and threat-based approach. Providers must weigh factors such as whether a vulnerability is likely reachable over the internet and how far it can be exploited. In early December, FedRAMP plans to start a quarterly security inbox emergency test to collect progress reports, and a service that fails to respond goes into remediation status on the FedRAMP marketplace for at least 30 days.

FedRAMP officials wrote that the primary concern of the U.S. government is that certified providers migrate to the new approach swiftly, safely and appropriately. They said the program will not take unnecessary administrative action against services that work safely and in good faith to adopt the rules. They also wrote that the urgency of the threat has only increased since then, pointing to the recent Black October incidents across the global information security community. Matt Bruggeman, director of GTM Federal at A-LIGN, told Federal News Network that the change is drastic compared with how vendors worked before and that it has been a pretty big uplift, with many providers looking for new third-party tools.

The July CISA directive was developed in reaction to the quickly evolving cyber capabilities of models like Anthropic's Claude Mythos. FedRAMP officials wrote that the mandatory migration is only the first of many migrations providers will need to make over the coming years and that yearly paperwork exercises are no longer appropriate or sufficient. FedRAMP Director Pete Waterman said earlier this year, after a Hugging Face hack by OpenAI agents, that vendors who only equate FedRAMP with compliance are cooked. Under the FedRAMP 20X initiative, the program is shifting to more automated, real-time security monitoring rather than large authorization document packages.

Articles.Title: FedRAMP pushes new cyber vulnerability rules to keep pace with AI

stories.Summary:
First Parish on the Common at 75 The Great Road in Bedford will hold a free, multigenerational “Food for Thought” conversation about artificial intelligence and how it is shaping people’s lives on Saturday, Nov. 21, from 6 to 8 p.m. at the church. The Bedford Citizen reported the event on Nov. 13, 2026, under the theme “AI, AI, Oh My! Navigating Our Brave New World.” The evening will be a conversation about the impact of artificial intelligence on the daily lives of children and adults alike.

First Parish will provide pizza and salads, and everyone is free to bring a side dish or dessert to share. Nathan Sellers, director of faith development for children at First Parish, said the church intends to host these conversations regularly throughout the church year. An earlier session in November 2025 focused on the effects of bullying online, at school, at work, and in society at large. to 7:30 p.m. in Anderson Hall at HCC’s Emerging Technologies Building. The presentation is titled “AI Today and Tommorow,” according to the Kentucky New Era. The 90-minute presentation will explore the current state of artificial intelligence, emerging opportunities and its potential effects on local businesses, employment, education and everyday life. The event will feature Dr. Ryan Hall, AI and innovation lead for strategy and governance at Owensboro Community and Technical College and the Kentucky Community and Technical College System.

Hall brings experience in artificial intelligence, workforce innovation and educational leadership. He also helps guide Kentucky’s 16 community and technical colleges through AI implementation and strategy. The presentation is designed for a broad audience and will conclude with an opportunity for attendees to participate in a community Q&A session. The event is free and open to the public, according to a press release. The Bedford event is one of the conversations First Parish intends to host regularly throughout the church year, Sellers said.

stories.Headline: TSMC creates 500 million dollar fund to invest in chip startups and upstream partners
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. announced plans to establish a new venture fund on November 13, 2026, to support promising chip startups. This strategic move aims to identify and back the next industry titans similar to Broadcom or Nvidia during the current artificial intelligence boom. The world's largest contract chipmaker intends to use this financial vehicle to broaden its existing ecosystem of partners. By investing in these emerging companies, the firm hopes to secure its position within the rapidly evolving semiconductor landscape. The company will allocate 500 million dollars to this new fund for investing in chip startups and upstream partners.

These resources are specifically designed to aid suppliers and other critical entities that contribute to the chipmaking process. This initiative represents an effort to formalize the investment activities of the organization as demand for chips remains insatiable. The fund will target companies that possess the potential to grow into major players within the global technology market. Kevin Zhang, who serves as the senior vice president and deputy co-chief operating officer, discussed these plans during an interview in Tokyo.

He spoke with Nikkei Asia on the sidelines of the Nikkei Forum Global Management Dialogue 2026 to explain the vision. Zhang stated that the company does not only want to support the current version of Nvidia but also the future version. He believes that fostering new talent and innovation is essential for the continued growth of the entire semiconductor industry. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Chris Miller says post-Jensen Nvidia must reshuffle leadership and reset Washington ties
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published an opinion piece by Chris Miller on 15 November 2026 under a headline about what a post-Jensen Nvidia will look like. The article as supplied consists only of a paywall page, so the body text is not available. The headline says a post-Jensen Nvidia must reshuffle its leadership, reset its ties in Washington and recognize that even the most valuable US company cannot dictate US foreign policy. No further details of what happened, who did it or when are given in the available text.

The only date the articles give is the publication date of 15 November 2026, and the only name they give is Jensen Huang, referred to in the headline as Jensen. The headline sets out three tasks for Nvidia after his era: reshuffling its leadership, resetting its Washington ties and accepting limits on its influence over US foreign policy. The articles give no numbers beyond that date and no other named people. They do not say what prompted the piece or what specific changes are required.

The article is attributed to Chris Miller, who is identified as the author in the byline. No statements from Nvidia, its leadership or US officials are included in the available text, so there is nothing to paraphrase from them. The headline itself frames the argument that the company cannot dictate US foreign policy. Beyond that framing, the articles do not say who is responsible for the changes or what anyone said about them.

The context the articles provide is limited to the paywall notice, which offers subscription access to the full piece. The articles do not say what happens next, whether Nvidia has responded or when any leadership change might occur. Because the body of the article is not available, the story cannot be supported beyond the headline and byline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Amazon algorithm recommends AI-generated Social Distortion biography that misgenders Mike Ness
stories.Summary:
A 2026 article in The Guardsman describes how the writer came to Philip K. Dick's 1965 novel "The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch" after failing to find a book about the punk band Social Distortion. The Amazon algorithm then recommended a book called "Social Distortion: Biography," which reviewers rated one star and described as AI-generated. One comment said the book repeatedly called lead singer Mike Ness "her" instead of "him." The writer links this to reporting by Alexandra Alter in The New York Times last June, which found 2,168 self-published Amazon books with more than 50% AI-generated content, including 970 novels with more than 90% AI-written pages.

In October 2026, the Spanish newspaper El País published an analysis by journalist Kiko Llaneras finding that one in three best-selling self-published books were generated by AI. Both journalists used the software Pangram to detect AI content, which the article calls the most accurate and reliable tool for the job. Pangram was also the official tool in two recent literary scandals. Haitian-Canadian author Thélyson Orélien was removed from the Prix Goncourt, awarded by the Académie Goncourt, over AI use and plagiarism. Peruvian writer David Silva Rojas, winner of the Almadía-Ventosa Arrufat prize for short novels, was accused by El País of using 99% AI, according to a Pangram diagnostic, and while his prize was not withdrawn, presentations of the novel in Spain were canceled pending an investigation.

The writer says Dick understood the risks of technology's evolution, including AI and addiction to it, and to creating content from pre-standardized patterns. People ask large language models like ChatGPT for everything from math problems to book analyses and accept the first answer, which the writer says could distort reality. The article notes that in the novel's final pages human and AI realities collide, and the only way to survive is through pleasure, which fewer humans can feel. It ends by asking whether AI can describe the experience of seeing Social Distortion live.

Articles.Title: How Philip K. Dick Predicted the Future of Artificial Intelligence in literature

stories.Headline: AI-generated posts falsely claim Paolo Maldini returns to AC Milan as head coach
stories.Summary:
Viral posts on Instagram and Threads claimed that AC Milan legend Paolo Maldini had returned to the club as head coach of its men's first team, and the posts were designed to look like genuine football appointment announcements. The creators included a disclaimer reading "CONCEPT ART • AI | FICTIONAL SCENARIO", which showed the announcement was an AI-generated concept rather than a real development. Realistic-looking graphics and the emotional appeal of a legendary figure returning home made the posts easy to confuse for real news, according to a report published on 15 November 2026. The report said the claim was entirely fictional. AC Milan officially appointed Portuguese manager Rúben Amorim as head coach of its men's first team on 16 June 2026, after Massimiliano Allegri left the club.

The club welcomed the former Manchester United and Sporting CP manager as part of its plans to rebuild the team. Paolo Maldini never pursued a coaching career, and he served as the club's technical director until June 2023. He also briefly took the role of technical director at the Italian Football Federation in July 2026 but resigned after just 16 days. The report said AI-generated content is increasingly blurring the lines between football news and digital fiction, because convincing visuals, familiar announcement templates and legendary names can make fabricated stories look like genuine breaking news. It said the prospect of a beloved former player returning to the dugout can be particularly tempting for supporters who are emotionally invested in their clubs.

It added that not everything carrying the look and language of a transfer exclusive deserves an instant celebration or a share. A quick check of official club announcements and credible sports publications can save fans from falling for an elaborate digital prank, the report said. The report said that while AI can recreate the excitement of a dream managerial appointment, it cannot make that appointment real. Maldini's return to AC Milan might make a wonderful fictional football story, but Amorim is the man in the hot seat, it said.

Articles.Title: AI has football fans fooled with a fictional Paolo Maldini return to AC Milan as Rúben Amorim remains in charge
