stories.Headline: BVDW publishes a 25-page AI workplace etiquette guide with 17 sections
stories.Summary:
Germany's Bundesverband Digitale Wirtschaft (BVDW) published its first "KI-Knigge" on November 5, 2026, a 25-page etiquette guide for artificial intelligence at work. The document tells employees when to skip the chatbot altogether and how to behave when software summarises a meeting. It also says who should own an AI agent before the agent is allowed to act. The full title is "Der BVDW-KI-Knigge: Verhaltenskodex für den nachhaltigen, sozialen und verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit KI in der Arbeitswelt." The guide borrows its structure from the environmental, social and governance framework companies already use for sustainability reporting.

The guide is 25 pages long and was published on November 5, 2026. It has seventeen numbered sections: four under Environmental, five under Social and eight under Governance. By PPC Land's count those sections contain 94 orientation points, 23 environmental, 26 social and 45 governance. The final section on agentic AI systems, with ten points, is the longest single list in the document. The guide takes its name from Adolph Freiherr Knigge, whose 1788 book "Über den Umgang mit Menschen" made his surname German shorthand for a manual of good manners.

The guide was written inside BVDW's Lab Responsible AI for Business, a unit of the association's Working Group Digital Responsibility. Its lead author is Maike Scholz of Deutsche Telekom, who heads the lab. Scholz said AI can take work off our hands but not the responsibility for its use. She said the guide shows how responsible AI use in everyday working life can succeed, and that resources, human interaction and clear responsibilities must be thought about together. BVDW, which represents more than 600 member companies, presents the document as practical recommendations for companies that want to integrate AI deliberately along the three sustainability dimensions.

The authors write that they are convinced enabling users should come before bans. They say the guide is meant not as a set of rules but as guidance from practice for practice. Readers are addressed with the informal German "Du," and each chapter ends with orientation points rather than obligations. The guide reaches anyone in a company who drafts social posts, summarises meetings, generates images or hands tasks to AI agents. Several of its points mirror labelling duties that the EU AI Act has applied since August 2, 2026.

The environmental chapter opens with the premise that AI systems require considerable computing power and therefore energy. It says selecting AI tools and checking their environmental impact is primarily the responsibility of companies. Section E2 states that a search query consumes only about a tenth of the resources of a generative AI query, with no source given. The guide says uniform standards for measuring and reporting the energy consumption of AI workloads have yet to be created. Section E3 recommends capping iterations with a fixed upper limit of prompt runs per task, for example a maximum of three attempts.

Nothing in the guide is binding, so what changes depends on whether employers turn its pointers into house rules on approved tools, human sign-off and documentation. BVDW says the guide will be adapted as needed to new findings, requirements and practical experience. The guide's closing outlook repeats that technological, regulatory, commercial and ethical conditions around AI keep shifting. The imprint on the last page states that the paper was produced using artificial intelligence, without saying which tools were used or for which parts.

stories.Headline: McGraw says AI penetration testing cannot replace independent CMMC assurance
stories.Summary:
The suspension of the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Phase 2 third-party assessment requirements has reignited the question of whether automated, artificial intelligence-based penetration testing could replace independent assessment, Terrence J. McGraw wrote in a November 13, 2026 commentary for Federal News Network. McGraw is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and chief executive officer of Cape Endeavors. The July 2026 CMMC reform effort called for discussion of the existing state of commercial cybersecurity and self-attestation. McGraw said that should be taken as a policy question, not as an indication that AI penetration testing will become a federal requirement. The underlying obligations of safeguarding covered defense information under Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement 252.204-7012 and National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171 remain in force for contractors.

McGraw wrote that a test continually probing a system is far more relevant than one that happens only every three years, but the two approaches answer very different questions. He said the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified vulnerability exploitation as a leading initial access path. He cited a Cape Endeavors analysis, published in a recent white paper using a hypothetical scenario of 500 hosts and 20 web apps, suggesting a model token cost of around $395 for a single on-demand test cycle versus around $4,200 per month for a high frequency continuous design. He said those are illustrative compute costs only, not actual market quotes or all-in contractor prices, and do not include vendor margins, infrastructure, human review or the engineering effort to fix issues found. He said a requirement to test continuously would turn a one-off assessment cost into a perpetual operating cost for small and midsize businesses in the defense industrial base.

McGraw said a penetration test is not in any way a complete analysis of how controlled unclassified information is protected, because many breaches result from stolen credentials, compromised third parties or misuse of legitimate access. He said independent assessments look at documented controls, interview people and examine evidence of implementation, but can only assess a particular point in time. He said a contractor can have a sophisticated test platform and still control which systems are tested, how it is configured and what results are reported. He cited a law firm Arnold & Porter example of a contractor who reported a perfect score in stark contrast to a later Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center evaluation. He said the gap between self-reported cybersecurity scores and government-assigned scores has been a factor in False Claims Act enforcement.

McGraw said the better approach is layered assurance: independently confirm required controls and the stated CUI boundary, test exposed technical controls continuously or after significant change, and run detection and response exercises. He said discovery finding CUI outside the approved boundary should modify the assessment scope, and a response exercise showing malicious activity went undetected means a clean vulnerability scan should not be taken as evidence of readiness. He said AI can speed up technical validation and make it more frequent but cannot on its own prove all appropriate safeguards are in place, all CUI is in the right place or the organization will deal with compromise appropriately. He said the point is to stop treating either human assessment or machine testing as the complete answer. He said contractors should keep an accurate inventory of CUI and the systems that process it, maintain system security plans and plans of action, minimize unnecessary exposure and document changes and remediation.

McGraw wrote that attackers do not wait for an assessment window and exploit exposed devices, misconfigurations and unpatched vulnerabilities when an opening appears. He said automated penetration testing can help close that timing gap by repeatedly checking reachable assets, attempting exploitation within allowed bounds and retesting the fix. He said for some technical controls, evidence that an attack actually failed may be more convincing than a policy stating the control should be in place. He said a tool probing the network perimeter will not see sensitive data copied to an unauthorized collaboration site, sent via normal email or left on an unmanaged device. He said a successful exploit does not tell whether defenders would detect and contain a skilled attacker already inside.

McGraw said there should not be any assumption today of a universal Level 2 AI testing mandate, and contractors can still make good decisions at this stage. He said better scoping will lead to lower security risk and fewer systems to test, and fewer recurring misconfigurations will mean fewer alerts to investigate and fewer issues to retest. He said federal policymakers should define the assurance outcome first and then pick the tool, asking whether an approach will verify implementation, find CUI outside authorized boundaries, find exploitable weaknesses and measure detection and response. He said credible evidence and clear accountability for exclusions and outstanding findings are needed, along with a look at the ongoing cost to the contractor base. He said if government policy eventually defines the scope, frequency or class of service providers that can carry out testing, contractors would have very little flexibility in managing that obligation.

Articles.Title: AI penetration testing cannot replace independent cybersecurity assurance - Federal News Network

stories.headline_source: AI penetration testing cannot replace independent cybersecurity assurance

stories.Headline: US warns China uses total mobilization strategy to steal AI and semiconductor technology
stories.Summary:
United States authorities have warned that Beijing is executing a total mobilization strategy to steal domestic artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. This aggressive information war involves government agencies, private companies, and ordinary citizens using methods like honey traps, investments, and cyberattacks. A high-profile scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national named Alice Huang revealed that large quantities of semiconductors were illicitly funneled to China. In 2024, Google engineer Ding Linwei was arrested for allegedly stealing 2,000 pages of confidential AI and supercomputing infrastructure documents. These combined efforts aim to close the technological and military gap between China and the United States.

The operation requires massive human capital, with a European intelligence agency estimating that China deploys approximately 600,000 intelligence and security personnel. This workforce includes the Ministry of State Security, the Ministry of Public Security, and the People's Liberation Army intelligence department. In 2021, an operative named Lai Liren recruited Qian Yuanshi, who had moved to the US in 2015, to photograph the Kitsap naval base in Washington state. In 2023, the wife of Qian photographed a roster of Chinese-American recruits at a US Navy recruiting office in Alhambra, California. These activities are part of a broader effort to secure restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 chips through budgets exceeding 23 billion yuan.

The Ministry of State Security and other agencies are responsible for managing these vast espionage operations across the globe. After their arrests, Qian Yuanshi and Lai Liren stated that they had no freedom to say no to the directives of the Ministry of State Security. The White House accused China in April of using tens of thousands of proxy accounts to extract data from American artificial intelligence systems. Anthropic reported that three Chinese AI companies used over 16 million queries to train their own models using the Claude chatbot. The FBI further estimated that government-backed Chinese hackers outnumber the total US cybersecurity workforce by at least fifty times.

President Xi Jinping views these technologies as core elements for national development despite China spending over 100 billion dollars on semiconductors. United Nations data shows the US holds 75 percent of the top 500 AI supercomputers, while China holds only 15 percent. Evidence from Employment Labs indicates that firms like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used advanced Blackwell GPUs despite strict US export controls. MI5 revealed in September that a China-linked institution exploited over 100 British researchers to transmit academic findings to intelligence agencies. The US continues to monitor these gray zone operations as Beijing leverages total information warfare to bolster its domestic AI capabilities.

Articles.Title: China AI Espionage — US Warns of Total Mobilization for Tech Theft

stories.headline_source: China AI Espionage — US Warns of Total Mobilization for Tech Theft

stories.Headline: Taiwan sees higher consumer spending than South Korea despite shared AI chip boom
stories.Summary:
Taiwan experienced a significant rise in consumer spending during the first three quarters of this year, while South Korea saw much slower growth. This divergence occurred despite both nations benefiting from a global boom in artificial intelligence chips. Private consumption in Taiwan increased by 5.4 percent on-year, whereas the corresponding figure for South Korea was only 2.1 percent. These different outcomes reflect how each country's industrial and employment structures distribute the financial gains from the semiconductor industry.

The disparity is driven by the fact that Taiwan employs 910,000 IT manufacturing workers, representing 10.6 percent of its total workforce. In contrast, South Korea has 390,000 such workers, which accounts for only 1.9 percent of its labor force. Taiwan also saw export growth driven by shipment volumes, while South Korea's growth relied more on price increases, with average export prices jumping 182 percent. Additionally, the Taiwanese government distributed approximately 420,000 won per person between November last year and April this year to stimulate spending.

The research department of the Bank of Korea published a report explaining that semiconductor profits in South Korea remain concentrated among high-income earners. These individuals typically spend a smaller portion of their earnings, which limits the overall recovery of domestic demand. The report stated that it is essential to strengthen the spending power of the middle class and reduce costs for low-income households. This approach is necessary to address a K-shaped economic divide where only certain sectors and income groups prosper.

The report further noted that South Korea's semiconductor boom gained momentum in the second half of last year, trailing Taiwan by about one year. Despite a 1.0 percent growth in GDP during the third quarter, private consumption in South Korea actually declined by 0.2 percent. The Bank of Korea warned that domestic demand will remain limited unless the benefits of the chip boom spread to other industries. Future recovery depends on whether the wealth generated by high-tech exports can reach middle and lower-income households.

Articles.Title: AI chip boom jump-starts Taiwan's consumer spending, but not Korea's

stories.headline_source: AI chip boom jump-starts Taiwan's consumer spending, but not Korea's

stories.Headline: Ukraine health ministry prepares medical AI rules as survey shows 80.5% of clinicians use the tools
stories.Summary:
The Health Ministry of Ukraine began preparing new rules for medical artificial intelligence on November 13, 2026. This action follows a survey showing that 80.5% of clinicians in the country already use these tools. The government wants to create a formal legal framework for these systems. This will ensure that technology is used safely across the healthcare sector.

The new bill will require the classification of AI tools based on their specific risk levels. It will establish strict requirements for the transparency and safety of all medical systems. The rules will also define the accountability of both the providers and the users. These measures follow a survey of 7,000 healthcare professionals, 300 patients, and 39 industry representatives.

Minister of Health Viktor Liashko is responsible for the development of this legislation. He stated that the ministry is working on a bill to set clear rules for the development of these systems. Liashko emphasized that medical professionals must supervise all decisions suggested by AI. He also noted that the personal medical data of patients must be protected.

One example of current technology is CheckEye, which analyzes retinal images in 30 seconds. This tool was tested on 873 patients in the Chernihiv and Odesa regions. The ministry intends to present the proposed bill for public discussion in the near future. This will allow stakeholders to review the safety and accountability standards.

The company recorded total quarterly revenue of THB246.41 million, which was up THB7.34 million, or 3%, from the third quarter of 2025. Total costs and expenses fell by THB18.54 million, or 7%, to THB232.09 million over the same period. The financial turnaround was attributed to growth in online media, a 7% reduction in costs and expenses, and new marketing strategies.

The company is implementing an AI push by applying Small AI projects to its workflows as part of a broader strategy to become a Media Tech Company. Nation Group also aims to operate under its Agile & Intelligence Organization concept, developing the agility and flexibility needed to respond to a rapidly changing world. The group intends to build on its content strengths and media network to expand its marketing services with leading Thai companies and global media organisations. It also plans to further develop its seminars and international networking forums to create opportunities for knowledge exchange and business connections.

Shine Bunnag, chairman of Nation Group's executive committee and chief executive officer, said the company had worked hard to restructure its organisation and business to prepare for the future. He said this particularly involved controlling costs and applying artificial intelligence to workflows through Small AI projects. He added that the company is focusing on expanding its agency team to bid for government contracts, and that revenue has grown significantly this year, though several weaknesses still require further adjustment and improvement. He also said that although AI is a powerful tool, it cannot replace every aspect of human work, and that journalists with specialist expertise and creative production teams are qualities AI cannot replace.

Shine said that although technology is changing how the media works, credibility has remained the company's foundation for 56 years. He said Nation Group will uphold its journalistic principles and professional ethics, delivering accurate and comprehensive news while continuing to scrutinise and verify the facts. He added that the aim is to provide valuable information that helps the public make informed decisions. The company also plans to build on its strength in producing substantive content that benefits society, with greater emphasis on analysis and in-depth reporting across major current issues.

stories.Headline: Researcher Sisi Tao proposes a five-tier framework setting age-gated generative AI limits for students aged 3 to 18
stories.Summary:
A perspective study published in AI, Brain and Child on November 14, 2026, introduces a five-tiered framework for generative artificial intelligence exposure for students aged 3 through 18. The study was authored by researcher Sisi Tao. The model links specific artificial intelligence permissions, quantitative cut-off times, and mandatory independence ratios to neurodevelopmental and cognitive milestones. It moves past polarized debates between absolute classroom prohibition and unrestricted adoption. The blueprint establishes an evidence-based continuum grounded in developmental psychology.

Tier 0 covers ages 3 to 5 and mandates zero direct student interaction, with all technology use adult-mediated and back-stage. Tier 1 covers ages 6 to 7 with a cap of 15 minutes per day and an independent work ratio of at least 95 percent. Tier 2 covers ages 8 to 10 at approximately 30 minutes daily with an independence ratio of 90 percent or higher. Tier 3 spans ages 11 to 13 with a daily limit of 60 minutes and an 80 percent independence threshold. Tier 4 governs ages 14 to 18 with a daily ceiling of 120 minutes and a minimum 70 percent independence ratio, requiring a formal Artificial Intelligence Usage Statement with each assignment.

Educational policymakers must enforce regulation by design, requiring software vendors to incorporate age-gated usage locks matching tiered daily exposure limits as a prerequisite for procurement in public school districts. Technology developers are urged to end direct preschool engagement tools and instead engineer transparent, privacy-preserving teacher resources that operate across varied network bandwidths. Educators are tasked with developing process-oriented curricula emphasizing explicit bias detection checklists, student agency, and oral evaluations. Parents serve as home gatekeepers by aligning domestic device habits with school cut-offs, monitoring family conversational assistants, and curbing uncritical trust or personal disclosure patterns. The author emphasizes that the proposed quantitative thresholds represent theory-driven hypotheses and testable heuristic baselines rather than definitive physiological constants.

In the United States, a presidential executive order promotes system-wide artificial intelligence integration in K-12 schooling despite an absence of age-specific bans. Approximately 40 percent of national education systems restricted smartphone use in schools by 2024, while UNESCO guidance recommends a minimum age threshold of 13 for classroom artificial intelligence tools. An electroencephalography study showed declining neural functional connectivity and post-exposure cognitive debt when individuals write with continuous artificial intelligence assistance. Generative models frequently present factual inaccuracies, fabricated scholarly citations, and systemic societal stereotypes as authoritative output. The framework synthesizes five classical developmental psychology frameworks: Piaget's cognitive stage theory, Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, Erikson's psychosocial theory, Kohlberg's stages of moral reasoning, and Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory.

The author utilized an adapted best-fit framework synthesis methodology, integrating empirical literature from PsycINFO and ERIC using targeted Boolean strings covering generative technology, digital media, and developmental neuroscience in cohorts aged 3 to 18. Four evidence streams were triangulated to set boundaries: Piagetian representational transitions, longitudinal magnetic resonance neuroimaging showing cortical volume peaks and synaptic pruning in frontal and parietal regions, empirical attention spans and executive function trajectories, and practical K-12 grade bands. A four-tier model was rejected because it would artificially collapse the transition around ages 6 to 7 from preoperational to concrete operational thought. A six-tier structure would introduce artificial breaks within adolescence that lack neuroscientific warrant, given that longitudinal neuroimaging demonstrates executive function development follows a protracted, continuous trajectory from age 13 to 18. Historical parallels include the introduction of portable electronic calculators and internet search engines, when observers feared the erosion of fundamental arithmetic and inquiry skills.

Key limitations include the framework's foundation in Western developmental psychology, necessitating future cross-cultural research to explore adaptations within non-Western and collectivist educational settings. Because the model reflects current text-based systems, rapid transitions toward autonomous agentic and multimodal platforms will require regular recalibration. Long-term empirical studies remain essential to test the ecological validity of the suggested cut-off values, track cross-device exposure, and design inherently artificial-intelligence-resistant pedagogies such as collaborative problem solving, embodied physical experiments, and process portfolios. The article states that students must retain intellectual agency as educational technology evolves. The articles do not state any implementation date or adopting institution for the framework.

stories.Headline: Trump administration rebrands artificial intelligence as super intelligence
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 13, 2026, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave a briefing on the White House lawn in Washington. This event occurred during a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States caused by a telecommunications failure. While discussing the travel disruption, Mullin corrected a reporter by insisting that the administration calls artificial intelligence "SI" or "Super Intelligence." He stated that officials cannot rule out any cause for the coast-to-coast aviation crisis at this point. The secretary used this brief press interaction to promote President Donald Trump's campaign to rename the technology.

The rebranding process began in July 2025 when Trump expressed dissatisfaction with the word artificial during his AI Action Plan launch. In December 2025, he suggested the phrase supreme intelligence while signing an order directing the Department of Justice to combat state laws. On September 19, 2026, he used Truth Social to poll options including Extreme Intelligence and Superior Intelligence. Trump officially adopted the term Super Intelligence during a September 22, 2026, speech at the United Nations General Assembly. On September 29, 2026, he signed an executive order titled Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence to enforce the change.

President Trump stated that the term artificial implies a defect and that the technology is actually pure genius. He believes the new terminology reflects transformative capabilities and limitless opportunities for the American people. Trump asserted that whoever wins Super Intelligence wins, and he intends to maintain global technological dominance over China. A State Department official subsequently instructed diplomats to change all references in documents and positions to the new term. Michael Kratsios of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy also adopted the branding during his UN remarks.

Social media users and technology writer Charlie Warzel criticized Mullin for prioritizing branding during a major aviation emergency. Harvard political scientist Ryan Enos noted that prioritizing regime approved rhetoric during a crisis is a sign of authoritarianism. Emily Tucker of Georgetown Law suggested the renaming might preempt arguments or make it harder to resist abuses of power. Professor Dave Karpf argued that the insistence on new words shows Trump is out of his depth regarding the technology. Jenna Ruddock of Free Press claimed industry leaders play along to secure lucrative government contracts and regulatory fast tracks.

Trump has a history of renaming entities, such as changing the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. He ordered the Department of Defense to be called the Department of War in September 2025. Other changes include renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America and suggesting the Trump Strait for the Strait of Hormuz. Industry leaders like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang have supported the shift to Super Intelligence. Musk specifically announced he would rename the SpaceXAI unit to SpaceXSI to align with the administration.

The federal government is now instructed to not acknowledge the term artificial intelligence in any official applicable setting. The administration continues to push for the rest of the world to adopt the term Super Intelligence in their documents. It remains unclear if the White House has the actual power to enforce this terminology change globally. The articles leave open whether the telecommunications failure that stopped all flights was actually caused by an SI related error. The cause of the Friday air travel crisis remains unknown as of the time of publication.

stories.Headline: Megaspeed hires external legal counsel to investigate media reports on its AI cloud business
stories.Summary:
On November 15, 2026, the Singapore-based company Megaspeed hired external legal counsel to investigate media reports regarding its global operations, supply chain, and AI cloud business. This new legal review follows a separate announcement from November 12, 2026, regarding the company's cooperation with the United States Department of Commerce. The company also confirmed that Alice Huang, a former chairperson and chief executive officer, left her position effective August 30, 2025. These internal actions occur while the Singapore Police Force and Singapore Customs continue an independent investigation that began in February 2025.

The current situation requires Megaspeed to conduct a comprehensive census of its graphics processing units through a separate United States law firm to verify export-control compliance. Singaporean authorities are investigating whether servers purchased by Megaspeed and other companies were routed through Malaysia to destinations that contradicted original declarations. This probe involves six individuals who have not been in Singapore since February 2025, as well as the company's controllers. Alice Huang received a stern warning and was barred from re-entering Singapore on February 26, 2026, after police found insufficient evidence of criminal offenses but determined she provided inaccurate information.

Chairman and CEO James Tan Yong Pong stated that the company is ready to cooperate with relevant United States authorities and has already worked with the Bureau of Industry and Security. Megaspeed maintains that the media reports lack verifiable evidence and asserts that its supply-chain controls are designed to follow all applicable local and international laws. The Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs noted that while it does not enforce unilateral foreign controls, it will not condone the use of fraud to circumvent such regulations. The ministry also mentioned that the United States server supplier Supermicro provided limited cooperation during the ongoing investigation.

Megaspeed operates as a regional partner for the computing-power cloud business of Nvidia, providing GPU compute and virtual servers for machine learning and AI workloads. Singaporean officials have requested assistance from the FBI and the United States Department of Justice several times since September 2025 to track the servers. The company will continue to review the reporting and communicate with its stakeholders as the legal and official investigations proceed. Future outcomes depend on whether the GPU census and the police inquiry can substantiate the compliance claims made by the company.

stories.Headline: States pass 115 AI measures as AMA and medical boards draft human oversight rules
stories.Summary:
State lawmakers and professional organizations are developing new approaches to responsible AI use, often focusing on human oversight and accountability for these tools. A new report from the Transparency Coalition, an AI-policy advocacy organization, identified 115 AI-related measures that legislatures in 30 states passed this year. As of mid-October, 108 had been signed into law and seven were awaiting a governor's signature. The report ranked human oversight of AI in health care and AI disclosure requirements among the most common issues states addressed.

Eight states, for example, enacted laws limiting health insurers' ability to rely solely on AI or automated systems to deny or reduce coverage, including prior authorization for health insurance claims. At least five states have enacted laws this year restricting AI in mental health care, generally requiring therapy to be provided by a licensed human professional. California also enacted a law requiring health facilities to ensure clinicians retain independent judgment when using clinical AI tools. Most of these mental health laws are already in effect, while Rhode Island's and California's take effect in January 2027.

In October, the American Medical Association released a governance framework for agentic AI outlining questions for AI systems that take on clinical functions, including what evidence supports their use, what oversight is appropriate, and who is accountable for their risks and outcomes. The AMA says these questions will guide its work on liability, licensure, and regulation. The framework does not set requirements for physicians or AI developers. Separately, the Federation of State Medical Boards convened a workgroup in Washington in early October to begin developing recommendations for state medical boards overseeing the use of clinical AI tools.

The FSMB group is focusing on systems that perform clinical functions, such as diagnosis and prescribing, with limited or no direct physician supervision. FSMB's leadership has argued in the past that AI should be governed through existing medical accountability structures, with physicians remaining accountable for their use of AI. Draft recommendations are expected in the coming weeks or months and will be open for feedback before adoption. Once adopted, they will not be binding, though state boards and legislators could use them to shape policy.

In October, the health policy journal Health Affairs issued a policy for AI use that reflects standards many academic journals have put in place since 2023. The policy prohibits authors who publish in the journal from listing AI as an author or using it in place of human judgment. It also requires authors to review AI-assisted work, remain responsible for its content, and disclose all AI use. The journal also recommends against using AI tools to manage citations and references, citing the tendency of some AI systems to generate inaccurate or nonexistent references.

The results of the 2026 midterm elections could further influence state efforts to regulate AI and how they interact with federal policy. The Trump administration has previously urged Congress to adopt a national framework for AI regulation that would preempt existing state laws it considers unduly burdensome, but broad preemption may be less likely given Democratic control of Congress beginning in January. Many congressional Democrats have previously opposed overriding state AI laws without federal regulations in place. Some Democrats in the incoming Congress have indicated they will pursue new legislation related to AI, including requiring experts to evaluate AI safety and clarifying when technology companies can be held liable for harmful AI outputs.

stories.Headline: Researchers map biological foundation model limits and warn that wet-lab ground truth remains essential
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, researchers Tian Cai, Andrew Kleist, Jaimin Patel, Duccio Malinverni, Alexander K. Taylor, and colleagues released a preprint titled AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems. The study maps the operational boundaries of biological foundation models across five design elements. It establishes where autonomous AI pipelines succeed, where they fail, and why wet-lab experimental ground truth remains indispensable for computational biology teams. The preprint is arXiv:2611.17015v1. It is slated for the Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science.

Investigators from St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and the University of California, Los Angeles examined the rapid integration of biological foundation models into autonomous agentic workflows. Foundation models trained on hundreds of millions of nucleotide sequences, protein structures, and single-cell transcriptomes include ESM2, AlphaFold, AlphaGenome, Geneformer, scGPT, and Evo. Researchers increasingly interact with these architectures through agentic systems that orchestrate multi-step analyses using large language models and external tool protocols. The authors formalize a model's knowledge boundary as the precise range of inputs, tasks, and biological conditions over which its predictions remain valid. This boundary is dictated by five interrelated design elements: input data, model architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis.

The authors show that foundation model outputs cannot be universally trusted. Because foundation models are frequently repurposed far beyond their original pre-training scope, these architectural constraints travel with them into downstream agentic workflows. The preprint synthesizes extensive empirical evidence comparing biological foundation models against simpler computational baselines across diverse modalities. Protein models capture hydrophobic and electrostatic residue clustering from evolutionary co-variation, but likelihood scores heavily reflect historical phylogenetic sampling bias rather than intrinsic fitness. Tokenization choices also impose hard limits, as multi-nucleotide tokens obscure single-nucleotide variants while rank-based gene encoding discards quantitative expression magnitude.

Attention mechanisms capture long-range interactions at quadratic computational cost, but context windows remain constrained. While models like AlphaGenome process up to one megabase, inter-chromosomal regulation falls outside their scope. AlphaFold2 relies heavily on multiple sequence alignments and frequently fails to predict the structural disruption caused by destabilizing point mutations. Self-supervised masked and autoregressive objectives reward statistical correlation rather than causal biological mechanisms. Sequence-to-function models such as Enformer, Borzoi, and AlphaGenome struggle to explain inter-individual expression variance and often predict the wrong direction of effect.

In single-cell perturbation experiments, simple linear models and training data averages regularly match or outperform un-fine-tuned foundation models like Geneformer and scGPT. Benchmarks frequently suffer from data leakage and lack simple baseline controls. Examining four integration pathways, foundation models as tools, text representations of measurements, encoder embeddings, and fine-tuning verifiers, the authors identify instances where language model agents generate fluent rationales that directly contradict the foundation model tools they invoke. For wet-lab and computational biology groups, the preprint delivers vital operational cautions. As research organizations build automated pipelines, uncritical adoption of foundation model predictions introduces subtle errors into experimental designs.

Autonomous agents can propagate failures across multi-step analyses without signaling uncertainty, threatening computational reproducibility across discovery campaigns. To safeguard scientific rigor, research leaders must audit training data provenance to verify that target organisms, cell states, and molecular assays fall within a model's validated operational domain. The authors advocate establishing standardized, machine-readable boundary statements, modeled on model cards, that document context lengths, tokenization strategies, pre-training corpora, and baseline benchmark comparisons. The authors also conclude that computational biology should not wait for an all-encompassing foundation model. Instead, research workflows should orchestrate portfolios of specialized models coupled with automated self-driving laboratories that generate targeted physical ground truth whenever an inquiry crosses into boundary territory.

stories.Headline: JPCERT/CC finds about 1,000 servers in Japan hosting AI tools for global website attacks
stories.Summary:
Japanese experts discovered approximately 1,000 servers in Japan that were equipped with artificial intelligence tools for attacking websites globally. The Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center conducted this investigation alongside several foreign cybersecurity companies. Specialists began checking these suspicious servers in early October and found tools designed to find vulnerabilities and steal configurations. These servers were either located in physical premises or managed through various virtual frameworks.

The investigation revealed that most of the servers hosted artificial intelligence platforms, including the Artex penetration-testing tool. One specific server contained a programming-support tool created by the American company Anthropic PBC, which showed how attackers weaponized artificial intelligence. Other publicly accessible servers held programs for testing system vulnerabilities and analyzing the internal structure of smartphone applications. Attackers used these tools to analyze applications and attempt unauthorized access through interfaces that exchange information with external systems.

Ken Sajo, an analyst at JPCERT/CC, stated that artificial intelligence is currently in the early stages of being used for cyberattacks. He warned that the number of more sophisticated attacks will likely increase in the future. This discovery follows a general warning from the heads of the largest artificial intelligence companies before the United Nations Security Council. They cautioned that artificial intelligence may pose a threat to all of humanity if appropriate measures are not taken.

stories.Headline: South Korean exam candidate Han admits using AI to cheat on tax accountant test
stories.Summary:
A top scorer on the national tax accountant exam in South Korea admitted on Sunday, November 15, 2026, that he used generative artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, identified by the surname Han, confessed to using a microcamera to photograph questions and a smartphone to receive answers from an AI tool. He achieved a near-perfect score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, missing only one answer out of 160 questions. This admission follows months of suspicion regarding his performance during the qualification exams held in April and July.

The scandal has created urgent pressure for officials organizing the annual national college entrance exam scheduled for this Thursday. The government must now implement countermeasures to prevent similar AI-assisted cheating during this high-stakes event. This situation is particularly sensitive because standardized tests in South Korea largely determine the career trajectories and social mobility of students. The Seoul metropolitan police agency has already assigned investigators to the case after receiving a written confession from Han through his lawyer.

A senior official from the presidential office stated that the government views the matter very seriously and is working hard to prepare for the upcoming college exam. The presidential chief of staff for policy planned an emergency meeting on Sunday afternoon to address concerns about potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged public anxiety on Friday and promised that the government would oversee the process closely. Her office stated that they would prepare thoroughly to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted in a fair and stable manner.

stories.Headline: An opinion piece argues AI exposes limits of traditional schooling and proposes three shifts for schools
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Daily Sabah on November 15, 2026, is an opinion piece arguing that artificial intelligence has exposed the limits of what schools have traditionally treated as learning. The author writes that students can now obtain explanations, generate essays, solve mathematical problems and explore complex questions within seconds. Tasks that once required considerable learning can now be done, at least superficially, with a few prompts. The piece asks what learning means when answers are readily available, and whether easy access to knowledge makes people smarter or intellectually weaker.

The author argues that AI does not determine the future of learning, because our conception of learning decides whether it becomes an instrument of growth or decline. The article proposes three shifts for schools: moving from standardized learning to personalizable learning, shifting from answering questions to finding and solving meaningful problems, and moving from individual competition to human interdependence. It says knowing an answer is not the same as understanding a problem, and producing an essay is not the same as having something meaningful to say. It adds that all students still need a reasonable foundation for participating in society, beyond which education should let different learners pursue different forms of excellence.

The author acknowledges that concerns about AI weakening effort, memory and critical thinking are legitimate but not new, comparing them to earlier worries about writing, printed books, calculators, computers and the internet. The piece contrasts two students using AI to write an essay, one who submits a lightly adjusted generated text and learns little, and one who uses AI to explore evidence, challenge assumptions and improve writing while remaining responsible for the argument. It says AI can weaken thinking when it replaces intellectual engagement and deepen understanding when it enables more meaningful engagement. The author is developing two initiatives with colleagues and educators, YEE AI, an AI-supported learning platform, and Courageous Minority, an international community of teachers and school leaders.

The article says educational transformation cannot wait for entire systems to change, and that teachers can begin by redesigning learning experiences in their own classrooms. It describes the two initiatives as complementary, with YEE AI exploring how technology can support a new educational paradigm and Courageous Minority exploring how educators can bring that paradigm to life in real classrooms and schools. The piece closes by asking whether schools are educating children to perform tasks or helping them become capable human beings who can live meaningful lives and contribute to the world. It states that AI makes many traditional educational tasks easier but does not make becoming human any easier.

Articles.Title: Learning after AI: When answers are there, what is education for? | Daily Sabah

stories.Headline: Developer Sam Brovda shuts down AI-coded sports trivia game statback after 172 commits
stories.Summary:
Sam Brovda, a former sales professional who builds software on the side with AI coding agents, pushed 172 commits to a daily sports trivia game called statback between June 18 and July 16, and 155 of those commits carry a line crediting Claude Opus 4.8 as co-author. The game gave every player the same 3x3 grid of nine card backs each day, with the player's name, birthplace and at first the team redacted, and the player had to identify each athlete from the stat lines with three tries per card and optional hints that cost points. It began with baseball and by the end of the first day covered MLB, NBA and NFL, using Next.js, Supabase, Vercel, PostHog, Resend for email and web push, with rookie cards, foil parallels, serial numbers and print runs, including a Gold parallel limited to 10 per drop. Brovda wrote that the first day's commits read like a roadmap, covering the game itself, a vintage clubhouse interface, a binder that swings open, lineups from the MLB Stats API, a monthly leaderboard, magic-link accounts, Google sign-in and holo card finishes.

Hints were the hardest part and were rebuilt repeatedly, with a June 19 commit requiring every hint to be factually valid, a June 20 swap to Claude-generated trivia covering 888 of the 930 players in the pool, and a stray placeholder artifact that reached live text that same day. On June 21 he rebuilt the hints from Wikipedia and Wikidata, grounding clues for 914 of the 930 players, and the final commit on July 16 still concerned hints, because once the team column showed on every card the scouting-report hints named the player's own team on 60% of entries. He changed the daily difficulty mix at least five times, from a 3/4/2 split with a guaranteed white whale to 2/4/3, then a recalibration that re-rolled boards people were already playing, which he reverted before adding a fix that pins each daily lineup the first time it is served, then re-applied the recalibration and later a 1/3/3/2 spread. On July 3 PostHog analytics showed average hints per board had jumped from about 4 to about 12 and perfect 9/9 boards had dropped from about 41% to about 20%, so he dialed back to a mostly modern 2/2/4/1 spread.

A June 24 commit marked critical addressed a store-wipe bug in which a failed database read was treated as an empty store and a fallback write could overwrite the whole database with empty defaults, and within 40 minutes three more commits added a guard blocking any write that would cut the core data in half, hourly snapshots in a 48-slot ring and a plan to move off one big JSON document onto real tables. Two days later a performance commit named the same root cause for slow gameplay, since everything lived in a single roughly 1MB JSON document and every write competed for one row. On June 27 he fixed phone overheating caused by the foil shimmer animation looping a CSS variable that forced constant full repaints, and the same day he fixed cards flipping backwards twice because the first fix was not enough. Sharing changed repeatedly, including a June 20 switch to plain text plus a link because recipients preferred readable text over an image, a version number on share URLs the next day after learning X and iMessage cache link previews for days, and referral codes that give both people a Scout foil card when a friend joins.

Brovda wrote that the agent will happily build a shortcut architecture that works until real people use it, and that an AI will produce content fast but will not check it against what is already on screen, so you have to do that yourself. He said the only reason he knew he had overshot on difficulty was shipping the analytics before tuning, and that most of his commit history is fixing what he built, with none of the fixes fancy and all of them coming from watching the product and the numbers and then telling the agent exactly what was wrong. He shut statback down because maintaining it was a headache and it was a side project, with every fix opening up another one, though he said it taught him how to work with an agent, what breaks when real people show up and what to check before trusting what it built. He is now building a consumer mobile app, which he described as a real project, and called statback the practice run.

stories.Headline: A researcher releases SignDrop exploit that disables Windows antivirus and EDR defences
stories.Summary:
A Windows zero-day exploit called SignDrop was publicly released on GitHub on 15 November 2026, according to a TechGig report published the same day. The exploit disables third-party antivirus and Endpoint Detection and Response, or EDR, defences on affected systems. Rather than relying on conventional memory corruption flaws, it weaponises the core logic of legitimate operating system security mitigations. SignDrop abuses self-referential trust within the Windows I/O subsystem and the kernel minifilter architecture, the report says.

The exploit forces the operating system to initiate a file creation request within the exact execution context of a target high-integrity process. This grants authorisation without secondary signature inspection, which leads to a tamper protection bypass and privilege escalation. The vulnerability creates a blind spot where security software still displays a healthy status icon in the system tray while actually being neutralised. Microsoft and endpoint security vendors now face an emergency triage cycle, and the report says remediation requires a structural redesign of how the Windows I/O subsystem evaluates process provenance at the ring-zero kernel level.

The report states that proper remediation requires explicit cryptographic verification on payload data streams, moving beyond reliance on process ID and certificate provenance. Security teams are told to implement aggressive compensatory controls to mitigate active exploitation while that work is pending. These include rigid Access Control List hardening on security directories and enforcing Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity. Organisations also need to deploy strict Application Control Policies and configure Out-of-Band Telemetry Watchdogs, according to the report.

The disclosure marks the eleventh zero-day from a single researcher within six months, which the report says highlights a systemic failure in vendor-researcher incentive alignment. The articles do not name the researcher or the affected Windows versions, and they give no timeline for a Microsoft fix. No statement from Microsoft or from any endpoint security vendor is included in the coverage. The report frames the flaw as requiring urgent structural redesign of the Windows I/O subsystem rather than patches alone.

stories.Headline: Developers tune pitch speed and prosody to make AI voices sound more natural
stories.Summary:
Voice AI developers can make text-to-speech output sound more natural by fine-tuning pitch, speed and prosody with configurable engines, according to a TechGig report published on November 15, 2026. The report says developers are focusing on voice quality to improve user experience in chatbots, audiobook platforms and smart assistants. A natural-sounding voice helps users feel they are interacting with a helpful companion rather than a machine, the report says. Pitch and intonation control how the voice rises and falls so sentences sound like real conversations, while duration and pace manage the length of each phoneme to prevent a robotic stutter.

Prosody, which the report describes as stress patterns on words, adds emotion and emphasis to speech, and background noise and reverberation can add realism or make audio sound synthetic. Developers should use configurable text-to-speech engines that allow per-utterance adjustments to pitch, speed and prosody, the report says. Adjusting pitch and speed prevents the voice from keeping a single register or constant speed, which mimics natural conversation. Embedding SSML tags directly into text can control prosody and pauses, which the report calls crucial for realistic speech, and experimenting with emotion parameters such as stability and similarity boost can push the voice toward specific emotional tones.

Advanced customisation includes layering additional neural processing for emotion, prosody and background effects, which the report says improves realism for long-form content. The report lists common pitfalls as over-tuning, ignoring context, not testing across devices and skipping voice-quality audits. Over-tuning can make the voice sound unnatural, and ignoring context means the same settings may not suit all content types. Testing on target hardware and gathering feedback from real users are essential to ensure voice quality, according to the report.

stories.Headline: Crissyfield finds exposed sensitive data in 159,041 Lovable projects without login
stories.Summary:
An analysis of 159,041 Lovable projects found many cases where sensitive data could be accessed without any user login, according to research by Crissyfield in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on these findings on November 2, 2026, in German, and TechGig published its account of the research on November 15, 2026. The investigation specifically looked into how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected from outside access. The finding highlights a gap between the platform's ease-of-use marketing and its terms, which place data security responsibility on customers.

Lovable's marketing emphasizes that technical knowledge is not needed to build projects, which can imply that the platform handles security for its users. However, Lovable's Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling squarely on the customers themselves. This creates a troubling gap between the platform's promise of an easy-to-use service and the security responsibilities customers are expected to undertake. The analysis covered 159,041 Lovable projects in total, and numerous instances of exposed sensitive data were found among them.

The research was carried out by Crissyfield in collaboration with Handelsblatt, and Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026, in German. Lovable itself is described as placing responsibility for applications and data handling on its customers through its Terms & Conditions. The platform's marketing, which stresses that technical knowledge is not needed, can imply that security is handled for users. The articles do not say what Lovable or Crissyfield said beyond these points, and they give no statement from either party.

The articles describe the gap between Lovable's marketing of an easy-to-use platform and the security duties its terms assign to customers. They do not say what happens next, whether the exposed projects were fixed, or whether Lovable or Crissyfield plans further action. No response from Lovable to the findings is given in the articles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jiachuan Peng leads study finding synthetic medical images can train vision models
stories.Summary:
A retrospective study led by Jiachuan Peng and twelve other authors evaluated whether a general-purpose image generation and editing model called Nano Banana could supply synthetic medical images for training vision models. The work covered four imaging modalities, namely chest radiography, fundus photography, CT and carotid ultrasound, and it was posted to the arXiv preprint server on 15 November 2026. Models for chest radiography, fundus photography and CT were trained only on synthetic images and then validated externally on real-world data against models trained on real data. Carotid ultrasound models were trained on a private Human Phenotype Project cohort of people aged 40 to 75 years, both with and without synthetic augmentation. Clinicians also rated how plausible the generated images appeared.

Synthetic-only models reached AUROCs of 0.877 for pneumonia with 14,863 cases, 0.963 for retinal detachment with 1,149 cases and 0.711 for renal calculus with 4,122 cases, which the authors describe as comparable to real-data-trained models. However, the calibration and net benefit of those synthetic-only models were not consistently more favorable than those of the real-data models. With mixed synthetic and real training, a carotid ultrasound model produced an ordinal vascular age index that split 633 external subjects into subgroups differing in BMI and glucose, both with p values below 0.01. To stress-test shortcut learning, the researchers edited a moderate tessellated pattern into fundus photographs, which lowered the true-class probability for central serous chorioretinopathy from 0.996 to 0.822. Clinician-guided editing raised low-quality CT plausibility from 3.10 out of 5 to 4.30 out of 5.

The authors conclude that synthetic data can complement real data in model training, subgroup representation and model testing through controlled editing. They state that its clinical value should be assessed with calibration, decision curve analysis and clinician review rather than discrimination alone. Evaluation in the study used AUROC, AUPR, calibration and decision curve analysis, alongside the clinician ratings of image plausibility. The abstract does not name any funder, regulator or deployment partner, and it gives no timetable for clinical use. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the authors' recommendation that synthetic medical images be judged on calibration, decision curve analysis and clinician review.

stories.Headline: XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 15, 2026 describes a new framework for estimating how much confidence to place in machine learning predictions used for resource management. The authors are Mahmoud Sanad, Mohammed Bakr Sikal, Osama Abboud, Heba Khdr and Jörg Henkel, and the paper is titled XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction. The work addresses the problem that machine learning-based resource management models degrade when they encounter out-of-distribution inputs at runtime. Existing approaches in the literature rely on a single global error margin that is overly conservative and fails to distinguish reliable predictions from catastrophic failures.

The proposed framework is called Lightweight Runtime EXplainability, or LEX, and the authors describe it as the first post-hoc XAI framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in machine learning-based resource management. LEX clusters the embeddings of the training input space using a Gaussian Mixture Model and associates per-cluster prediction error bounds to input samples. This enables fine-grained runtime confidence signals without retraining, according to the abstract. The framework was evaluated on a state-of-the-art LSTM-based IPS forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake across 34 benchmark applications.

According to the abstract, LEX achieves approximately 94% containment on unseen workloads and produces approximately 17% tighter per-input confidence bounds than global baselines. The authors state that LEX has negligible runtime overhead. They say the framework advances the field by providing explainable and reliable input-specific confidence signals of machine learning predictions. This, they write, makes machine learning-based resource management resilient to out-of-distribution inputs at runtime.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2611.13199, and the posting date given is November 15, 2026. The abstract presents LEX as a post-hoc method, meaning it works without retraining the underlying model. The authors frame the contribution as the first such framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in this setting. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the publication of the paper and its stated results.

stories.Headline: Researchers release khammoon, a lightweight Thai morpheme segmenter trained on a linguistic guideline
stories.Summary:
Warit Sirichotedumrong, Adisai Na-Thalang, Chanakan Wittayasakpan, Kritsadha Phatcharoen and Kunat Pipatanakul posted a paper on arXiv on 15 November 2026 describing khammoon, a Thai morpheme segmenter built from a linguistic guideline. Thai is written without spaces between words, so segmentation is a foundational step in most Thai natural language processing pipelines, according to the abstract. Existing tools mainly reproduce the word-level conventions of corpora such as BEST, but the notion of a word in Thai lacks a unified linguistic consensus, and those conventions struggle with productive compounding, leading to arbitrary boundaries and ambiguity in downstream representations. The authors instead propose operating at the morphological level, focusing on khammoon, which they call the smallest atomic unit that carries meaning.

Segmenting at the morphemic level gives an explicit and consistent morphological representation that the authors say eliminates compounding ambiguity. Models trained on morphemes perform on par with or exceed word-level baselines across part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition and sentiment classification, showing that linguistic consistency improves representation quality without a downstream performance penalty. To put the representation into practice, the authors translated linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement, a kappa of about 0.99, scaled annotation with a large language model and corrected systematic errors with human labels. They then trained khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, which achieved a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text.

The paper lists Warit Sirichotedumrong and four other authors as responsible for the work, and the abstract states that the guideline, datasets, model and library are all publicly released. The authors frame the morpheme-level approach as a response to the lack of consensus on what counts as a Thai word and to the compounding problems that follow from word-level conventions. The abstract presents the downstream results as evidence that linguistic consistency need not cost performance, and it describes the segmenter as lightweight and suited to CPU inference. The articles give no further details on release dates, licensing or future plans beyond the public release of the guideline, datasets, model and library.

stories.Headline: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
stories.Summary:
Genming Cui, Xiangyu Li, Zixu Hao, Xin Ding, Yunxin Liu and Ting Cao posted a paper on arXiv on 15 November 2026 describing SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method for low-bit LLM agents. The authors say low-bit quantization cuts the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success, and that examining failed rollouts showed quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions. Those oversights produce environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references, and the authors say correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult. Offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while the student's own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts.

SteerDistill has a full-precision teacher guide the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refine its guidance using feedback from student execution, which the authors call closed-loop teacher steering and describe as producing locally verified behavioral corrections. The method internalizes these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67 to 2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ²-Bench it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours, and it produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

The paper lists Genming Cui, Xiangyu Li, Zixu Hao, Xin Ding, Yunxin Liu and Ting Cao as its authors, and the abstract presents the closed-loop teacher steering and the training scheme as the authors' own contributions. The authors state that the teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and refines that guidance from student execution feedback, and that training without guidance lets the student run unassisted. They report the gains above the strongest quantized baseline and the comparison with QeRL as their results, and they say SteerDistill stays within one point of BF16. The abstract gives no further statements from the authors beyond these descriptions and figures.

The context the abstract gives is that low-bit quantization lowers inference cost for LLM agents while risking task success, and that failed rollouts show quantized agents diverging from full-precision references. The authors frame offline data and the student's own rollouts as inadequate sources of correction in the student's failure contexts, which is the gap SteerDistill is meant to fill. The reported results cover five agentic benchmarks and three models under W4A16, with the τ²-Bench comparison against QeRL and its 67% reduction in training GPU hours. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's posting on arXiv.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose using multimodal large language models to automate explainable AI evaluation
stories.Summary:
Eoin M. Kenny, Salim I. Amoukou, and Tom Bewley published a research paper on November 15, 2026, regarding the evaluation of Explainable AI. The authors investigated whether Multimodal Large Language Models could serve as surrogate human participants to automate the assessment of explanation techniques. This study addresses the ongoing struggle to find a reliable way to measure how useful AI explanations actually are for users. The researchers aimed to find a middle ground between unreliable proxy metrics and the high cost of human testing.

The proposed methodology introduces a purpose-grounded evaluation framework that applies the same metrics to both human users and artificial models. To test this approach, the team conducted extensive empirical trials across fourteen different Multimodal Large Language Models and five specific purpose-grounded areas, including model improvement. The results showed that while all tested models trended positively, the variants from OpenAI and Qwen demonstrated the highest levels of alignment. These specific models are therefore the recommended choices for practitioners who wish to automate the evaluation process.

The researchers explained that human evaluation is the gold standard but remains expensive, difficult to scale, and challenging to reproduce. They argued that current proxy metrics provide very little information about the actual utility of an explanation for a human user. The authors stated that their insights are not intended to replace traditional user testing entirely in the research process. Instead, they believe this method helps researchers complement their current work and reduces the heavy reliance on proxy metrics.

The study provides conceptual insights into why and when these large models can be trusted to automate the evaluation of explainable AI. By using these surrogates, the field can move toward more scalable and reproducible ways of measuring how AI explains its decisions. The authors expect that this framework will allow for more frequent and detailed testing of XAI techniques before they reach human subjects. This shift could potentially accelerate the development of AI systems that are more transparent and easier for people to understand.

stories.Headline: Pichai endorses Grok's Gemini 4 Hydrogen cost efficiency assessment
stories.Summary:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai endorsed an assessment of Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen model that was shared by xAI's Grok, according to a TechGig report published on November 14, 2026. The exchange began when an X user with the handle @itsvishaltwt posted a ranking of several AI models and argued that cost efficiency, rather than intelligence alone, would decide how widely AI models are adopted. Grok agreed with that assessment and said pricing and efficiency matter when AI models are deployed at scale. Grok described Gemini 4 Hydrogen as delivering performance close to leading models while offering lower costs and higher speeds, and it suggested that Gemini 4 Carbon remains the better option for demanding tasks where users are willing to spend more. Pichai replied to Grok's assessment on X with the brief comment, "Nice summary @grok!"

Pichai had earlier introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen as a model built to deliver AI capabilities for everyday tasks, coding, and agentic workflows. According to Pichai, Gemini 4 Hydrogen completes tasks up to 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash. The model also offers four thinking levels, which let users choose how much reasoning is applied to different tasks. Google said Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini app, and Search. Paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also reach it through Google's Antigravity platform.

Pichai is the Google CEO who responded positively to the assessment, and Grok is the xAI system that agreed with the user's argument about cost efficiency. Grok stated that pricing and efficiency are important factors when AI models are deployed at scale, and it placed Gemini 4 Hydrogen close to leading models at lower cost and higher speed. Pichai's public reply on X was limited to a short endorsement of Grok's summary. The report ties the exchange to growing competition among AI companies over performance, speed, and pricing.

The articles describe the episode as a sign that AI companies are increasingly competing on the balance between model capabilities, response speed, and operating costs, alongside improvements in reasoning and overall performance. The report gives no further details on the rollout timeline beyond saying the model is rolling out across the listed Google products and platforms. It also does not say how Gemini 4 Carbon compares in price or speed beyond Grok's remark that it suits demanding tasks for users willing to spend more. No next steps beyond the rollout and the public exchange are stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: Nvidia appoints Colette Kress as interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on November 12, 2026, with immediate effect. His sudden departure followed media reports concerning alleged personal relationships with a Singapore-based businesswoman named Alice Huang. US authorities suspect Alice Huang has connections to Chinese intelligence, though these suspicions are not established facts. Nvidia appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive to lead the company. The firm has also initiated a search to find a permanent replacement for the chief executive role.

The crisis brings attention to Nvidia business activities in China and the financial arrangements supporting AI infrastructure. Alice Huang is an executive associated with Megaspeed, which is a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly resisted efforts by other officials to strengthen enforcement against companies diverting processors to China. On November 11, Axios reported this resistance, and on November 12, Reuters reported White House officials discussed removing Lutnick. Lawmakers from both major US political parties have called for greater examination of Commerce Department export restrictions.

KC Rajkumar, an analyst at Lynx Equity Strategies, warned that uncertainty could affect earnings expectations across the sector. He suggested that investors are struggling to assess the consequences of the departure for the AI supply chain. Rajkumar stated that the limited reaction among other semiconductor stocks does not mean investors have fully assessed the consequences. He believes that current earnings expectations might not adequately reflect the possibility of reduced AI infrastructure investment. The analyst indicated he intends to remain cautious and is positioning for the possibility of further declines.

The situation affects semiconductor manufacturers and infrastructure providers who rely on financing arrangements between Nvidia and other industry participants. Rajkumar warned that a reduction in such financing could lower demand for Nvidia processors and other data centre equipment. If projects lose financial backing, companies might be required to revise their expected revenue and earnings. American chipmakers could also face reduced access to Chinese customers if US authorities introduce additional export limitations. These combined effects of weaker demand and tighter controls could be more significant than either development alone.

The background involves renewed scrutiny of US semiconductor export policies and how authorities monitor attempts to circumvent restrictions. Rajkumar previously maintained a positive outlook on AI-related semiconductor stocks before this leadership crisis occurred. He noted that valuations for several semiconductor stocks have become more attractive following these recent market developments. However, he questioned if lower share prices are sufficient to encourage investors to increase their exposure. The analyst is now concerned about the reliability of future earnings forecasts rather than valuations in isolation.

Analysts may revise semiconductor industry growth forecasts, particularly for the year 2027, as more information becomes available. Upcoming investor conferences are expected to provide more data on company spending plans and customer demand. A change in leadership at the Commerce Department or a reversal of policies could have further consequences. It remains open whether a widespread wave of project cancellations has actually occurred in the AI industry. The extent of the financial effects remains uncertain until further company disclosures and policy developments are released.

stories.Headline: Wuhan researchers develop machine learning models to identify small cell lung cancer in small lung nodules
stories.Summary:
Researchers from several institutions in Wuhan, China, conducted a multicenter study to identify small cell lung cancer in peripheral solid lung nodules. The team developed machine learning models to distinguish this specific cancer from non-small cell lung cancer before surgery. This research was published in the European Journal of Medical Research on November 15, 2026. The study aimed to provide a noninvasive alternative to biopsies for patients with nodules measuring 3 centimeters or less.

The process required analyzing 510 patients divided into a training set of 327, an internal test set of 141, and an external test set of 42. Experts extracted 1,223 radiomic features from pretreatment computed tomography images using specific algorithms to filter the data. They trained eight different classifiers, finding that a Logistic Regression-based model performed best on its own. This was then combined with clinical variables to create a hybrid model with an area under the curve of 0.983 in the external test set.

The authors, including Siqing Liao, Xinghui Cao, and Dan Lv, stated that the hybrid model distinguishes cancer subtypes with high accuracy. They noted that this tool could support individualized preoperative evaluation and treatment planning for patients. The researchers received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China and other regional health commissions. They explained that current guidelines for upfront surgery might be inappropriate for those with small cell lung cancer.

This new method maintains strong discrimination even for patients with negative lymph nodes or nodules smaller than 2 centimeters. By providing a noninvasive way to differentiate cancer types, the model helps doctors avoid unnecessary or incorrect surgical approaches. The study protocol was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and approved by an Institutional Review Board. Future applications may integrate these clinical-radiomics features into standard preoperative lung cancer screenings.
